docs.title: Scriberig
docs.text:
Scriberig is a structured knowledge and agent platform for working with code, documents, PDFs, sessions, project decisions, tool results, and other domains through one common model.

Its central idea is:

Store meaning as structured knowledge. Treat files, transcripts, user interfaces, and model context as projections of that knowledge.

Instead of making files or chat transcripts the primary source of truth, Scriberig models knowledge as typed entities, relations, immutable revisions, and snapshots. Supported files remain normal human-editable projections: changes made in external editors can be parsed and reconciled back into semantic changes.

The same foundation is intended to support ordinary applications as well as agents. Storage, querying, domain adapters, projections, CLI, API, TUI, reusable web libraries, and the full editor are designed as layers over shared capabilities. Agents are consumers of those capabilities rather than privileged owners of the system.

Key goals include:

  • structured, progressively disclosed access instead of requiring agents to read large raw files;
  • immutable revisions, snapshots, branches, semantic diffs, and explicit migrations;
  • local incremental updates and reusable derived results;
  • bidirectional projections for source files and documents;
  • one interaction model across code, documents, PDFs, sessions, and future domains;
  • reusable Rust and web libraries that remain useful without the agent runtime;
  • CLI, API, TUI, web, and agent surfaces that evolve together.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
crates/        Rust libraries and runtime crates
apps/          Native executable composition roots
web/packages/  Reusable TypeScript/React packages
web/apps/      Complete browser applications
tools/         Repository linting and developer automation
tests/         Cross-layer conformance and end-to-end tests
design/        Level 1-3 architecture and implementation documents

docs.title: Design documents
docs.text:
The project is currently being specified from architecture down to implementation tasks under design/:

  • design/level-1/ — durable architecture, principles, and system-level decisions;
  • design/level-2/ — concrete crate boundaries, schemas, protocols, algorithms, and package layouts;
  • design/level-3/ — focused implementation instructions and acceptance criteria for implementation agents.

The intended result is a system where humans, agents, compilers, editors, and third-party applications can work with different views of the same persistent semantic state without each inventing a separate storage or mutation model.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text:
rustup show
cargo check --workspace --all-targets
corepack enable
pnpm --dir web install
python3 -m pip install pre-commit
./tools/install-hooks.sh

docs.title: Quality checks
docs.text:
Run the complete local quality gate with:

./tools/check.sh

Apply safe automatic fixes and formatters with:

./tools/fix.sh

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
Build all Rust workspace targets with:

make build

Build and install the srig executable into Cargo's bin directory with:

make install

docs.title: Local app
docs.text:
Start or reuse the API and web application, create the ignored SQLite database under playground/dev-app-runtime/, and open the editor in your browser with:

make dev

Stop the processes started by that command with:

make dev-stop

The Make targets work on Linux and Windows. Repeating make dev reuses the running services; make dev-stop stops them. The current API exposes a health endpoint while semantic API operations remain under development. Logs and the local database stay in playground/dev-app-runtime/.

Repository-specific source and agent rules live in the top-level AGENTS.md and are refined by nested AGENTS.md files.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig is a general system for storing, understanding, editing, and navigating structured knowledge.

The system is designed for both humans and software agents. It must support source code, documents, sessions, PDFs, project decisions, tool results, and future domains without giving each domain a separate storage architecture.

The central idea is simple:

Store meaning as structured knowledge. Treat files, transcripts, user interfaces, and model context as projections of that knowledge.

Scriberig is therefore not primarily a file editor, a chat application, or an agent harness. Those are products and interfaces built on top of a shared knowledge system.

This document defines the vision and architectural principles that all lower-level designs and implementations must preserve.

docs.title: 2. The Core Premise
docs.text:
Scriberig has one universal typed knowledge store.

Different domains specialize that store with schemas and relations.

Examples:

  • a paragraph is an entity;
  • a Markdown section is an entity;
  • a source-code function is an entity;
  • an AST expression is an entity;
  • a PDF page is an entity;
  • a table row or cell is an entity;
  • an agent session is an entity;
  • a session branch is an entity;
  • a project decision is an entity;
  • a migration is an entity;
  • a style is an entity.

Relations connect these objects.

Examples:

  • contains;
  • calls;
  • references;
  • derived_from;
  • described_by;
  • supersedes;
  • produced_by;
  • belongs_to.

Domain-specific systems define which entity types and relations are useful, but they do not replace the universal storage model.

This allows the same fundamental operations to work across domains.

For example, an agent or application should be able to inspect, traverse, search, compare, describe, render, branch, and modify knowledge using one general interaction model whether the target is code, a document, a PDF, or a session.

docs.title: 3. Goals
docs.text: Scriberig should make the following possible.

docs.title: 3.1 Structured access instead of raw file access
docs.text:
An agent should normally work with semantic objects rather than unrestricted byte or text access.

For example, instead of reading a large Markdown file, an agent can first list its top-level sections, inspect a selected section, see how many paragraphs or tables it contains, and read only the required objects.

For code, an agent can inspect modules, functions, conceptual code groups, statements, and expressions progressively.

The system should make the cheapest representation useful enough for the agent to decide what to inspect next.

docs.title: 3.2 Human compatibility
docs.text:
Humans must remain free to use ordinary tools.

Users may edit source files, Markdown files, and other supported projections with external editors.

Scriberig must import those changes back into the semantic store instead of requiring all edits to happen through a custom editor.

The system must not trap a project inside a proprietary editing environment.

docs.title: 3.3 Stable history
docs.text:
Knowledge must have durable identity and history.

The system must support:

  • immutable revisions;
  • snapshots;
  • branches;
  • migrations;
  • semantic diffs;
  • concurrent work;
  • merges;
  • rollback and inspection of historical state.

docs.title: 3.4 Efficient incremental work
docs.text:
A local change should not force unrelated knowledge to be recomputed, rerendered, reanalyzed, or reread by an agent.

Unchanged semantic objects should remain reusable across snapshots.

Derived results should be reusable whenever their exact dependencies have not changed.

docs.title: 3.5 One platform, many consumers
docs.text:
The storage and knowledge libraries must be useful without any agent runtime.

A user may use Scriberig only as:

  • a versioned semantic database;
  • a structured document system;
  • a source-code analysis system;
  • a projection engine;
  • a query system;
  • an API server;
  • a reusable UI library.

The full agent product is one consumer of these capabilities, not the owner of them.

docs.title: 3.6 First-class reusable interfaces
docs.text:
CLI, server API, TUI, web libraries, the full web editor, and agent tools must evolve together.

User-level capabilities should be implemented vertically across the supported surfaces rather than existing only in one interface for long periods.

The full Scriberig editor should use the same public libraries and APIs made available to third parties.

docs.title: 4. Non-Goals
docs.text: The following are not foundational goals.

docs.title: 4.1 Replacing every external tool
docs.text: Scriberig does not need to replace existing compilers, language servers, PDF parsers, editors, formatters, or databases when they can be integrated effectively.

docs.title: 4.2 Treating every domain identically
docs.text:
The storage and interaction model is universal, but domain semantics are not.

A Rust function and a PDF table are different kinds of knowledge and may require different parsers, renderers, validators, and relations.

The goal is shared foundations, not forced uniformity.

docs.title: 4.3 Making raw storage representation the public API
docs.text:
Consumers should use stable semantic APIs rather than depend directly on database tables or backend-specific details.

The internal persistence implementation must be able to evolve without forcing all clients to change.

docs.title: 4.4 Eliminating textual representations
docs.text:
Text files remain important because they are portable, familiar, editable, reviewable, and compatible with existing tools.

The change is that they are treated as projections rather than the only canonical representation of meaning.

docs.title: 5. Fundamental Concepts
docs.text: Scriberig distinguishes three different questions.

docs.title: 5.1 What thing is this?
docs.text:
An entity identifies conceptual continuity.

A function, paragraph, session branch, or decision may continue to be the same conceptual entity while its content changes over time.

This is represented by an EntityId or an equivalent stable handle.

docs.title: 5.2 What exact state is this thing in?
docs.text:
A revision identifies an exact immutable state of an entity.

Revisions do not change in place.

A change creates another revision.

This is represented by a RevisionId or equivalent immutable identity.

docs.title: 5.3 What exact state is the whole knowledge universe in?
docs.text:
A snapshot identifies a complete consistent state of the knowledge store.

A snapshot determines which revision of each relevant entity is current for that snapshot.

Any canonical change creates a new snapshot identity.

This is represented by a SnapshotId or equivalent root identity.

These three concepts must not be conflated.

Stable entity identity provides local continuity. Immutable revision identity provides exactness. Snapshot identity provides global certainty.

docs.title: 6. Principle: Knowledge Is Structured
docs.text:
Canonical knowledge should be represented in forms that preserve meaningful structure.

Examples include:

  • sections and paragraphs instead of only Markdown bytes;
  • tables, rows, and cells instead of only text ranges;
  • functions, statements, and expressions instead of only source lines;
  • session branches, decisions, and tool results instead of only transcript strings.

The canonical representation should preserve the distinctions that matter to the domain.

The system should not aggressively normalize semantically or syntactically meaningful choices merely because two forms may currently behave similarly.

docs.title: 7. Principle: Revisions Are Immutable
docs.text:
Canonical revisions are never edited in place.

A change produces a new revision.

Historical revisions remain addressable while retained by history, branches, snapshots, or other roots.

Immutability enables:

  • reliable caching;
  • reproducible analysis;
  • branch isolation;
  • exact historical references;
  • safe concurrent work;
  • deterministic comparison;
  • structural sharing.

Implementations may optimize physical storage, but they must preserve the logical immutability of revisions.

docs.title: 8. Principle: Local Stability and Global Certainty
docs.text:
A change deep in the knowledge graph must not unnecessarily redefine the conceptual identity of every semantic ancestor.

For example, editing the text of a paragraph should not imply that the containing document is a new conceptual document. Editing an expression should not imply that the containing function is a new conceptual function.

Local entities retain stable identity while receiving new revisions.

At the same time, the top-level snapshot must change whenever canonical knowledge changes.

This is intentional.

A snapshot identity is a compact assertion about the entire visible state of knowledge.

Therefore:

  • local revisions are used for fine-grained caching and incremental work;
  • the global snapshot is used for consistency, reproducibility, synchronization, branching, and change detection.

The system should preserve both properties rather than choosing one at the expense of the other.

docs.title: 9. Principle: Projections Are Functions of Semantic State
docs.text:
Files, transcripts, UI views, and model context are projections of semantic state.

Conceptually:

projection = render(semantic_state, projection_configuration)

Examples:

Markdown graph + Markdown style -> .md
Code graph + source style -> source file
Session graph + chat style -> transcript
Session graph + context policy -> model context
Knowledge graph + UI state -> browser view

Formatting and presentation configuration should not become semantic content unless the domain explicitly requires them to be meaningful.

A style change should not normally change the semantic identity of the underlying knowledge.

docs.title: 10. Principle: Supported Projections Are Bidirectional
docs.text:
Where editing is supported, projections must work in both directions.

Rendering converts semantic state into an external representation.

Import and reconciliation convert an edited external representation into semantic changes.

Conceptually:

semantic state
    -> render
projection
    -> external edit
edited projection
    -> parse and reconcile
semantic migration
    -> new snapshot

External edits should not be blindly accepted as a replacement for canonical state.

They should be interpreted as proposed semantic changes relative to known previous state.

When both the semantic state and an external projection have changed independently, reconciliation should use a three-way model and surface conflicts instead of silently overwriting one side.

docs.title: 11. Principle: Changes Are Explicit
docs.text:
Canonical changes should be represented as explicit migrations or equivalent transitions between snapshots.

A migration records what changed and where the new state came from.

Possible sources include:

  • human edits;
  • agent edits;
  • API clients;
  • CLI commands;
  • web editing;
  • imports;
  • merges;
  • automated transformations.

All write paths should converge on the same change model.

The browser editor, CLI, TUI, external file watcher, agent runtime, and API server must not each invent separate mutation semantics.

docs.title: 12. Principle: Derived Knowledge Is Separate and Provenanced
docs.text:
Not every useful fact belongs in canonical state.

Examples of derived knowledge include:

  • compiler analysis;
  • symbol resolution;
  • call graphs;
  • control-flow and data-flow information;
  • PDF extraction indexes;
  • descriptions;
  • summaries;
  • model-generated interpretations;
  • rendered intermediate representations;
  • validation results.

Derived knowledge should record:

  • what it was derived from;
  • the exact revisions or configuration it depends on;
  • the producer or method used;
  • enough provenance to distinguish authoritative facts from generated interpretations.

Derived knowledge should be recomputable.

When its dependencies are unchanged, it should be reusable even if unrelated parts of the global snapshot changed.

docs.title: 13. Principle: Progressive Disclosure Is the Default Agent Interface
docs.text:
Agents should not be forced to reconstruct high-level structure from large raw inputs.

The system already knows structure and should expose it directly.

An agent should typically navigate from coarse information to fine detail.

Examples:

Project
  -> subsystem
    -> module
      -> function
        -> code group
          -> statement
            -> expression

Document
  -> section
    -> subsection
      -> paragraph/table/list
        -> row/cell/item

Session
  -> branch/topic
    -> episode
      -> turn
        -> message/tool result

Container objects should expose short descriptions, useful counts, relations, and stable handles before exposing full content.

Tool results should make useful next navigation actions obvious.

docs.title: 14. Principle: One Interaction Grammar Across Domains
docs.text:
The agent and external applications should learn one general way to interact with the knowledge store.

The universal interaction vocabulary should support concepts such as:

  • inspect;
  • list;
  • follow relations;
  • find;
  • query;
  • describe;
  • compare;
  • inspect history;
  • render;
  • branch;
  • propose a change;
  • validate;
  • commit or merge.

Domain-specific schemas may expose specialized relations and operations, but they should extend the common model rather than create unrelated access systems.

This makes it possible for a simple agent to navigate code, sessions, PDFs, documents, and future domains with the same basic tool discipline.

docs.title: 15. Principle: Sessions Are Knowledge
docs.text:
Agent sessions are stored in the same universal system as project artifacts.

A session is not fundamentally a flat transcript.

It may contain structured objects such as:

  • goals;
  • human inputs;
  • agent outputs;
  • observations;
  • decisions;
  • questions;
  • tool invocations;
  • tool results;
  • branches;
  • branch results;
  • summaries;
  • tasks;
  • references to project entities.

Session branches are first-class objects.

A branch should have a short description of its purpose and, when completed, its outcome.

Completed exploratory branches may be omitted from normal model context and represented by compact branch summaries while remaining fully retrievable.

This allows long-running work without requiring the permanent context to grow as a flat transcript.

docs.title: 16. Principle: Files and Line Numbers Are Not Primary Semantic Handles
docs.text:
Files remain important projections, but semantic identity should not normally depend on file location or line number.

A function moved to another file may still be the same conceptual function.

A paragraph shifted by inserted text may still be the same conceptual paragraph.

Agents and applications should prefer stable semantic handles.

File paths and line positions may be supplied as useful projection metadata, but they should not be the primary identity system when a semantic object exists.

docs.title: 17. Principle: Validation Precedes Promotion
docs.text:
Proposed changes should be validated before they become the promoted project state when the domain supports validation.

Validation may include:

  • structural checks;
  • parser checks;
  • schema checks;
  • compiler checks;
  • type checking;
  • linting;
  • tests;
  • application-specific invariants.

Agent work should normally occur on isolated branches or workspaces derived from a known snapshot.

Failed attempts must not corrupt the base snapshot.

Successful work can be compared, reviewed, validated, and merged explicitly.

docs.title: 18. Principle: Consumers Are Peers
docs.text:
The CLI, API server, TUI, browser editor, external applications, and agent runtime are peers over the same application capabilities.

No interface should contain unique core business logic that other interfaces cannot reuse.

The server is not the conceptual owner of the system. It is one adapter exposing application operations remotely.

The full web editor is not privileged. It should be implemented with the same public client, model, and UI libraries intended for third-party applications.

An agent is also not privileged. It is a consumer of the same semantic APIs available to ordinary programs, with permissions and capabilities determining what it may access.

docs.title: 19. Principle: Develop Capabilities Vertically
docs.text:
A user-facing capability should evolve across the supported surfaces together.

For example, when semantic diff becomes a product capability, the design should consider its presence in:

  • core application operations;
  • protocol types;
  • server API;
  • CLI;
  • TypeScript client;
  • reusable web libraries;
  • reference web application;
  • agent tools where appropriate.

Not every internal primitive requires every surface, but product-level capabilities should not accumulate exclusively in one interface.

This keeps the public libraries capable enough to build the full product and prevents the web application or agent runtime from depending on private shortcuts.

docs.title: 20. Principle: Reusable Platform Below Integrated Product
docs.text:
Scriberig should be useful in layers.

A consumer may stop at the immutable storage layer.

Another may use the universal graph and query model.

Another may add Markdown, code, PDF, or projection support.

Another may consume the API and reusable web libraries.

The integrated Scriberig product adds sessions, agents, UI, orchestration, and opinionated workflows on top.

Lower layers must not depend on higher product layers.

In particular:

The knowledge store must not know that agents exist.

Domain adapters must also remain useful without the agent runtime.

docs.title: 21. Principle: Domain Adapters Specialize, They Do Not Fork the Architecture
docs.text:
Each supported domain may provide:

  • schemas;
  • parsers;
  • renderers;
  • reconciliation logic;
  • validators;
  • derived indexes;
  • specialized queries;
  • semantic operations;
  • UI views.

But these should plug into the common storage, revision, snapshot, migration, query, and projection systems.

A new domain should not require a new persistence model or a completely separate agent access protocol.

docs.title: 22. Principle: Cache Exact Inputs, Not Incidental Containers
docs.text:
Caching should depend on the smallest immutable inputs that determine a result.

For example:

  • a rendered semantic fragment may depend on an object revision and style revision;
  • a function summary may depend on the function revision and summary profile;
  • a compiler analysis may depend on a function revision plus exact relevant dependency revisions and toolchain configuration;
  • a session branch summary may depend on the branch revision and summary profile.

The global snapshot should not be used as a cache key when only a local revision is relevant.

This prevents unrelated changes from invalidating useful work.

docs.title: 23. Principle: Provenance and Trust Are Visible
docs.text:
The system must distinguish between sources of information.

Examples include:

  • user-authored;
  • parser-derived;
  • compiler-derived;
  • static-analysis-derived;
  • system-generated;
  • model-generated.

An agent should be able to tell whether a statement is an authoritative structural fact or an interpretation generated by another model.

Important conclusions and project decisions should retain references to the sessions, branches, tools, or artifacts from which they were derived.

docs.title: 24. Principle: The System Is Inspectable at Multiple Levels
docs.text:
Users and developers should be able to inspect the same state at different abstraction levels.

The integrated editor should eventually support views such as:

  • raw entity and relation browsing;
  • revision and snapshot inspection;
  • migration history;
  • semantic document views;
  • source-code views;
  • projection views;
  • session and branch views;
  • agent commands scoped to selected semantic objects.

A selection in one view should resolve to the same semantic entity used by the other views.

This makes the system debuggable and allows low-level and high-level operations to coexist.

docs.title: 25. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Lower-level designs must preserve these invariants unless a later Level 1 decision explicitly replaces them.

  • Canonical knowledge is structured and typed.
  • Conceptual entity identity is distinct from exact revision identity.
  • Revisions are immutable.
  • A snapshot represents one exact consistent global state.
  • Canonical changes produce new snapshots.
  • Local semantic identity should remain stable across unrelated or presentation-only changes.
  • Files and transcripts are projections, not the universal storage primitive.
  • Supported editable projections can be reconciled back into semantic changes.
  • Formatting and style are separate from semantic content unless a domain explicitly makes them meaningful.
  • Changes from all write surfaces converge on a common migration/change model.
  • Derived knowledge records provenance and dependencies.
  • Derived results can be reused when their exact dependencies remain unchanged.
  • Agents use progressive semantic disclosure by default.
  • Sessions and their branches are stored as structured knowledge.
  • Domain adapters reuse the common storage and interaction architecture.
  • Storage and domain libraries remain useful without an agent runtime.
  • CLI, API, web, TUI, and agent surfaces consume shared application capabilities.
  • The reference web application uses public reusable libraries rather than private product-only mechanisms.
  • Validation can occur on isolated branches before a result is promoted.
  • Historical and concurrent states remain explicitly addressable.

docs.title: 26. Measures of Success
docs.text: The architecture is succeeding when the following statements are true.

docs.title: 26.1 A large project can be navigated without reading it all
docs.text: An agent can locate and inspect a small relevant semantic region without loading an entire repository, document, or session into context.

docs.title: 26.2 Formatting changes are cheap
docs.text: Changing a rendering style does not invalidate semantic identity or unrelated model understanding.

docs.title: 26.3 Local edits remain local
docs.text: Editing one paragraph, expression, or session branch preserves unrelated revisions and derived caches.

docs.title: 26.4 Global change is still detectable immediately
docs.text: A snapshot identity provides a compact way to determine whether canonical knowledge changed at all.

docs.title: 26.5 External tools remain usable
docs.text: Users can edit supported projections with ordinary editors and import those changes without abandoning semantic history.

docs.title: 26.6 Multiple consumers use the same platform
docs.text: The CLI, API, browser, TUI, agent runtime, and third-party applications use the same underlying operations and semantic references.

docs.title: 26.7 The integrated editor is reproducible by public APIs
docs.text: The official web application can be built from the same reusable packages available to other applications.

docs.title: 26.8 Agent history does not grow without structure
docs.text: Completed exploratory work can collapse to descriptions and results while remaining retrievable through session branches.

docs.title: 26.9 The storage layer remains independently valuable
docs.text: A consumer can use the knowledge store, revisions, snapshots, queries, and domain adapters without installing or running an agent.

docs.title: 27. Design Direction
docs.text:
The intended architecture can be summarized as:

                     Universal Knowledge Store
                              |
              entities + revisions + relations
                              |
                         snapshots
                              |
        +---------------------+----------------------+
        |                     |                      |
    domain models        derived knowledge       sessions
        |                     |                      |
        +---------------------+----------------------+
                              |
                    application operations
                              |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
          |                   |                   |
        CLI/API             Web/TUI             Agents
          |                   |                   |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
                              |
                       semantic changes
                              |
                          migrations
                              |
                         new snapshot

External projections such as files participate through render and reconciliation paths rather than bypassing this model.

The architecture should remain understandable from this diagram even as individual domain adapters and product surfaces become sophisticated.

docs.title: 28. Guidance for Lower-Level Design
docs.text:
Level 2 documents may choose concrete architectures, crate boundaries, schemas, algorithms, protocol types, and library APIs as long as they preserve the principles in this document.

Level 3 documents may define exact implementation tasks, acceptance tests, files to modify, and focused instructions for implementation agents.

When implementation pressure conflicts with a principle in this document, the conflict should be made explicit. A local implementation shortcut should not silently redefine a Level 1 architectural decision.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig uses one universal typed knowledge model for all supported domains.

The same underlying model must be able to represent source code, Markdown, PDFs, sessions, agent branches, decisions, tool results, styles, migrations, derived analysis, and future domains without introducing a separate persistence architecture for each one.

The purpose of this document is to define the domain-independent concepts that every specialization builds on.

The central rule is:

A domain adds meaning through schemas, types, relations, constraints, and projections. It does not replace the universal knowledge model.

This document intentionally stays above concrete Rust types, SQL tables, API endpoints, and parser implementations. Those belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Design Goals
docs.text: The universal model must support the following properties.

docs.title: 2.1 One substrate for different domains
docs.text: A paragraph, function, PDF page, session branch, decision, table cell, tool result, and style are different kinds of knowledge, but they should participate in the same storage, history, query, provenance, and navigation systems.

docs.title: 2.2 Strong domain meaning without forced uniformity
docs.text:
The model must be universal without pretending that all objects behave the same way.

A Rust expression is not interchangeable with a PDF table cell. A session branch does not have the same constraints as a Markdown section.

Domains specialize the shared substrate with their own schemas and operations.

docs.title: 2.3 Stable semantic access
docs.text: Applications and agents should work with semantic objects and relations rather than reconstruct meaning from filenames, line numbers, byte ranges, or transcript positions whenever a richer object exists.

docs.title: 2.4 Progressive disclosure
docs.text:
The model must support coarse-to-fine navigation.

A consumer should be able to inspect a project, document, module, function, branch, or page before deciding which children or relations to follow.

docs.title: 2.5 Exact history and reproducibility
docs.text: The model must work with immutable revisions and snapshots so that historical references identify exact states rather than whatever happens to be current when they are read.

docs.title: 2.6 Efficient derived knowledge
docs.text: Descriptions, summaries, compiler analysis, render intermediates, embeddings, validation results, and other derived data must be attachable to exact immutable inputs and reusable while those inputs remain unchanged.

docs.title: 2.7 Reusable outside the agent product
docs.text:
Nothing in the knowledge model may require an agent runtime.

The store, graph, schemas, queries, domains, and projections must remain useful to ordinary applications.

docs.title: 3. Model Overview
docs.text:
The universal model is a typed graph of semantic entities and relationships interpreted within a snapshot.

Figure 1. A snapshot resolves semantic entities to immutable revisions. The same substrate supports canonical structure, derived knowledge, universal interaction, and independently specialized domains.

Conceptually:

Snapshot
   |
   v
Entity -> Revision
   |
   +-- properties
   +-- relations --------> Entity
   +-- collections ------> Entity, Entity, Entity, ...
   +-- descriptions
   +-- provenance
   +-- derived knowledge

Different domains define different entity types and relation meanings.

Examples:

Document --contains--> Section
Section  --contains--> Paragraph
Table    --rows------> TableRow
TableRow --cells-----> TableCell

Module   --contains--> Function
Function --body------> CodeGroup
CodeGroup --contains-> Statement
Function --calls-----> Function

PDFDocument --pages--> PDFPage
PDFPage     --contains--> Paragraph
PDFPage     --contains--> Figure

Session --branches--> Branch
Branch  --contains--> Turn
Decision --derived_from--> Branch

Migration --base_snapshot--> Snapshot
Migration --result_snapshot--> Snapshot

The graph is not required to be a tree.

Containment may be tree-like in some domains, but references, provenance, dependencies, calls, lineage, and other relationships naturally form a graph and may contain cycles.

docs.title: 4. Entities
docs.text:
An entity identifies a conceptual thing that may persist through change.

Examples include:

  • a project;
  • a document;
  • a paragraph;
  • a table;
  • a row;
  • a cell;
  • a module;
  • a function;
  • a code group;
  • a statement;
  • a PDF page;
  • a session;
  • a session branch;
  • a decision;
  • a migration;
  • a rendering style.

An entity answers the question:

What thing is this?

An entity does not by itself imply one exact historical state.

Its exact state is determined by its revision in a given snapshot.

This distinction is important because conceptual continuity and exact content are different concerns.

For example, the same conceptual function may be edited many times. The function entity remains the stable semantic handle while each exact state is represented by a separate immutable revision.

docs.title: 5. Revisions
docs.text:
A revision is one exact immutable state of an entity.

Revisions answer the question:

What was this thing exactly at this point in history?

A revision may contain:

  • typed properties;
  • references to other entities;
  • collection membership;
  • domain-specific structural data;
  • metadata that is considered canonical for that domain.

A revision never changes in place.

A semantic edit creates another revision.

The relationship between entity identity and revision identity allows consumers to choose the correct level of reference.

Use an entity reference when continuity matters:

Function process_payment

Use an exact revision reference when reproducibility matters:

Function process_payment at revision R17

The detailed identity and storage rules for entities, revisions, and snapshots are defined separately in the identity and snapshot design.

docs.title: 6. Snapshots
docs.text:
A snapshot represents one complete consistent view of canonical knowledge.

Conceptually, a snapshot resolves entities to exact revisions:

Snapshot S42

Document D  -> Revision DR8
Paragraph P -> Revision PR3
Function F  -> Revision FR19
Branch B    -> Revision BR5
Decision X  -> Revision XR2

Figure 2. Entity identity expresses conceptual continuity. Revision identity expresses one exact immutable state. Snapshot identity fixes the exact revisions visible in one consistent knowledge world.

The knowledge graph must always be interpreted relative to an explicit or implicit snapshot.

This avoids ambiguity such as asking for "the children of this function" without defining which historical state of the project is being observed.

Consumers may commonly work against a current snapshot, but the underlying model must make historical snapshot selection possible.

docs.title: 7. Entity Types
docs.text:
Every entity has a type defined by a schema.

Examples:

Document
Section
Paragraph
Table
TableRow
TableCell

Module
Function
Parameter
Statement
Expression
Comment

PDFDocument
PDFPage
Figure

Session
Branch
Turn
Decision
ToolInvocation
ToolResult

Types provide semantic meaning and determine which properties, relations, operations, validations, and projections are available.

The universal store should not contain hard-coded knowledge of every domain type.

Instead, domains register or provide schemas understood by higher layers.

The model therefore separates:

universal graph machinery

from:

domain vocabulary

docs.title: 8. Properties
docs.text:
Properties represent typed values that belong directly to a revision.

Examples:

Paragraph.text
Function.name
Comment.kind
Branch.status
Style.max_width
PDFPage.number
Decision.state

Properties are appropriate for values whose meaning belongs locally to the entity revision.

Properties should not be used to encode relationships that need independent identity, traversal, history, provenance, or reuse.

For example, this is conceptually weaker:

Function {
    called_function_names: ["foo", "bar"]
}

than an explicit relation:

Function --calls--> Function foo
Function --calls--> Function bar

when the called functions are themselves known entities.

The schema defines which properties are required, optional, scalar, structured, ordered, or constrained.

docs.title: 9. Relations
docs.text:
Relations connect entities.

A relation has a type and a semantic direction.

Examples:

contains
calls
references
derived_from
supersedes
implements
produced_by
validated_by
rendered_from
belongs_to

Relations are first-class parts of the knowledge model rather than conventions hidden inside text fields.

This enables universal operations such as:

follow(entity, relation)
parents(entity)
related(entity)
find paths
query by relation
inspect provenance

Domains define what a relation means and which source and target types are valid.

A relation may be canonical or derived.

For example:

Section --contains--> Paragraph

may be canonical document structure, while:

Function --calls--> Function

may be derived from compiler or static-analysis output.

The graph layer must preserve that distinction.

docs.title: 10. Direction and Reverse Navigation
docs.text:
Canonical relationships should have a clear ownership direction.

For containment, the preferred direction normally points from container to contained entity:

Section --contains--> Paragraph

The paragraph does not need to store the section as part of its own canonical identity merely so that reverse navigation is possible.

Reverse navigation can be provided by indexes:

parents(Paragraph) -> Section

This prevents unnecessary revision churn when an entity is moved between containers.

The same principle applies to many relations.

A relation should be stored in the direction that best represents canonical ownership or semantic responsibility. Reverse traversal should normally be derived.

docs.title: 11. Collections
docs.text:
Many semantic structures contain ordered or unordered groups of entities.

Examples:

  • paragraphs inside a section;
  • rows inside a table;
  • cells inside a row;
  • parameters of a function;
  • statements inside a block;
  • pages in a PDF document;
  • turns inside a session branch.

Collections must be represented explicitly enough to preserve the semantics that matter.

An ordered collection must preserve order.

An unordered collection must not gain accidental semantic meaning from physical storage order.

The model should distinguish:

contains these entities

from:

contains these entities in this sequence

The detailed physical representation of collections belongs to lower-level design.

At the knowledge-model level, the important invariant is that collection semantics are explicit.

docs.title: 12. Containment Is Not the Whole Graph
docs.text:
Containment provides useful hierarchical navigation, but Scriberig must not reduce all knowledge to one ownership tree.

Consider a function:

Module
  -> contains Function
       -> contains CodeGroup
            -> contains Statement

The same function may also participate in:

Function --calls--> Function
Function --references--> Type
Function --described_by--> Description
Function --changed_by--> Migration
Function --mentioned_in--> SessionBranch

Likewise, a paragraph may belong to a document hierarchy while also being referenced by a decision, summary, annotation, session, or external projection.

The universal model is therefore a graph with hierarchical views, not a single universal tree.

docs.title: 13. Schemas
docs.text:
Schemas define how a domain specializes the universal model.

A schema may define:

  • entity types;
  • property definitions;
  • relation types;
  • valid relation endpoints;
  • collection semantics;
  • required and optional structure;
  • validation rules;
  • canonical versus derived fields;
  • description strategies;
  • supported projections;
  • supported semantic operations;
  • schema version.

For example, a Markdown schema may say that a Section can contain ordered block entities and may have a heading.

A Rust schema may define functions, parameters, statements, expressions, comments, attributes, and syntax-specific relationships.

A session schema may define branches, turns, goals, decisions, tool invocations, and tool results.

Schemas should be evolvable without changing the universal storage architecture.

docs.title: 14. Domain Adapters
docs.text:
A domain adapter translates between external domain representations and the universal knowledge model.

A domain adapter may provide:

  • parsing;
  • schema definitions;
  • canonicalization;
  • rendering;
  • reconciliation;
  • validation;
  • semantic operations;
  • derived analysis;
  • domain-specific queries;
  • domain-specific UI views.

Examples:

Markdown adapter
Rust adapter
PDF adapter
Session adapter

The adapter is responsible for preserving the distinctions that matter to its domain.

The universal store should not need to understand Markdown headings, Rust macro syntax, or PDF layout rules directly.

docs.title: 15. Canonical Knowledge
docs.text:
Canonical knowledge is the state that participates in snapshots and semantic history.

A domain must define what it considers canonical.

For Markdown, canonical knowledge may include:

  • sections;
  • paragraphs;
  • lists;
  • tables;
  • links;
  • code blocks;
  • meaningful inline structure.

For source code, canonical knowledge may include:

  • chosen syntax;
  • functions;
  • statements;
  • expressions;
  • comments;
  • macro invocations;
  • attributes;
  • human-oriented code-group structure where that structure is intentionally preserved.

Canonical knowledge should preserve choices that matter to the author or domain.

The model must not automatically collapse two representations merely because some compiler or renderer currently considers them equivalent.

docs.title: 16. Derived Knowledge
docs.text:
Derived knowledge is computed from canonical knowledge or external evidence.

Examples include:

  • symbol resolution;
  • type information;
  • call graphs;
  • control-flow graphs;
  • data-flow graphs;
  • compiler diagnostics;
  • PDF text extraction indexes;
  • embeddings;
  • summaries;
  • descriptions;
  • model-generated explanations;
  • validation results;
  • render intermediate representations.

Derived knowledge must identify its dependencies and provenance.

Conceptually:

DerivedObject
  source: Function F at Revision R17
  producer: rust-analyzer configuration C
  profile: call-graph-v2
  result: ...

Derived knowledge is not automatically authoritative merely because it is stored in the same database.

Consumers must be able to distinguish canonical state from parser facts, compiler facts, user-authored annotations, and model-generated interpretations.

Figure 3. Derived artifacts remain separate from canonical semantic state. They point to exact immutable inputs and record their producer and configuration through provenance.

docs.title: 17. Provenance
docs.text:
Knowledge should carry enough provenance to answer:

  • where did this come from?
  • who or what produced it?
  • which exact revisions were used?
  • which tool, parser, compiler, model, or configuration produced it?
  • is it canonical, imported, inferred, generated, or validated?

Possible provenance sources include:

user
authoritative_import
parser
compiler
static_analysis
agent
model_summary
system
external_tool
migration

Provenance is especially important because one universal store may contain both hard facts and uncertain interpretation.

For example:

Function F calls Function G
source: compiler_analysis

and:

Function F purpose:
"Retries failed payment requests"
source: model_generated

must remain distinguishable.

docs.title: 18. Descriptions
docs.text:
Important entities should be able to expose short descriptions for navigation.

Examples:

Function
"Validates an order and persists a payment."

Paragraph
"Explains why snapshots change globally."

PDFPage
"Contains the report's methodology and first results table."

Branch
"Investigates render-cache invalidation."

Descriptions are primarily attention and navigation aids.

They let humans and agents choose what to inspect without loading full content.

Descriptions may be:

  • user-authored;
  • parser-derived;
  • compiler-derived;
  • statically inferred;
  • model-generated.

Their provenance must be visible.

Generated descriptions should normally be derived knowledge rather than part of the canonical semantic identity of the described entity.

docs.title: 19. Summaries and Multiple Levels of Detail
docs.text:
The same entity may have several useful representations at different information costs.

For example, a function may expose:

identity and one-line description
structural overview
code-group overview
statement-level structure
full syntax
rendered source

A session branch may expose:

title
purpose
outcome
important decisions
turn list
full transcript

A document section may expose:

title
short description
child counts
subsections
paragraph summaries
full block content

The universal model should allow these derived representations to coexist and be selected intentionally.

This is the basis for progressive disclosure.

docs.title: 20. Semantic Handles
docs.text:
Every important object returned through APIs should have a stable semantic handle.

A consumer should be able to receive:

Function F
CodeGroup G
Paragraph P
Branch B
TableRow R

and use those handles in later operations.

Handles should be preferred over incidental coordinates such as:

src/foo.rs:183
page 17 character 421
transcript turn 291 byte 88

Projection coordinates remain useful metadata for humans and integrations, but they should not replace semantic identity when a semantic object exists.

docs.title: 21. Files Are Not a Special Knowledge Primitive
docs.text:
A file may be:

  • an external projection of semantic knowledge;
  • an imported source artifact;
  • a binary blob;
  • a container selected by a domain's layout rules.

The universal knowledge model should not assume that a file is the fundamental unit of meaning.

For example, a function may remain the same conceptual entity when moved from one source file to another.

A document may have Markdown, HTML, plain-text, and web-editor projections without becoming four independent semantic documents.

File paths are therefore domain or projection metadata rather than universal semantic identity.

docs.title: 22. Sessions Use the Same Model
docs.text:
Sessions are not a separate persistence system.

A session domain specializes the same knowledge model used by documents and code.

Typical entities include:

Session
Branch
Goal
HumanInput
AgentOutput
Observation
Decision
Question
ToolInvocation
ToolResult
BranchResult
Summary
Task

Typical relations include:

Session --contains--> Branch
Branch --contains--> Turn
Decision --derived_from--> Branch
Branch --touches--> Function
ToolResult --produced_by--> ToolInvocation

A session may directly reference project entities without copying their content into a transcript.

This gives agent history exact semantic references and lets branches remain compactly summarized while still fully retrievable.

docs.title: 23. Project Knowledge Uses the Same Model
docs.text:
Facts, decisions, hypotheses, tasks, and open questions may also be represented as entities.

For example:

Decision D19
  text: "Canonical syntax revisions are immutable."
  status: accepted

D19 --derived_from--> Branch B81
D19 --affects--> StorageArchitecture
D19 --supersedes--> Decision D11

This allows durable knowledge to be promoted from sessions without relying on transcript search as the primary memory mechanism.

A current decision and the historical discussion that produced it remain connected but distinct.

docs.title: 24. Styles Are Knowledge Objects
docs.text:
Styles and projection configurations may also be represented in the universal store.

Examples:

RustStyle
MarkdownStyle
ChatStyle
AgentContextPolicy
UIProjectionConfiguration

A style can have stable semantic identity and immutable revisions like other entities.

The semantic content being rendered does not normally change when only its style changes.

This allows multiple projections of the same knowledge for different users or applications without duplicating the underlying semantic objects.

docs.title: 25. Migrations Relate States, Not Just Text
docs.text:
A migration is structured knowledge about change.

It connects a base snapshot to a resulting snapshot and may describe the semantic operations involved.

Examples:

replace paragraph revision
insert entity into collection
remove relation
move collection member
rename symbol
change expression
merge branches

Migrations may reference the entities they affect and the session, user, agent, command, or external edit that produced them.

This allows history itself to participate in the knowledge graph.

docs.title: 26. Universal Queries
docs.text:
Because domains share one graph model, a common query vocabulary can work across them.

Examples:

inspect(entity)
children(entity)
relations(entity)
follow(entity, relation)
find(scope, query)
history(entity)
diff(a, b)
describe(entity)

Domain-specific queries may add stronger semantics:

find_callers(function)
find_references(symbol)
list_paragraphs(section)
list_rows(table)
list_branches(session)

These specialized queries should build on the same universal identity, snapshot, relation, and provenance model.

docs.title: 27. Universal Operations and Domain Operations
docs.text:
The same distinction applies to editing.

Universal operations may describe graph-level changes such as:

create entity
set entity revision
add relation
remove relation
insert collection member
remove collection member
reorder collection

Domain operations may express stronger intent:

rename heading
replace paragraph
insert table row
rename symbol
extract function
complete branch
supersede decision

Higher-level operations are preferable when they capture useful domain meaning and can be validated more strongly.

All operations ultimately produce explicit semantic changes and a new snapshot rather than bypassing the common change model.

docs.title: 28. Universality Does Not Mean a Single Giant Schema
docs.text:
The universal knowledge model must not become one enormous schema containing every possible field for every possible domain.

Instead:

Universal Model
  |
  +-- common identity and history
  +-- common graph concepts
  +-- common provenance
  +-- common query/navigation model
  |
  +-- Markdown schema
  +-- Rust schema
  +-- PDF schema
  +-- Session schema
  +-- future schemas

Figure 4. The universal layer stays small. Domain schemas preserve strong semantics while reusing the same identity, graph, provenance, history, and interaction concepts.

Domains should be independently evolvable where possible.

The universal layer should contain only concepts that genuinely need to be shared.

docs.title: 29. Universality Does Not Mean Lowest-Common-Denominator Semantics
docs.text:
A danger in universal data models is reducing every object to generic key-value pairs and generic edges until domain meaning is lost.

Scriberig should avoid this.

A Function, Paragraph, Branch, and TableRow should remain strongly typed domain concepts.

The universal substrate provides common machinery, while schemas preserve domain semantics.

The goal is:

One interaction grammar, not one undifferentiated data type.

docs.title: 30. Canonical Graph and Derived Indexes
docs.text:
The canonical graph should remain conceptually separate from indexes built to make navigation efficient.

Useful derived indexes may include:

entity -> parents
entity -> reverse relations
symbol -> references
function -> callers
type -> implementations
entity -> descriptions
entity -> migrations
entity -> sessions mentioning it
file path -> projection
branch -> touched entities

Indexes are allowed to be backend-specific and optimized aggressively.

They must remain rebuildable from canonical knowledge and declared derived sources.

Applications should not confuse index representation with semantic truth.

docs.title: 31. Knowledge Scope
docs.text:
Not every object in the database must belong to one project tree.

The store may contain multiple scopes such as:

  • projects;
  • imported documents;
  • sessions;
  • shared styles;
  • reusable schemas;
  • cached derived objects;
  • external references.

Snapshots or roots define which knowledge belongs to a particular consistent view.

This is another reason the universal model should be treated as a graph rather than a filesystem-shaped hierarchy.

docs.title: 32. Cross-Domain Relations
docs.text:
A major benefit of one store is that relations may cross domain boundaries.

Examples:

SessionBranch --touches--> Function
Decision --affects--> Module
Paragraph --describes--> ArchitectureConcept
PDFTable --supports--> Decision
Migration --produced_by--> AgentBranch
ToolResult --references--> SourceFunction

Figure 5. Session, code, document, PDF, migration, and project-knowledge entities can reference one another directly through typed relations while retaining independent identity and history.

These cross-domain relationships should not require copying objects between separate databases.

They are ordinary typed relations in the same knowledge system.

This is one of the strongest reasons to begin from a universal model rather than integrate several isolated domain stores later.

docs.title: 33. External References
docs.text:
Not all referenced knowledge must be owned by the local store.

The model should allow references to external resources where necessary, such as:

  • URLs;
  • Git commits;
  • package identities;
  • external database records;
  • remote documents;
  • tool-specific identifiers.

External references should be explicit and typed.

Where an external object is imported into canonical knowledge, the imported entity should retain provenance linking it back to its source.

docs.title: 34. Validation
docs.text:
Schemas and domain adapters define validity constraints.

The universal model itself can enforce only generic graph invariants.

Domain validation may include:

  • required properties;
  • allowed relation endpoints;
  • collection cardinality;
  • structural constraints;
  • parser validity;
  • compiler validity;
  • application-specific invariants.

A proposed revision may exist temporarily in a branch or workspace while invalid, depending on product policy, but promotion to a canonical project state may require validation.

The knowledge model must make validation status explicit rather than assuming all stored objects are valid by definition.

docs.title: 35. Agent-Oriented Consequences
docs.text:
The universal knowledge model is especially useful for agents because it provides one consistent navigation discipline.

An agent can learn operations such as:

inspect
list
follow
find
describe
diff
history
branch
propose change
validate

and apply them to different domains.

The entity being inspected advertises its type, available relations, child counts, descriptions, and domain capabilities.

The agent does not need a completely unrelated tool philosophy for code, PDFs, sessions, and documents.

This reduces tool complexity while preserving specialized domain meaning.

docs.title: 36. Human-Oriented Consequences
docs.text:
The same universal model benefits human-facing applications.

A full editor may select one entity and show several synchronized views:

semantic structure
raw database representation
rendered projection
history
relations
migration activity
agent context

A selection of a function, paragraph, branch, or table row can be represented by the same semantic handle even though each domain has a different visual editor.

This enables integrated tools without requiring them to invent separate identity and history systems.

docs.title: 37. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Lower-level designs must preserve the following rules.

  1. All domains use the same fundamental entity, revision, snapshot, relation, provenance, and query concepts.

  2. Domain schemas add meaning without replacing the universal storage model.

  3. Entity identity represents conceptual continuity; revision identity represents exact immutable state.

  4. Knowledge is interpreted within a snapshot.

  5. Relations are first-class and typed.

  6. Containment is one relation pattern, not the entire knowledge model.

  7. Reverse navigation must not require embedding mutable parent identity into children.

  8. Canonical and derived knowledge remain distinguishable.

  9. Derived knowledge records exact dependencies and provenance.

  10. Descriptions and summaries support progressive disclosure but do not silently become canonical truth.

  11. Files, line numbers, transcript positions, and other projection coordinates are not primary semantic identity when a semantic entity exists.

  12. Sessions use the same knowledge model as project artifacts.

  13. Cross-domain relationships are ordinary graph relationships.

  14. Schemas preserve strong domain semantics rather than reducing everything to untyped key-value data.

  15. Indexes and caches are rebuildable representations, not canonical truth.

  16. The universal model remains useful without an agent runtime.

docs.title: 38. What This Document Does Not Decide
docs.text:
This document deliberately does not specify:

  • the physical database backend;
  • the exact Rust crate layout;
  • SQL tables;
  • binary encodings;
  • the exact content-addressing algorithm;
  • the snapshot-map implementation;
  • API transport formats;
  • parser libraries;
  • renderer implementations;
  • concrete agent tool names;
  • UI component structure.

Those decisions belong in lower-level design documents.

The purpose here is to define the semantic contract those implementations must satisfy.

docs.title: 39. Summary
docs.text:
Scriberig begins with one universal typed knowledge graph.

The graph contains stable semantic entities whose exact states are represented by immutable revisions and interpreted within snapshots.

Entities have typed properties, relations, and collections. Schemas specialize those primitives into meaningful domains such as Markdown, source code, PDFs, sessions, and project knowledge.

Canonical knowledge is separated from derived analysis and interpretation. Provenance identifies where knowledge came from and how reliable or authoritative it is. Descriptions and summaries provide cheap navigation while exact semantic handles allow precise follow-up operations.

The universal model is deliberately richer than a generic key-value database and deliberately more general than any one AST, document tree, transcript format, or filesystem layout.

Its purpose is to provide one durable semantic substrate on which specialized domains, projections, applications, and agents can all operate.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig must preserve two properties that are easy to confuse:

  • local semantic objects need stable identity across ordinary change;
  • the system also needs an exact immutable identity for every historical state.

A paragraph should still be the same conceptual paragraph after its text is edited. A function should still be the same conceptual function after an expression changes. A session branch should remain the same branch while work is appended to it.

At the same time, an exact historical reference must never silently resolve to newer content, and the system must be able to identify whether anything in canonical knowledge changed between two points in time.

Scriberig therefore distinguishes three identities:

EntityId
RevisionId
SnapshotId

They answer different questions:

EntityId   -> What thing is this?
RevisionId -> What exact state is this thing in?
SnapshotId -> What exact state is the whole knowledge universe in?

These identities must remain distinct throughout storage, query, projection, caching, sessions, agents, and external APIs.

This document defines their meaning and the architectural rules that follow from them. Concrete hash algorithms, Rust types, database layouts, and persistent-map implementations belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Core Rule
docs.text:
The central rule is:

Stable semantic identity is local. Exact immutable state is revisioned. Global certainty is provided by snapshots.

A change to one object should not unnecessarily redefine every semantic object that contains or refers to it.

However, every canonical change must produce a new global snapshot identity.

Scriberig deliberately keeps both properties:

local stability
+
global certainty

This is not a compromise between two models. It is a separation of concerns.

The next figure is the anchor for the whole document. The key thing to notice is that each identifier exists for a different job: entity identity preserves continuity, revision identity preserves exact local state, and snapshot identity preserves exact global state. The rest of the document keeps these concerns separate.

Figure 1. The three identity layers: conceptual continuity, exact local state, and exact global state.

docs.title: 3. Entity Identity
docs.text:
An entity represents conceptual continuity.

Examples include:

  • a document;
  • a section;
  • a paragraph;
  • a table row;
  • a source-code module;
  • a function;
  • a statement;
  • a session;
  • a branch;
  • a decision;
  • a style;
  • a PDF page.

An EntityId answers:

Which conceptual thing are we talking about?

For example:

Function F

may have many historical states:

Function F
├── revision R1
├── revision R2
└── revision R3

The entity remains the stable handle when continuity matters.

Changing the body of the function does not automatically create a new conceptual function.

The same principle applies to documents and sessions.

Editing the text of a paragraph should normally create a new revision of the same paragraph entity. Adding work to a session branch should normally create a new revision of the same branch entity.

docs.title: 4. Entity Identity Is Not Content Identity
docs.text:
An entity must not be identified solely by a hash of its current content.

If entity identity were equal to content identity, every edit would destroy continuity.

For example:

Paragraph:
"Sessions form a tree."

changed to:

Paragraph:
"Sessions form a persistent tree."

would appear to be an unrelated paragraph rather than a new state of the same conceptual paragraph.

Scriberig needs to represent both facts:

same conceptual paragraph

and:

different exact content

Therefore entity identity and revision identity are separate.

docs.title: 5. Revision Identity
docs.text:
A revision represents one exact immutable state of an entity.

A RevisionId answers:

What was this entity exactly in this state?

For example:

Entity P

Revision PR1:
  text = "Sessions form a tree."

Revision PR2:
  text = "Sessions form a persistent tree."

PR1 and PR2 are different immutable states of the same entity P.

A revision never changes in place.

If canonical state changes, another revision is created.

Historical revisions remain exact while retained by snapshots, branches, history, references, or other roots.

docs.title: 6. Revisions Should Be Content-Addressable
docs.text:
Revision identity should normally be derived from the canonical content that defines the revision.

Conceptually:

RevisionId = hash(canonical revision representation)

The exact hashing and canonical serialization rules are implementation details, but the architectural property is important:

The same exact canonical revision should have the same immutable identity.

This enables:

  • deduplication;
  • deterministic comparison;
  • safe cache reuse;
  • structural sharing;
  • exact dependency tracking;
  • reproducible derived analysis.

Content addressing applies naturally to immutable revision state.

It does not replace stable entity identity.

docs.title: 7. What Belongs in a Revision
docs.text:
A revision contains the canonical state of one entity for its domain.

Depending on the entity type, this may include:

  • scalar properties;
  • ordered or unordered relationships;
  • collection membership;
  • domain-specific structural state;
  • canonical comments or annotations;
  • references to other semantic entities;
  • canonical configuration that is meaningfully part of the entity.

A revision should contain only information that is required to define that entity's canonical state.

Derived indexes, caches, summaries, compiler analysis, render results, and incidental physical storage details should not be included merely because they are convenient to compute alongside the entity.

docs.title: 8. Parentage and Position Are Not Intrinsic Child Identity
docs.text:
A child entity should not normally include its parent or its position inside the parent as intrinsic identity.

For example, this is undesirable as a universal rule:

Paragraph P
parent = Section S
position = 4
text = "..."

If another paragraph is inserted before P, the paragraph itself has not changed.

If P is moved to another section, its text may still represent the same conceptual paragraph.

Containment and order should therefore normally be represented by the container, collection, or relation that owns those facts.

Conceptually:

Section S
children = [P1, P2, P3]

rather than:

P1.position = 1
P2.position = 2
P3.position = 3

This allows moves and insertions to affect the structure that actually changed without manufacturing new revisions for otherwise unchanged children.

docs.title: 9. Content Change and Structural Change Are Different
docs.text: Scriberig should distinguish between changing the content of an entity and changing how entities are structurally related.

docs.title: 9.1 Content change
docs.text:
Suppose a section contains paragraph P.

The paragraph changes from:

P@R1
"Objects are immutable."

to:

P@R2
"Objects are immutable and content addressed."

The section may still contain the same conceptual entity P.

Only the current revision of P changed.

docs.title: 9.2 Structural change
docs.text:
Suppose a section contains:

[P1, P2]

and a new paragraph is inserted:

[P1, P3, P2]

Now the section's membership or ordering changed.

The structure that owns that collection must receive a new revision.

P1 and P2 need not change.

This distinction substantially reduces unnecessary revision churn and gives semantic meaning to changes.

The important contrast in the next figure is that content change preserves the same conceptual entity while structural change creates new relationship or collection state around mostly unchanged children. That is the pattern that prevents unnecessary ancestor churn.

Figure 2. Content change updates an entity revision; structural change updates the relationship or collection that owns ordering or membership.

docs.title: 10. Semantic Containment Must Not Be the Storage Merkle Tree
docs.text:
Scriberig knowledge forms a semantic graph.

For example:

Project
  contains Module
    contains Function
      contains Statement
        contains Expression

It would be possible to define every parent revision as a recursive hash of all descendant revision IDs.

Then editing one expression would force a chain such as:

Expression E1 -> E2
Statement  S1 -> S2
Function   F1 -> F2
Module     M1 -> M2
Project    P1 -> P2

Persistent data structures make such path copying technically manageable, but this should not be the universal semantic identity rule.

The problem is conceptual rather than merely computational.

Changing an expression does not necessarily mean the function is a different conceptual function. Changing a paragraph does not mean the document is a different conceptual document.

Therefore:

Semantic containment and storage snapshot structure are separate concerns.

The semantic graph expresses meaning.

The snapshot structure provides exact global state.

They must not be forced to be the same tree.

docs.title: 11. Snapshot Identity
docs.text:
A snapshot represents one exact consistent state of canonical knowledge.

A SnapshotId answers:

What exact state is the whole visible knowledge universe in?

Conceptually, a snapshot resolves stable entities to immutable revisions:

Snapshot S42

Document D   -> Revision DR8
Paragraph P  -> Revision PR3
Function F   -> Revision FR19
Branch B     -> Revision BR5
Decision X   -> Revision XR2

A snapshot is therefore not just another semantic parent object.

It is a consistent global resolution context.

The knowledge graph is interpreted relative to a snapshot because an entity by itself identifies continuity, not one exact historical state.

docs.title: 12. Snapshot as Persistent Revision Map
docs.text:
The conceptual snapshot model is a persistent mapping:

EntityId -> RevisionId

A new canonical change produces another mapping that differs only where required.

For example:

Snapshot S1

F  -> FR7
P1 -> PR3
P2 -> PR8
B  -> BR2

After editing only P2:

Snapshot S2

F  -> FR7
P1 -> PR3
P2 -> PR9
B  -> BR2

Only one entity resolution changed.

The physical implementation should use persistent structural sharing so that creating S2 does not require copying the entire map.

The exact data structure is a lower-level concern.

Architecturally, snapshots must behave as immutable persistent maps with efficient sharing between related states.

The next figure should be read as a resolution table, not as a semantic parent-child tree. The key point is that a snapshot is a world-state map: most bindings are unchanged and structurally shared, while only the bindings whose exact local state changed need new targets.

Figure 3. A snapshot is a persistent map from stable entity identities to exact immutable revisions.

docs.title: 13. Global Snapshot Change Is Intentional
docs.text:
Every canonical change must produce a different snapshot identity.

This is a strength.

A snapshot ID becomes a compact fingerprint for the complete visible canonical state.

If:

Snapshot A == Snapshot B

then the system can treat canonical knowledge as exactly the same state.

If:

Snapshot A != Snapshot B

then something changed.

A consumer can then ask for the semantic difference between the snapshots rather than assuming every object changed.

This provides a cheap answer to a global question without sacrificing local stability.

docs.title: 14. Snapshot Identity Should Be Content-Derived
docs.text:
A snapshot should have an immutable identity derived from its exact mapping and any canonical metadata required to interpret that mapping.

Conceptually:

SnapshotId = hash(snapshot state)

The physical structure may use a persistent Merkle map, trie, tree, or equivalent mechanism.

The architectural requirements are:

  • the same exact snapshot state has the same exact identity;
  • changing any canonical entity resolution changes the snapshot identity;
  • unchanged portions are structurally shareable;
  • two snapshots can be compared without treating all contained entities as changed;
  • historical snapshots remain exact.

docs.title: 15. Local Stability and Global Certainty
docs.text:
The three identities work together as follows:

EntityId
  stable conceptual continuity

RevisionId
  exact immutable local state

SnapshotId
  exact immutable global state

This gives Scriberig two useful kinds of stability.

docs.title: 15.1 Local stability
docs.text:
A consumer can keep referring to:

Function F

across ordinary edits, formatting changes, file moves, and unrelated project changes.

docs.title: 15.2 Historical exactness
docs.text:
A consumer can refer to:

Function F at Revision R

and know that the target cannot silently change.

docs.title: 15.3 Global exactness
docs.text:
A consumer can attach work to:

Snapshot S

and know exactly which revision of every visible canonical entity formed the working world.

All three are required.

docs.title: 16. References Must Declare Their Required Exactness
docs.text:
Different operations require different kinds of references.

Use an entity reference when the operation is about conceptual continuity.

Examples:

Open function F.
Show the current paragraph P.
Follow branch B.

Use a revision reference when exact immutable content matters.

Examples:

Summarize function F at revision FR7.
Render paragraph revision PR3.
Compare revision PR3 with PR9.

Use a snapshot reference when a consistent world view matters.

Examples:

Run analysis against snapshot S42.
Start an agent branch from snapshot S42.
Render the project as it existed at snapshot S42.

A public API should not hide this distinction behind ambiguous identifiers.

docs.title: 17. Entity Resolution Is Snapshot-Scoped
docs.text:
An entity reference by itself does not determine one exact state.

To inspect canonical state, the system resolves it within a snapshot:

resolve(Snapshot S42, Entity F) -> Revision FR19

Consumers may have an implicit current snapshot for convenience, but the underlying operation remains snapshot-scoped.

This rule prevents subtle ambiguity in history, branches, concurrent agent work, and external clients.

For reproducible operations, the snapshot should be explicit.

docs.title: 18. Historical References Must Never Drift
docs.text:
A reference to an exact revision or snapshot must always resolve to the same immutable state.

The following must never happen:

Revision R

means one body today and another body tomorrow.

Likewise:

Snapshot S

must never be retargeted to newer knowledge.

Mutable names such as:

main
current
latest
preferred-style

may exist as aliases or pointers, but they are not revision or snapshot identities.

The system must make this distinction explicit.

docs.title: 19. Named Roots and Aliases Are Mutable Pointers
docs.text:
Users and applications need convenient names for changing state.

Examples include:

main
current-project
active-session
preferred-rust-style

Such names may point to different entities, revisions, or snapshots over time depending on their purpose.

They are mutable references, not immutable identities.

Conceptually:

main -> Snapshot S41

later becomes:

main -> Snapshot S42

S41 and S42 themselves remain immutable.

This separation allows familiar mutable workflows without weakening historical exactness.

docs.title: 20. Structural Sharing
docs.text:
Related snapshots and revisions should reuse unchanged immutable state.

For example:

Snapshot S1
  P1 -> PR1
  P2 -> PR2
  P3 -> PR3

After changing only P2:

Snapshot S2
  P1 -> PR1
  P2 -> PR4
  P3 -> PR3

PR1 and PR3 are shared.

The persistent snapshot structure should also reuse unchanged internal storage nodes.

Structural sharing is important because it makes immutable history practical rather than requiring complete copies of the knowledge universe for every change.

The logical model must permit aggressive sharing even if physical storage later uses additional optimizations.

docs.title: 21. Change Propagation Is Moved to the Right Layer
docs.text:
A deep semantic edit does cause one unavoidable global change:

Snapshot S1 -> Snapshot S2

That propagation is intentional.

It means the system has a single exact answer to:

Has any canonical knowledge changed?

What should be avoided is unnecessary semantic propagation such as:

Expression changed
therefore Function entity changed
therefore Module entity changed
therefore Project entity changed

The correct model is:

local entity revision changes where canonical local state changed
+
structural revisions change where relationships or membership changed
+
new global snapshot

This gives precise local invalidation and exact global change detection at the same time.

The next figure contrasts the anti-pattern with the intended design. Readers should notice that the system still gets a single global change signal, but that signal comes from the snapshot layer rather than from redefining every semantic ancestor as a new conceptual object.

Figure 4. Change propagation is intentionally global at the snapshot layer, not at every semantic ancestor.

docs.title: 22. Caches Must Depend on the Smallest Exact Inputs
docs.text:
The global snapshot identity must not be used indiscriminately as a cache key.

Doing so would make every global change invalidate every local cached result.

Instead, cache keys should use the smallest immutable inputs that actually determine the result.

Examples:

function summary
  depends on Function revision

paragraph rendering
  depends on Paragraph revision + Style revision + renderer version

symbol analysis
  depends on relevant code revisions + toolchain configuration

branch summary
  depends on Branch revision + summary profile

The snapshot ID is appropriate for results that truly depend on the entire snapshot.

This distinction is essential for incremental performance.

docs.title: 23. Dependency Sets Preserve Cache Validity Across Snapshot Changes
docs.text:
A derived result may depend on multiple exact inputs.

For example:

Analysis A

depends_on:
  Function F@FR7
  Type T@TR4
  Trait X@XR2

An unrelated function may change, producing a new global snapshot.

Analysis A remains valid if all of its declared immutable dependencies remain unchanged.

Therefore:

A new snapshot does not imply that all derived knowledge is stale.

Derived results should record exact dependency revisions and configuration so that validity can be determined precisely.

This rule applies to compiler analysis, render caches, summaries, descriptions, model-generated understanding, query caches, and other derived artifacts.

docs.title: 24. Relationships May Have Their Own Revisioned State
docs.text:
Not all canonical state belongs naturally inside a leaf entity.

Some state describes relationships or collections between entities.

Examples include:
