  • ordered children of a section;
  • parameters of a function;
  • rows of a table;
  • branches belonging to a session;
  • file layout of a projected module;
  • membership in a conceptual group.

Such structure may be represented as revisioned state owned by a container or by a first-class collection or relation entity.

The exact representation is domain-dependent.

The important rule is:

A child does not need a new revision merely because a relation around it changed.

This enables moves, reorderings, and regroupings without unnecessary content churn.

docs.title: 25. Graph Cycles Must Not Break Revision Identity
docs.text:
The semantic knowledge graph may contain cycles.

Examples include:

Function A calls Function B
Function B calls Function A

or mutually recursive definitions.

Revision identity therefore cannot depend on naively recursively hashing the entire reachable semantic graph.

Canonical revision identity must be defined over a bounded canonical representation whose references can be encoded without requiring infinite recursive expansion.

Domains with cyclic canonical structures may require component-level canonicalization or other explicit rules.

The universal model must permit cycles without forcing the whole graph into one recursive content hash.

docs.title: 26. Derived Relations Do Not Automatically Affect Canonical Revision Identity
docs.text:
Some relationships are derived rather than canonical.

Examples include:

  • symbol resolution;
  • inferred type;
  • call graph edges discovered by analysis;
  • reverse-reference indexes;
  • control-flow edges;
  • semantic search indexes;
  • model-generated descriptions.

Changes in a derived representation must not automatically produce new canonical entity revisions.

Derived information should identify the exact canonical revisions and configuration from which it was computed.

This prevents rebuildable analysis state from contaminating semantic identity.

docs.title: 27. Styles Follow the Same Immutable-State Principle
docs.text:
Styles and projection configurations may also have stable conceptual identity and immutable revisions.

For example:

Style entity: preferred-rust-style

Revision SR1:
  width = 100
  indent = 4

Revision SR2:
  width = 120
  indent = 4

A mutable alias may identify the currently preferred style while old style revisions remain exact.

Rendering can then depend on immutable inputs such as:

semantic revision
style revision
renderer version

Formatting preference changes do not need to change underlying semantic revisions.

docs.title: 28. Sessions Use the Same Identity Model
docs.text:
Sessions are not exceptions to the identity rules.

A session is a semantic entity.

A branch is a semantic entity.

Turns, decisions, tool invocations, results, and summaries may also be entities where useful.

Appending work to a branch creates a new branch revision.

The branch entity remains stable.

A completed branch summary can refer to the exact branch revision it summarizes.

An agent invocation can record the exact snapshot from which it began.

This makes sessions reproducible and allows later agents to distinguish:

what branch was meant

from:

which exact state of that branch was observed

docs.title: 29. Agent Work Must Be Snapshot-Based
docs.text:
An agent should begin meaningful work from a known snapshot.

Conceptually:

AgentRun
base_snapshot = S42

The agent may produce one or more candidate successor snapshots on an isolated branch or workspace.

If canonical state advances independently, the system can compare the agent's base snapshot with the new current snapshot and perform an explicit merge or reconciliation.

The system must not silently reinterpret the agent's earlier observations against newer state.

This is the foundation for safe concurrent agent work.

docs.title: 30. External Editing Uses the Same Model
docs.text:
A projected file also corresponds to a known snapshot and exact rendered inputs.

When a user edits the file externally, the system can distinguish:

B = snapshot/projection state from which the file was rendered
D = current database snapshot
F = externally edited projection

Reconciliation can then infer a migration from known state rather than treating the file as an unrelated replacement.

When imported changes are accepted, they produce new revisions and a new snapshot.

The immutable base snapshot remains available for three-way comparison.

docs.title: 31. Snapshot Diffs Are Semantic Change Discovery
docs.text:
Because snapshot identities answer only whether global state differs, the system also needs a way to discover what differs.

Conceptually:

diff(Snapshot A, Snapshot B)

should identify changed entity resolutions and relevant structural changes.

For example:

3 entities changed

Paragraph P
  PR3 -> PR4

Function F
  FR8 -> FR9

Branch B
  BR2 -> BR3

Higher-level domain diffing may then explain the meaning of those revision differences.

Snapshot comparison must not assume that every entity in a different snapshot changed.

docs.title: 32. Branching Does Not Copy the World
docs.text:
A branch begins from an immutable snapshot and later points to successor snapshots.

Conceptually:

        S1
       /  \
      S2   S3

The branches share all unchanged revisions and persistent snapshot structure.

Creating a branch should therefore be cheap regardless of project size.

The branch records history and intent around snapshot transitions; it does not require cloning all semantic objects.

This property is important for agent experiments, alternative edits, validation workspaces, and concurrent users.

docs.title: 33. Merge Is Defined Over Shared Historical State
docs.text:
When two branches descend from a common snapshot:

        S1
       /  \
      S2   S3

Scriberig has the information required for semantic three-way comparison:

base  = S1
left  = S2
right = S3

Disjoint entity changes can often be combined automatically.

Changes to the same entity or structural relation may require domain-aware reconciliation.

A successful merge produces another immutable snapshot:

S2 ----\
        -> S4
S3 ----/

The exact migration and merge model is defined separately, but immutable snapshot ancestry is a prerequisite.

The next figure gives the mental model for branching and merge. Readers should notice that branches do not copy the whole world; they reuse a shared base snapshot and only add the exact successor states needed for each line of work.

Figure 5. Branching and merge over immutable snapshots with structural sharing.

docs.title: 34. Snapshot Scope May Be Defined by a Root Set
docs.text:
Not every Scriberig installation must necessarily place every stored object into one monolithic visible world.

A snapshot may describe the complete state of a defined root set or knowledge scope.

Examples might include:

  • one project;
  • one workspace;
  • one repository plus its active sessions;
  • one explicitly composed knowledge universe.

The scope rules must be deterministic and explicit.

Within that scope, the snapshot identity must represent the complete canonical state.

This allows the same storage system to host multiple independent or partially related knowledge worlds without forcing unrelated projects to invalidate one another.

docs.title: 35. Snapshots Are Not Necessarily User-Visible Commits
docs.text:
Snapshots are fundamental immutable states.

They may be created frequently as canonical changes occur.

A user-facing commit, checkpoint, milestone, or named branch is a higher-level concept that may point to a snapshot and attach metadata such as:

  • author;
  • message;
  • purpose;
  • validation status;
  • branch name;
  • review state.

The storage model should not require every internal snapshot to become a user-visible commit.

This keeps exact state tracking separate from workflow presentation.

docs.title: 36. Provenance Must Reference Exact State Where Required
docs.text:
When knowledge is derived, imported, summarized, validated, or produced by an agent, provenance should be able to identify exact revisions and snapshots.

For example:

Summary S
source = Function F@FR19
profile = summary-profile SP4

or:

Validation V
snapshot = S42
toolchain = T7

or:

Decision D
produced_in = Branch B@BR5
base_snapshot = S40

This prevents provenance from drifting as entities continue to evolve.

docs.title: 37. Retention and Reachability
docs.text:
Immutable revisions and snapshots can accumulate over time.

Retention policy determines which historical states remain addressable.

Potential retention roots include:

  • current named roots;
  • active branches;
  • saved snapshots;
  • published states;
  • session history;
  • migrations;
  • user bookmarks;
  • audit requirements.

Unreachable revisions and snapshot structure may eventually be reclaimed according to storage policy.

Garbage collection is a persistence concern, but identity semantics require one important guarantee:

An identity must never be reused to mean different content after collection.

If historical content is no longer retained, the system may report it unavailable. It must not reinterpret the identifier.

docs.title: 38. Identity Across Import and Reconciliation
docs.text:
When structured external content is imported, the parser can construct candidate semantic state but cannot always know stable entity continuity by syntax alone.

Reconciliation determines whether a candidate object represents:

  • a new revision of an existing entity;
  • a newly created entity;
  • a moved entity;
  • a split or merged structure;
  • an ambiguous case requiring intervention.

For example, editing a paragraph should normally result in:

same EntityId
new RevisionId

while inserting a genuinely new paragraph should result in:

new EntityId
new RevisionId

Stable identity must therefore be preserved by explicit reconciliation logic rather than guessed solely from content hashes.

docs.title: 39. Identity Across Moves
docs.text:
Moving an entity should not automatically change its entity identity or content revision.

Examples:

  • moving a paragraph between sections;
  • moving a function between files where the language permits it;
  • moving a session branch into another organizational grouping;
  • reordering table rows.

The containing structure or projection layout changes.

The moved entity may remain unchanged.

This distinction is especially important for caching, lineage, and agent references.

docs.title: 40. Identity Across Formatting Changes
docs.text:
Formatting changes in a projection should not normally change semantic entity or revision identity.

For example, these may represent the same canonical code structure under different styles:

foo(a,b,c)

and:

foo(a, b, c)

Likewise, Markdown spacing or table alignment may differ without changing canonical semantic content where the domain defines those differences as presentational.

A change only affects canonical revision identity when the domain's canonical model says meaningful state changed.

Projection configuration and style identity are separate concerns.

docs.title: 41. Identity Is Domain-Aware but the Framework Is Universal
docs.text:
The universal system defines the distinction among entity, revision, and snapshot identity.

Domains define what constitutes meaningful canonical change for their entity types.

For example:

  • a Markdown domain decides which formatting is semantic;
  • a Rust domain decides which syntax distinctions are canonical;
  • a PDF domain decides whether extracted layout or original binary structure is canonical;
  • a session domain decides which turn metadata belongs in canonical state.

The framework must not hard-code one domain's identity rules for all others.

However, every domain must respect the universal invariants around stable entities, immutable revisions, and exact snapshots.

docs.title: 42. Public Operations Should Expose Identity Deliberately
docs.text:
Universal operations should make identity scope visible.

Examples include:

inspect(entity, snapshot)
resolve(entity, snapshot)
inspect_revision(revision)
diff_revisions(a, b)
diff_snapshots(a, b)
history(entity)

Higher-level APIs may provide convenient defaults, but exact forms must remain available.

This is especially important for agents and distributed clients because implicit current state can change between operations.

A sequence of reads that must be consistent should operate against one known snapshot.

docs.title: 43. Concurrency Model
docs.text:
Immutability means concurrent writers do not need to overwrite the same stored revision.

Two consumers may start from the same snapshot:

S1

and independently create:

S2
S3

Both histories remain valid.

The conflict is not a low-level race over mutable object contents.

It is an explicit question of whether and how S2 and S3 should be merged or which named root should advance.

Mutable root updates may require transactional or compare-and-swap behavior, but the knowledge states themselves remain immutable.

docs.title: 44. Failure Model
docs.text:
Creating revisions and candidate snapshots must not corrupt existing states.

If an operation fails during parsing, validation, reconciliation, rendering, or persistence, previously valid revisions and snapshots remain unchanged.

Promotion of a new named current root should happen only after the successor snapshot is complete enough to satisfy the relevant transaction boundary.

This allows failed agent attempts, imports, and edits to remain isolated.

docs.title: 45. Required Invariants
docs.text:
All lower-level designs must preserve the following invariants.

  1. An EntityId identifies conceptual continuity, not exact content.
  2. A RevisionId identifies one exact immutable canonical state.
  3. A SnapshotId identifies one exact immutable global state within its defined scope.
  4. Revisions never change in place.
  5. Snapshots never change in place.
  6. Mutable aliases and named roots are not immutable identities.
  7. Historical revision and snapshot references never drift.
  8. A local content change does not automatically create new identities for all semantic ancestors.
  9. Structural changes affect the structure that owns the changed relationship or collection.
  10. Semantic containment is not required to be the physical snapshot Merkle structure.
  11. Every canonical change produces a new snapshot identity.
  12. Unchanged revisions are reusable across snapshots.
  13. Related snapshots structurally share unchanged storage state.
  14. Cache validity is based on exact dependencies, not merely on whether the global snapshot changed.
  15. Derived knowledge does not redefine canonical identity unless explicitly promoted into canonical state.
  16. Graph cycles must be supported without recursively hashing the entire reachable graph.
  17. External import and reconciliation preserve existing entity identity when continuity can be established.
  18. Moving or reformatting an entity does not automatically change its semantic revision.
  19. Concurrent work creates independent immutable successor states rather than mutating shared history.
  20. Collected identities are never reused for different content.

docs.title: 46. Consequences for the Rest of the Architecture
docs.text: This identity model determines several later designs.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: The storage layer must support immutable revision objects and persistent snapshot mappings with structural sharing.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: Changes are transitions between snapshots and can record lineage between revisions and entities.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text: Rendered files and views must record the snapshot and exact semantic or style inputs from which they were produced.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Caches should use revision identities and exact dependency sets rather than filenames, line numbers, or global snapshot IDs unless the result genuinely depends on the whole snapshot.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: Branches and turns can reference exact project snapshots while maintaining stable semantic handles for evolving session objects.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: Agent work begins from a known snapshot, uses stable entity handles for navigation, and exact revision references for reproducible observations.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text: Protocols must distinguish stable entity references from exact revision and snapshot references instead of exposing one ambiguous generic ID.

docs.title: 47. Summary
docs.text:
Scriberig uses three layers of identity because no single identity can correctly represent continuity, immutable local state, and immutable global state at the same time.

EntityId
  -> stable semantic thing

RevisionId
  -> exact immutable state of that thing

SnapshotId
  -> exact immutable state of the knowledge universe

The architecture intentionally avoids tying semantic parent identity to recursively hashed descendant state.

Instead, local entities remain stable, changed entities receive new immutable revisions, structural owners receive new revisions when their relationships change, and every canonical transition produces a new persistent snapshot.

This moves change propagation to the layer where it is useful.

Local identities remain stable enough for agents, applications, caching, and semantic references.

The global snapshot still changes whenever anything canonical changes, providing a compact, exact fingerprint for consistency, history, branching, synchronization, and reproducibility.

The result is the combination Scriberig needs:

Local stability for useful semantic identity, immutable revisions for exactness, and global snapshot identity for certainty.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig needs a persistence model that can store one universal knowledge system without coupling that system to agents, files, a specific domain, or a specific database engine.

The storage layer must support source code, documents, PDFs, sessions, branches, decisions, styles, migrations, derived analysis, and future domains through the same fundamental persistence rules.

This document defines those rules.

The central principle is:

Persist exact immutable state locally, preserve stable conceptual identity separately, and represent each complete consistent world with an immutable snapshot.

The storage layer must make the following simultaneously possible:

  • exact historical references;
  • local incremental updates;
  • global change detection;
  • structural sharing;
  • deterministic caching;
  • branching and concurrent work;
  • reliable recovery;
  • efficient querying;
  • eventual garbage collection;
  • replacement of the physical storage backend without changing the knowledge model.

This document intentionally does not prescribe SQL tables, Rust structs, page layouts, serialization libraries, or one database engine. Those belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Relationship to the Knowledge Model
docs.text:
The universal knowledge model distinguishes three questions:

What thing is this?                  -> Entity
What exact state is that thing in?   -> Revision
What exact state is the whole world? -> Snapshot

Persistence must preserve those distinctions.

Conceptually:

EntityId
   |
   | resolved in
   v
Snapshot ----------------------+
   |                            |
   v                            |
RevisionId                      |
   |                            |
   +-- canonical properties    |
   +-- canonical relations ----+
   +-- canonical collections

An entity is a stable semantic handle.

A revision is immutable exact content.

A snapshot is an immutable mapping that determines which revision of each entity is visible in one consistent state of the knowledge universe.

These concepts must not collapse into one recursively changing identifier.

Figure 1. Stable entity identity, exact revision identity, and global snapshot identity.

The important distinction is that the entity answers which conceptual thing is being discussed, a revision identifies one exact immutable state of that thing, and a snapshot selects the exact revisions that together form one complete world. An edit can therefore preserve semantic continuity while still producing exact local history and a new global state.

docs.title: 3. Storage Is a Platform Capability
docs.text:
The persistence system must be useful without any agent runtime.

A consumer may use it only as:

  • an immutable revision store;
  • a versioned graph database;
  • a document backend;
  • a source-code database;
  • a history and snapshot system;
  • an application database with semantic entities;
  • a substrate for custom domains.

Therefore the storage layer must not contain assumptions about:

  • prompts;
  • models;
  • tool calls;
  • agent context windows;
  • chat interfaces;
  • one particular source language;
  • one particular document format.

Agents, sessions, source code, PDFs, and other domains are users of the persistence model rather than privileged parts of it.

docs.title: 4. Logical Persistence Layers
docs.text:
The persistence model should be understood as several logical layers even if one physical database stores all of them.

+------------------------------------------+
| Semantic entities and typed relations    |
+------------------------------------------+
| Immutable entity revisions               |
+------------------------------------------+
| Snapshot entity -> revision map          |
+------------------------------------------+
| Derived indexes and caches               |
+------------------------------------------+
| Physical storage backend                 |
+------------------------------------------+

The layers have different guarantees.

docs.title: 4.1 Semantic entity layer
docs.text: Provides stable conceptual identity and domain meaning.

docs.title: 4.2 Revision layer
docs.text: Stores exact immutable canonical states.

docs.title: 4.3 Snapshot layer
docs.text: Defines one complete consistent view by resolving entities to revisions.

docs.title: 4.4 Derived layer
docs.text: Stores rebuildable indexes, reverse relations, search structures, cached renders, summaries, compiler information, and other accelerators.

docs.title: 4.5 Physical backend
docs.text:
Stores bytes, pages, records, transactions, and indexes using a concrete database implementation.

Higher layers must not depend on incidental details of lower layers.

Figure 2. Logical persistence layers and their dependency direction.

The reader should notice that semantic and domain code depends on persistence capabilities, not on a particular table layout or storage engine. This separation lets Scriberig replace or optimize physical storage, indexes, chunking, and cache strategies without changing the universal knowledge model exposed above them.

docs.title: 5. Immutable Revisions
docs.text:
Canonical revisions are immutable after creation.

An edit never changes an existing revision in place.

Instead:

Entity E

Snapshot S1:
E -> Revision R1

change E

Snapshot S2:
E -> Revision R2

R1 remains valid while retained by a reachable historical state.

This rule applies regardless of domain.

Examples:

Paragraph P -> new paragraph revision
Function F  -> new function revision
Branch B    -> new branch revision
Style S     -> new style revision
Decision D  -> new decision revision

Logical immutability is mandatory even if the physical backend internally compacts or rewrites storage pages.

docs.title: 6. Revision Identity and Deduplication
docs.text:
A revision identity should identify exact canonical content.

The storage model should support content-derived or otherwise deterministic revision identity so that equal canonical values can be recognized as equal states.

Conceptually:

RevisionId = identity(canonical revision representation)

This enables natural deduplication.

If the same canonical revision is produced twice, the store may reuse the existing revision rather than persist another logical copy.

This property supports:

  • structural sharing;
  • exact cache keys;
  • branch convergence;
  • reproducible references;
  • inexpensive reuse of unchanged knowledge.

The exact hashing algorithm and canonical encoding are implementation decisions, but the persistence model depends on one invariant:

A revision identifier must never silently refer to different canonical content.

docs.title: 7. Stable Entities Are Separate from Revision Identity
docs.text:
A revision identifies exact state, but applications often need continuity across change.

Therefore stable entity identity is maintained separately.

Example:

Function entity F

R1: original implementation
R2: timeout handling added
R3: parameter renamed

A consumer asking for F in the current snapshot means:

Resolve the conceptual function F to the revision visible now.

A consumer asking for F at R1 means:

Read the exact historical state R1.

This prevents two undesirable extremes:

  1. mutable objects whose historical meaning changes under existing references;
  2. content hashes being used as the only application-level identity, causing every edit to appear to create an unrelated conceptual object.

The persistence layer must support both continuity and exactness.

docs.title: 8. Snapshots
docs.text:
A snapshot is an immutable consistent mapping from semantic entities to exact revisions.

Conceptually:

Snapshot S

Entity A -> Revision A7
Entity B -> Revision B2
Entity C -> Revision C19
Entity D -> Revision D4

A canonical change produces a new snapshot.

The previous snapshot remains valid.

The snapshot is the unit used when exact global consistency matters.

Examples include:

  • an agent workspace base;
  • a validation run;
  • a projection render;
  • a semantic diff;
  • a branch point;
  • a merge base;
  • reproducible analysis;
  • synchronization between clients.

docs.title: 9. The Snapshot Map Is Not the Semantic Containment Tree
docs.text:
The persistence structure used to identify a complete snapshot must not be confused with the semantic graph itself.

Consider semantic containment:

Document
  -> Section
      -> Paragraph

If the paragraph text changes, the containing section and document remain the same conceptual entities.

The persistence model should therefore avoid requiring every semantic ancestor to receive a new conceptual identity merely because a deep descendant changed.

Instead, a snapshot can maintain an independent persistent mapping:

EntityId -> RevisionId

For example:

Snapshot S1

Document D  -> D@4
Section S   -> S@7
Paragraph P -> P@2

After changing only the paragraph:

Snapshot S2

Document D  -> D@4
Section S   -> S@7
Paragraph P -> P@3

The document and section revisions remain unchanged if their own canonical state did not change.

This gives Scriberig two desirable properties at once:

local semantic stability
+
global snapshot certainty

Figure 3. Local semantic stability combined with global snapshot certainty.

This is the central answer to the change-propagation problem. A deep edit need not recreate the conceptual identity or revision of every semantic ancestor; only entities whose own canonical state changed need new revisions. The top-level snapshot still changes intentionally, giving the system a compact fingerprint that says the complete canonical world is different.

docs.title: 10. Structural Changes and Content Changes Are Different
docs.text:
The storage model should preserve the distinction between changing an entity and changing a structure that refers to that entity.

Example content change:

Paragraph P

R1: "Objects are immutable."
R2: "Objects are immutable and content addressed."

The section containing P may not need a new revision because it still contains the same conceptual entity P.

Example structural change:

Section S

R1 children:
[P1, P2]

R2 children:
[P1, P3, P2]

Now the section's own structural state changed, so the section receives a new revision.

This distinction reduces unnecessary change propagation and gives diffs more useful semantics.

docs.title: 11. Persistent Snapshot Representation
docs.text:
Although a snapshot conceptually maps many entities to revisions, creating a new snapshot must not require copying the entire map.

The physical representation should support persistent structural sharing.

Conceptually:

Snapshot S1
    |
    +-- mostly shared mapping structure

Snapshot S2
    |
    +-- mostly the same mapping structure
    +-- changed path for Entity P

A small semantic change should create only a small amount of new snapshot-index state.

Suitable implementation techniques may include persistent trees, tries, Merkle structures, copy-on-write indexes, or equivalent mechanisms.

The specific data structure belongs in lower-level design.

The Level 1 requirement is:

Snapshot creation must scale with the changed portion of the entity-to-revision mapping rather than require duplication of the whole knowledge universe.

docs.title: 12. Global Snapshot Identity Is Intentionally Sensitive
docs.text:
The identity of the top-level snapshot should change whenever canonical state visible through that snapshot changes.

This is not undesirable invalidation. It is the purpose of the snapshot identity.

A snapshot identity provides a compact answer to:

Has anything canonical changed?

If two snapshot identities are equal, they represent the same complete canonical state.

If they differ, at least one canonical mapping differs.

This supports fast decisions such as:

  • whether a client is current;
  • whether an agent is still operating on its original base;
  • whether synchronization is required;
  • whether a three-way merge is needed;
  • whether two branches converged;
  • whether a validation result applies to the same complete state.

The snapshot identity is therefore intentionally coarse.

It must not be used as the default key for fine-grained caches.

docs.title: 13. Fine-Grained Reuse Must Depend on Exact Inputs
docs.text:
A change anywhere in the database changes the global snapshot, but unrelated derived results should remain reusable.

For example, if one paragraph changes, the following may still remain valid:

  • a summary of an unchanged function;
  • rendered output of an unrelated section;
  • compiler analysis of an unaffected module;
  • a branch summary whose source branch did not change;
  • an embedding of an unchanged PDF page.

Fine-grained caches should therefore depend on the smallest immutable inputs that determine their result.

Conceptually:

render cache:
(object revision, style revision, renderer version)

summary cache:
(source revision, summary profile, producer version)

analysis cache:
(exact dependency revisions, analysis configuration)

The global snapshot is used for world-level consistency.

Exact local revisions are used for incremental reuse.

docs.title: 14. Canonical and Derived Persistence
docs.text:
The database may contain both canonical and derived knowledge, but the storage model must distinguish them.

Canonical state participates directly in snapshot history.

Derived state is computed from canonical state, external artifacts, configuration, or other derived inputs.

Examples of derived persisted data include:

  • reverse-relation indexes;
  • full-text search indexes;
  • call graphs;
  • type information;
  • compiler diagnostics;
  • PDF extraction indexes;
  • embeddings;
  • descriptions;
  • summaries;
  • render caches;
  • pretty-print intermediate representations;
  • validation results;
  • model-generated explanations.

Derived persisted objects should identify their exact dependencies and producer configuration.

They should be removable and rebuildable without losing canonical knowledge.

Figure 4. Canonical state is authoritative; derived state is dependency-tracked and rebuildable.

The key operational distinction is retention and invalidation. Losing canonical state can destroy retained knowledge, while losing a derived cache should only cost recomputation. Derived results should therefore name the smallest exact revision set and producer configuration that determines them, allowing reuse across unrelated global snapshot changes.

docs.title: 15. Indexes Are Derived State
docs.text:
Indexes exist to make access efficient; they are not the authority for knowledge.

Examples include:

entity -> current revision in snapshot
child -> semantic parents
symbol -> references
function -> callers
entity -> migrations
entity -> descriptions
path -> projection
term -> matching semantic objects

If an index is corrupted or deleted, the system should be able to rebuild it from authoritative persisted state or other declared authoritative sources.

An implementation may maintain indexes transactionally for performance, but logical correctness must not depend on treating an index as independent canonical truth.

docs.title: 16. Relations and Reverse Navigation
docs.text:
Canonical relations should be persisted in the direction defined by their schema or domain ownership rules.

Reverse navigation should normally be implemented as derived indexing.

For example:

Section --contains--> Paragraph

is canonical structure.

The system may derive:

parents(Paragraph) -> Section

without storing Section as part of the paragraph's own revision.

This avoids unnecessary paragraph revision changes when the paragraph is moved between sections.

The same rule applies broadly:

Persist canonical ownership once; derive convenient traversal directions where possible.

docs.title: 17. Collections
docs.text:
Ordered and unordered collections are canonical state when the domain says their membership or order is meaningful.

A persistence implementation must preserve those semantics without forcing child identity to depend on position.

For example:

Section S revision R1:
[P1, P2, P3]

Section S revision R2:
[P3, P1, P2]

The section revision changes.

P1, P2, and P3 do not change merely because their positions changed.

Large collections should be representable with structural sharing so that inserting one element does not require duplicating an arbitrarily large collection representation.

The specific persistent sequence structure belongs in lower-level design.

docs.title: 18. Transactions
docs.text:
A visible snapshot must always represent a consistent committed state.

Operations that create or promote canonical state may involve several internal steps:

create revisions
update canonical relations or collections
update snapshot mapping
record migration metadata
update required indexes
publish new snapshot/root

Consumers must not observe a half-applied state.

The persistence layer therefore needs an atomic commit boundary.

Either the old snapshot remains current or the complete new snapshot becomes current.

A crash during preparation must not create a partially visible canonical world.

docs.title: 19. Current Roots and Named Roots
docs.text:
Snapshots are immutable, but applications need stable names that indicate which snapshots are currently important.

Examples may include:

project main
feature branch
agent workspace
active session
published revision
user bookmark

These names are references to immutable roots.

Conceptually:

main -> Snapshot S42

After a successful change:

main -> Snapshot S43

The named reference may move.

The snapshots do not.

Moving a named root should be atomic and may require an expected previous value so that concurrent writers cannot silently overwrite each other.

docs.title: 20. Concurrency
docs.text:
Immutability removes many low-level write conflicts.

Two consumers may start from the same snapshot and independently create new revisions and snapshots:

        S1
       /  \
     S2    S3

Neither branch mutates S1.

Conflict occurs only when deciding how a shared named root should advance or when semantic changes need to be merged.

The persistence layer should support optimistic concurrency through explicit base snapshots or expected root values.

A failed compare-and-promote operation is not data corruption. It means the caller's base is no longer current and reconciliation or merge may be required.

docs.title: 21. Branches Are Roots, Not Copies
docs.text:
Creating a branch or workspace should not duplicate the complete database state.

A branch begins by referencing an existing snapshot.

New work creates additional revisions and snapshots that structurally share all unchanged state.

Conceptually:

Snapshot S1
   |
   +--> Branch A -> S2
   |
   +--> Branch B -> S3

The storage cost of branching should be proportional to subsequent changes, not to the size of the project or knowledge universe at the branch point.

This property is important for:

  • agent exploration;
  • alternative implementations;
  • speculative transformations;
  • concurrent users;
  • validation workspaces;
  • merge experiments.

Figure 5. Named roots move atomically over immutable snapshots; branches share state instead of copying it.

The figure combines three persistence rules that must work together: snapshots remain immutable, named roots provide the mutable coordination point, and new branch states structurally share their base. Readers therefore observe either a complete old root or a complete promoted root, while concurrent branches can develop independently and later reconcile semantically.

docs.title: 22. Migrations and History
docs.text:
The persistence layer stores states; migrations explain transitions between states.

History must not be inferred solely from physical write order.

A migration or equivalent history object may record:

  • base snapshot;
  • resulting snapshot;
  • source of the change;
  • semantic operations;
  • provenance;
  • parent migrations or merge parents;
  • validation information;
  • user or agent metadata where appropriate.

The precise migration model is defined in the change and merge design.

For persistence, the important requirement is that historical topology remains explicit and queryable.

docs.title: 23. Reachability
docs.text:
Immutable persistence naturally accumulates historical state.

Retention should therefore be defined through reachability from protected roots.

Potential protected roots include:

  • current project roots;
  • named branches;
  • active workspaces;
  • retained session roots;
  • published revisions;
  • pinned snapshots;
  • bookmarks;
  • history that policy requires preserving.

An object or snapshot that remains reachable from a protected root must not be collected.

Reachability may cross domains because one universal store may contain project, session, provenance, and derived relationships together.

docs.title: 24. Garbage Collection
docs.text:
Garbage collection is a storage maintenance operation, not a semantic mutation of retained knowledge.

At a high level:

enumerate protected roots
        |
        v
mark reachable canonical state
        |
        v
apply retention policy
        |
        v
remove unreachable physical objects

Derived caches may have independent eviction policies because they are rebuildable.

Canonical revisions require stronger retention rules.

Garbage collection must never make a retained snapshot partially unreadable.

Implementations should prefer conservative retention when reachability or policy is uncertain.

Figure 6. Canonical retention is determined by reachability from protected roots.

The important boundary is between semantic history and physical maintenance. Garbage collection may remove unreachable storage and derived caches may be evicted more aggressively, but neither operation is allowed to alter the meaning or readability of any retained snapshot. When retention is uncertain, the safe behavior is to keep the canonical state.

docs.title: 25. Blobs and External Artifacts
docs.text:
Not every persisted artifact should be decomposed immediately into fine-grained semantic entities.

The store may need immutable blobs for:

  • original PDF files;
  • imported binaries;
  • images;
  • archives;
  • source artifacts awaiting parsing;
  • large opaque tool outputs.

A blob may participate in provenance relationships such as:

PDFDocument --derived_from--> Blob
ParsedDocument --produced_from--> Blob

Blob identity should follow the same exactness principles as other immutable persisted content.

Domain adapters decide whether and how blob contents are decomposed into semantic knowledge.

docs.title: 26. Large Values and Chunking
docs.text:
The logical model must not require one revision to correspond to one monolithic physical record.

Large values may be chunked, compressed, deduplicated, streamed, or stored through backend-specific large-object mechanisms.

Those optimizations must preserve the same logical revision identity and read semantics.

This is especially relevant for:

  • large documents;
  • binary blobs;
  • large session tool results;
  • generated indexes;
  • source trees;
  • rendered artifacts.

Physical chunking is an implementation detail, not a semantic boundary unless a domain deliberately promotes chunks into entities.

docs.title: 27. Canonical Encoding and Evolution
docs.text:
Exact revision identity requires a deterministic canonical representation.

That representation will evolve over the lifetime of the project.

The persistence architecture must therefore support explicit encoding or schema versions.

Evolution must distinguish:

same semantic state under a newer physical encoding

from:

actual semantic change

Storage migrations, schema migrations, and semantic migrations are different concepts and should not be conflated.

A backend upgrade must not invent semantic history merely because bytes were reorganized.

docs.title: 28. Backend Independence
docs.text:
The logical persistence model must not depend on one storage engine.

An initial implementation may use an embedded transactional database because it offers a practical local deployment model.

Other future implementations may use:

  • another embedded database;
  • a service-backed database;
  • an object store combined with indexes;
  • a distributed backend;
  • an in-memory backend for tests;
  • specialized archival storage.

The rest of Scriberig should depend on persistence capabilities rather than backend-specific queries or table layouts.

The required capabilities include concepts such as:

  • store and retrieve immutable revisions;
  • resolve entities in a snapshot;
  • create snapshots with structural sharing;
  • atomically move named roots;
  • enumerate history and reachability;
  • maintain or rebuild indexes;
  • transact safely;
  • verify integrity.

docs.title: 29. Integrity Verification
docs.text:
Because exact identity and historical reproducibility are foundational, the storage system should be able to verify its own integrity.

Verification may include checking that:

  • revision identifiers match their canonical content;
  • referenced revisions exist;
  • snapshot structures are internally valid;
  • protected roots resolve to complete states;
  • canonical collection invariants hold;
  • required history references exist;
  • derived indexes correspond to known authoritative inputs.

Integrity checks should be possible independently of agents and user interfaces.

docs.title: 30. Failure Recovery
docs.text:
The database must recover to a previously committed consistent state after interruption.

Important failure scenarios include:

  • process termination during a write;
  • machine restart;
  • storage exhaustion;
  • interrupted index rebuild;
  • interrupted projection import;
  • failed validation;
  • concurrent root promotion;
  • partially completed agent work.

Prepared but unpromoted immutable objects may remain physically present after failure. They are harmless if unreachable and may later be reused or collected.

What must never happen is publication of a root that depends on incomplete canonical state.

docs.title: 31. Storage and Projection State
docs.text:
Projection files are not the authoritative persistence mechanism for supported semantic domains.

The database stores canonical semantic state and enough projection metadata to detect and reconcile external changes.

Projection metadata may include logical facts such as:

  • which semantic root or entity a projection represents;
  • which snapshot was rendered;
  • which style or projection configuration was used;
  • an identity of the produced external representation;
  • whether the external representation has diverged.

The exact file-watching and reconciliation mechanisms belong in the projection design.

The persistence requirement is that an external file edit cannot silently mutate historical database revisions.

It must result in new semantic state if accepted.

docs.title: 32. Storage and Sessions
docs.text:
Sessions use the same persistence guarantees as other domains.

A session branch, decision, turn, tool result, or summary may be stored as semantic entities and immutable revisions.

The storage layer does not need special knowledge of conversational behavior.

This means session features inherit ordinary database properties:

  • exact historical references;
  • branches;
  • structural sharing;
  • provenance;
  • reachability;
  • semantic links to project entities;
  • fine-grained derived summaries;
  • snapshot-based reproducibility.

A session is therefore persisted as knowledge, not as a privileged append-only text transcript.

docs.title: 33. Storage and Agents
docs.text:
Agents must consume persistence through higher-level semantic capabilities.

They should not need direct access to physical database representation.

An agent may ask to inspect an entity, follow a relation, compare revisions, query history, or create a branch.

Those operations eventually use the persistence system, but physical layout remains hidden.

This preserves the ability to change:

  • database engines;
  • index strategies;
  • chunking;
  • compression;
  • snapshot data structures;
  • cache layouts;

without changing the agent interaction model.

docs.title: 34. Storage and Applications
docs.text:
Non-agent applications should have equal standing.

A command-line program, server, web application, IDE integration, domain-specific tool, or third-party library may use the same storage and graph capabilities.

The persistence API should therefore expose general operations rather than agent-specific convenience methods.

The full Scriberig product is a consumer of the database, not its owner.

docs.title: 35. Observability
docs.text:
The storage subsystem should expose enough operational information to understand its behavior without exposing backend internals as semantic API.

Useful observable concepts may include:

  • current named roots;
  • snapshot ancestry;
  • revision counts;
  • retained versus unreachable data;
  • cache sizes and hit rates;
  • index status;
  • pending maintenance;
  • integrity-check results;
  • transaction failures;
  • storage usage.

The exact metrics and diagnostics belong in lower-level design.

The architectural requirement is that persistence behavior can be inspected and debugged rather than acting as an opaque black box.

docs.title: 36. Security and Access Boundaries
docs.text:
A universal database may contain information with different visibility and trust requirements.

The persistence model should not assume that every consumer may read every entity or snapshot.

Authorization, capability scoping, and trust policy are defined elsewhere, but storage must preserve enough structure to support them.

In particular, implementations should avoid designs that require unrestricted backend access merely to perform normal semantic operations.

Higher layers should be able to expose bounded views without bypassing the persistence abstraction.

docs.title: 37. Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
All persistence implementations must preserve the following invariants.

  1. Canonical revisions are immutable.
  2. Stable entity identity is separate from exact revision identity.
  3. Snapshots are immutable consistent views.
  4. Any canonical change produces a different global snapshot state.
  5. A local semantic change must not force unrelated entity revisions to change.
  6. Snapshot representation must support structural sharing.
  7. Branches and workspaces begin from existing snapshots rather than copying the world.
  8. Named roots may move; immutable snapshots do not.
  9. Visible root promotion is atomic.
  10. Historical references continue to identify exact retained state.
  11. Derived indexes and caches are rebuildable.
  12. Fine-grained reuse depends on exact local inputs, not the global snapshot by default.
  13. Canonical relation direction and reverse indexing are distinct concerns.
  14. Child identity must not change merely because a parent or position changes unless the domain declares that context canonical.
  15. Garbage collection operates only on state not protected by retention roots or policy.
  16. Backend-specific details do not leak into the universal knowledge model.
  17. Agents are not required for storage operation.
  18. Files are not required for storage operation.
  19. A crash cannot expose a partially committed canonical snapshot.
  20. The store can verify the integrity of retained canonical state.

docs.title: 38. Consequences of the Model
docs.text:
This persistence model intentionally combines local stability with global certainty.

A deep edit may change only one semantic entity revision while still producing a new top-level snapshot identity.

That is a strength rather than a contradiction.

It means Scriberig can answer both:

Did this function change?

and:

Did anything in the canonical knowledge universe change?

without using the same identity for both questions.

It also means that caches, renderers, compilers, summaries, and agents can reuse unchanged local knowledge while synchronization, history, branching, and reproducibility operate against exact global snapshots.

The storage layer therefore does not merely hold data.

It provides the consistency model that allows every higher-level Scriberig capability to share one universal knowledge system without sacrificing incremental behavior.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig represents canonical knowledge as immutable revisions resolved through immutable snapshots.

That model makes state exact, but a usable system also needs an equally clear model for change.

The system must be able to answer:

  • what changed between two states;
  • why it changed;
  • which entity revisions were replaced or introduced;
  • whether a change came from a human, an agent, an importer, a merge, or another source;
  • what work was performed speculatively rather than promoted;
  • how two concurrent lines of work relate;
  • whether they can be combined automatically;
  • where a conflict exists when they cannot;
  • how historical lineage can be inspected without reconstructing it from physical write order.

The central rule is:

Canonical change is an explicit transition between immutable snapshots, not mutation of an existing snapshot.

This document defines the architectural model for those transitions.

It covers migrations, change lineage, semantic diffs, branches, workspaces, concurrency, common ancestors, merge, conflict representation, and promotion of completed work.

It intentionally does not define Rust types, SQL tables, wire formats, one diff algorithm, or one merge implementation. Those belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Relationship to Entities, Revisions, and Snapshots
docs.text:
The identity model distinguishes:

EntityId   -> What conceptual thing is this?
RevisionId -> What exact state is this entity in?
SnapshotId -> What exact state is the whole canonical world in?

A change operates across those layers.

For example:

Snapshot S1
Paragraph P -> Revision PR1

change paragraph P

Snapshot S2
Paragraph P -> Revision PR2

The entity P remains the same conceptual paragraph.

PR1 and PR2 are different immutable states.

S1 and S2 are different immutable global states.

The transition from S1 to S2 is represented by a migration or equivalent change object.

Conceptually:

S1 --Migration M1--> S2

The state and the explanation of the state transition are distinct objects.

The important point in the following figure is that a semantic edit does not collapse entity identity, revision identity, snapshot identity, and history into one thing. The paragraph remains entity P; only its exact revision changes, the enclosing world receives a new snapshot identity, and the migration records why the transition occurred.

Figure 1. A migration connects two exact immutable worlds while preserving stable semantic identity and unchanged local state.

docs.title: 3. State Does Not Explain History by Itself
docs.text:
Two snapshots can be compared to discover that they differ, but snapshot contents alone do not explain why one state followed another.

For example, the same final state may be reached by:

human edit
agent edit
import
refactoring
merge
reconciliation of an external projection

The resulting snapshot may be identical in every case.

Therefore Scriberig must not infer history solely from:

  • physical write order;
  • timestamps;
  • current entity revisions;
  • file modification times;
  • database transaction order.

History is explicit semantic data.

The system stores or derives explicit relationships such as:

base snapshot
result snapshot
change source
semantic operations
provenance
validation evidence
parent changes
merge parents

This makes historical topology queryable and reproducible.

docs.title: 4. Migration
docs.text:
A migration describes a canonical transition from one snapshot to another.

Conceptually:

Migration M

base:
  Snapshot S1

result:
  Snapshot S2

changes:
  Entity P: PR1 -> PR2

A migration answers:

How did this canonical state become that canonical state?

A migration is not the canonical state itself.

It is a first-class explanation of the transition.

The exact final authority remains the resulting snapshot and the revisions it resolves.

docs.title: 5. Migrations Are Immutable Historical Objects
docs.text:
Once a migration has been committed as history, its meaning must not change.

If a proposed operation is modified before acceptance, the system should treat the modified proposal as different work rather than rewriting committed history.

This preserves the same exactness property used elsewhere in Scriberig:

historical reference
    -> exact historical meaning

Committed migrations may therefore be content-addressable or otherwise immutable in the same architectural sense as revisions and snapshots.

The precise identity scheme belongs in lower-level design.

docs.title: 6. A Migration May Be More Semantic Than a Snapshot Diff
docs.text:
The minimal mechanical difference between two snapshots may be represented as changed entity resolutions:

P: PR1 -> PR2
Q: absent -> QR1

That information is useful but incomplete.

A domain may know that the same state transition represents:

RenameSymbol
SplitParagraph
MergeParagraphs
InsertTableRow
MoveFunction
ChangeExpressionOperator
ResolveDecision
CompleteTask

Scriberig should preserve higher-level semantic operations when they are known.

Therefore a migration may contain two complementary views:

exact state transition
+
semantic interpretation of the transition

The exact before and after states remain authoritative even if a higher-level interpretation is absent or incomplete.

docs.title: 7. Generic and Domain-Specific Change
docs.text:
The universal knowledge model needs domain-independent change primitives.

Examples include conceptual operations such as:

create entity
replace entity revision
add relation
remove relation
insert collection member
remove collection member
move collection member
replace collection structure

Domain adapters may describe the same transition more precisely.

For example:

Generic:
replace revision of expression E

Domain-specific:
change binary operator from Add to Multiply

Or:

Generic:
change ordered children of section S

Domain-specific:
insert paragraph P3 between P1 and P2

The universal change model must not require all domains to expose the same vocabulary, but every domain-specific change must ultimately resolve to a valid transition in the universal state model.

docs.title: 8. Change Sources and Provenance
docs.text:
A migration should be able to state where the change came from.

Possible sources include:

  • direct user action;
  • external file or projection reconciliation;
  • agent work;
  • CLI command;
  • API client;
  • web editor;
  • TUI action;
  • importer;
  • domain refactoring;
  • merge;
  • synchronization;
  • system maintenance that truly changes canonical semantics.

The source is provenance, not authority by itself.

A user edit and an agent edit both produce canonical state only through the same commit rules.

This is an important invariant:

All canonical write paths converge on the same migration and snapshot model.

No interface should have a privileged hidden mutation path.

docs.title: 9. Semantic Change and Representation Change
docs.text:
Not every externally visible change is a canonical semantic change.

Examples that may not change canonical state include:

  • formatting a source file differently under another style;
  • rendering the same session with another context policy;
  • changing whitespace that is not semantically represented;
  • rebuilding an index;
  • updating a cache;
  • changing physical database encoding without changing semantic meaning.

Those operations may create new projections, derived objects, or physical storage state without creating a semantic migration.

A semantic migration exists only when canonical knowledge changes.

This distinction prevents rendering, caching, storage maintenance, and semantic history from being conflated.

docs.title: 10. Change Sets Should Be Local Even When Snapshot Identity Is Global
docs.text:
Every canonical change creates a new snapshot identity.

That global sensitivity is intentional.

However, the migration should identify the smallest meaningful changed set rather than implying that every entity changed.

For example:

Snapshot S1 -> Snapshot S2

changed:
  Paragraph P

unchanged:
  all other visible entities

The global snapshot answers:

Did anything change?

The migration and semantic diff answer:

What changed?

These are separate questions and must remain separate in APIs, caches, agents, and user interfaces.

docs.title: 11. Semantic Diff
docs.text:
A semantic diff compares two exact states and describes their meaningful differences.

At the universal level, a diff may report:

entities created
entities removed from a scope
entity revisions changed
relations added or removed
collection membership changed
collection ordering changed

Domain-specific views may provide richer meaning.

For example, a source-code diff may report:

function signature unchanged
one condition changed
one error branch inserted
one function moved

A document diff may report:

section renamed
paragraph updated
table row inserted

A session diff may report:

branch completed
decision added
open task resolved

Textual diffs may still be rendered when useful, but they are projections of the semantic change rather than the universal change model.

docs.title: 12. Diff Does Not Require Direct Ancestry
docs.text:
A diff is a comparison between two states.

A migration is a historical transition.

They are related but not identical.

For example:

S1 -> S2 -> S3

The system may compute:

diff(S1, S3)

without there being a direct migration from S1 to S3.

Likewise, two sibling branch states may be compared:

       S1
      /  \
    S2    S3

with:

diff(S2, S3)

Therefore APIs and conceptual models must not use "diff" and "migration" interchangeably.

docs.title: 13. History Is a Directed Graph
docs.text:
Canonical history is not necessarily a single linear chain.

Branching creates multiple descendants of one snapshot:

       S1
      /  \
    S2    S3

A merge may produce a state with more than one historical parent:

S2 ----\
        -> S4
S3 ----/

History is therefore a directed acyclic graph of immutable states and explicit transitions, subject to the semantics of retained history.

A linear presentation may be useful for a UI, but it must not replace the actual topology.

The figure below makes the topology explicit. The reader should notice that immutable snapshots and migration edges form the durable history graph, while names such as main or feature are merely movable references into that graph. Branching therefore does not copy the database, and merging adds another descendant instead of rewriting either parent line.

Figure 2. Canonical history is a DAG of immutable snapshots and explicit transitions; branch names point into that graph rather than defining it.

docs.title: 14. Branches Are Named Lines of Work Over Snapshots
docs.text:
A branch is not a copy of the database.

A branch is a line of work anchored to immutable snapshots.

Conceptually:

main -> S1

create branch A from S1
create branch B from S1

A -> S2
B -> S3

All unchanged state is shared.

The branch name or branch entity may advance over time:

A -> S2
A -> S4
A -> S5

The snapshots do not move or mutate.

The branch reference advances to newer snapshots.

docs.title: 15. Branch Identity and Branch State Are Separate
docs.text:
A branch may itself be represented as a semantic entity with stable identity and evolving revision state.

For example, a session branch may have:

title
purpose
status
short description
outcome
related entities
resulting migration

Those properties can evolve while the branch remains the same conceptual branch.

Separately, the branch has or refers to a current working snapshot.

This follows the same identity rule as the rest of Scriberig:

stable entity identity
+
immutable revision state
+
immutable snapshot state

The exact representation of branch metadata and branch heads belongs in lower-level design.

docs.title: 16. Workspaces Are Branches for Isolated Work
docs.text:
A workspace is an isolated line of work based on a specific snapshot.

It may be used by:

  • an agent attempting an edit;
  • a human trying an alternative;
  • a refactoring tool;
  • an external importer;
  • a merge process;
  • a validation process;
  • a speculative transformation.

Conceptually:

base S1
  |
  +-- attempt S2
  |
  +-- attempt S3

Neither attempt mutates S1.

One may be promoted, both may be retained, or both may eventually become unreachable.

This makes speculative work cheap and safe.

docs.title: 17. Failed Attempts Are States, Not Corruption
docs.text:
An invalid or rejected workspace result does not damage the base state.

For example:

S1
├── S2  compile failed
├── S3  tests failed
└── S4  accepted

S1 remains exact throughout the process.

Whether failed attempts are retained is a policy decision.

Architecturally, the important rule is:

Failure before promotion must not partially mutate the base branch.

This applies equally to agent work, manual editing, projection reconciliation, and merge attempts.

docs.title: 18. Promotion Advances a Named Root
docs.text:
A branch or workspace becomes externally current by advancing a named root or equivalent current reference to a completed snapshot.

Conceptually:

main -> S1

After accepted work:

main -> S2

S1 remains immutable.

Promotion should be atomic.

A consumer must not observe a state where only part of the migration has become current.

This is the point at which prepared immutable work becomes the canonical state selected by that root.

docs.title: 19. Promotion Uses Optimistic Concurrency
docs.text:
A caller should normally state the snapshot it expects a named root to reference.

For example:

expected:
  main -> S1

promote:
  main -> S2

If main has already advanced to S3, silently overwriting it would lose concurrent work.

The promotion should fail as a concurrency event rather than corrupt history.

The caller can then:

  • inspect the new state;
  • rebase its work;
  • merge;
  • abandon the proposal;
  • create another branch.

This is a semantic concurrency boundary, not a low-level locking failure.

The workspace model is easiest to understand as a prepare-and-promote flow. The failed candidates in the next figure are legitimate immutable states but never become current; the successful candidate only becomes current if an atomic compare-and-promote confirms that the named root still points to the expected base.

Figure 3. Workspaces isolate speculative attempts, and optimistic promotion is the boundary where accepted work becomes current.

docs.title: 20. Concurrent Work Is Normal
docs.text:
Scriberig should assume that multiple actors may work from the same snapshot.

Actors may include:

  • multiple users;
  • multiple agents;
  • background importers;
  • filesystem reconciliation;
  • API clients;
  • web and TUI clients;
  • automated refactoring or validation systems.

Starting from:

S1

they may independently create:

       S1
      /  \
    S2    S3

This is not exceptional state.

It is the ordinary shape of concurrent immutable work.

The system must preserve both results until policy or an explicit operation decides what to do with them.

docs.title: 21. Common Ancestor
docs.text:
Combining concurrent states requires an explicit base.

Given:

       S1
      /  \
    S2    S3

S1 is the common ancestor used to determine what each branch changed.

Conceptually:

left changes  = diff(S1, S2)
right changes = diff(S1, S3)

Merge reasons about those two change sets, not merely about the final rendered representations of S2 and S3.

The common ancestor is essential because the same final value may mean different things depending on what each side started from.

docs.title: 22. Three-Way Merge
docs.text:
The default semantic merge model is three-way:

          base
         /    \
      left    right
         \    /
         merged

The merge process considers:

base snapshot
left snapshot
right snapshot

and attempts to produce:

merged snapshot

plus explicit merge provenance.

The merge result must not overwrite either input snapshot.

It creates another immutable state.

docs.title: 23. Disjoint Changes Should Merge Naturally
docs.text:
If two branches change unrelated entities, they should normally combine without conflict.

Example:

Base S1

Function F -> FR1
Paragraph P -> PR1

Left:

Function F -> FR2
Paragraph P -> PR1

Right:

Function F -> FR1
Paragraph P -> PR2

Merged:

Function F -> FR2
Paragraph P -> PR2

The universal snapshot model makes this case straightforward because the changed entity mappings are independent.

This should be the common inexpensive case.

docs.title: 24. Same Entity Does Not Always Mean Conflict
docs.text:
Two branches changing the same entity require deeper analysis, but they are not automatically irreconcilable.

Suppose both branches change a section revision.

One inserts a paragraph at the beginning.

The other inserts a different paragraph at the end.

A domain-aware collection merge may be able to preserve both.

Similarly, two source-code edits may affect different statements within the same function.

Therefore the merge model should allow progressively deeper reasoning:

snapshot-level changed entity detection
        |
        v
entity-level revision comparison
        |
        v
field/relation/collection comparison
        |
        v
domain-specific semantic merge

The system should not declare conflict earlier than necessary.

docs.title: 25. But Merge Must Not Invent Certainty
docs.text:
When two changes cannot be combined safely, the system must represent uncertainty explicitly.

It must not silently choose one side merely to produce a result.

Examples include:

  • both branches replace the same expression differently;
  • both rename the same entity to different names;
  • one branch deletes an entity that the other meaningfully edits;
  • two structural edits produce an ordering whose intended semantics are ambiguous;
  • domain invariants allow more than one plausible interpretation.

In these cases, the merge should produce structured conflicts or an unresolved merge workspace.

docs.title: 26. Conflicts Are Semantic Objects
docs.text:
A conflict should describe the semantic object and alternatives involved rather than only exposing textual conflict markers.

A generic conflict may contain conceptual information such as:

base entity
base revision
left revision
right revision
conflict kind
affected relation or collection
available domain interpretation
provenance for each side

A code conflict may refer to a function, statement, or expression.

A document conflict may refer to a section, paragraph, row, or cell.

A session conflict may refer to a decision, task, branch outcome, or other structured object.

Text conflict markers may be rendered for compatibility, but they are not the canonical conflict representation.

The merge pipeline below shows why a changed entity is not itself a conflict. Scriberig first compares each branch with the common base, combines independent changes directly, and progressively inspects overlapping changes at finer semantic scopes. Only an ambiguity that cannot be resolved safely becomes a conflict object.

Figure 4. Three-way semantic merge delays conflict until the smallest scope where the system cannot combine changes with confidence.

docs.title: 27. Conflict Scope Should Be Minimal
docs.text:
A conflict affecting one entity should not make unrelated merged state unusable.

Conceptually:

merged automatically:
  A
  B
  C

unresolved:
  D

merged automatically:
  E
  F

The system should preserve successful non-conflicting work while isolating unresolved semantic choices.

Whether an unresolved merge is allowed to become a canonical named root depends on policy and domain guarantees.

For ordinary project state, the default should be to resolve required conflicts before promotion.

docs.title: 28. Merge Produces Provenance
docs.text:
A merge result must record where it came from.

Conceptually:

S2 ----\
        -> S4
S3 ----/

The history should retain both parent lines.

The resulting migration or merge record should identify:

  • merge base where relevant;
  • left input;
  • right input;
  • automatic resolutions;
  • explicit resolutions;
  • unresolved conflicts if the result remains provisional;
  • validation evidence where appropriate.

This allows future consumers to understand whether state was created by ordinary linear change or by convergence of concurrent work.

docs.title: 29. Merge Is Not Textual File Merge
docs.text:
Files may be projections of canonical semantic state.

Therefore merging canonical knowledge should not normally be defined as:

merge rendered file A
with rendered file B

The preferred direction is:

semantic base
semantic left
semantic right
      |
      v
semantic merge
      |
      v
render projection

A domain adapter may use textual information as evidence during reconciliation, but the canonical result must be expressed in the semantic model.

This prevents formatting or projection choices from creating false semantic conflicts.

docs.title: 30. Reconciliation and Merge Are Related but Different
docs.text:
External projection reconciliation asks:

Given canonical semantic state and an externally edited representation, what semantic change did the user make?

Merge asks:

Given two semantic descendants of a common base, how can their changes be combined?

A projection reconciliation may itself require a three-way comparison when canonical state changed while the user was editing.

For example:

B = state used to render the user's starting file
D = current database state
F = semantic state parsed from the externally edited file

The system may then merge:

base  = B
left  = D
right = F

But reconciliation still has an additional responsibility: inferring semantic correspondence from an external representation.

The concepts should share merge infrastructure where appropriate without being treated as identical operations.

The next figure separates the two responsibilities. Reconciliation converts an edited representation back into a semantic candidate and must recover correspondence with canonical objects; only after that step can the ordinary three-way merge machinery combine the candidate with concurrent database changes.

Figure 5. Projection reconciliation infers semantic intent from an external representation, while merge combines already-semantic descendants of a common base.

docs.title: 31. Rebase Re-Expresses Work Against a New Base
docs.text:
A consumer may prefer to re-express a line of work on top of a newer base rather than create an explicit merge result.

Conceptually:

S1 -> S2    original work
 \
  -> S3     new current state

A rebase attempts to apply the semantic intent of:

S1 -> S2

onto:

S3

producing a new descendant:

S3 -> S4

S2 is not mutated or erased.

A rebase creates new history because the work is now interpreted relative to a different base.

The original branch may remain retained according to policy.

docs.title: 32. Replay Must Preserve Semantic Intent Where Known
docs.text:
A migration may contain richer semantic operations than a raw state difference.

When replaying or rebasing work, the system should prefer those semantic operations when they remain valid.

For example, a known operation:

RenameSymbol X to Y

is more useful to replay than blindly applying a textual replacement derived from one source projection.

Likewise:

InsertParagraph after P

carries clearer intent than a byte offset.

The exact algorithms are domain-specific, but the architectural principle is:

Preserve and reuse semantic intent whenever it is available and validated.

docs.title: 33. Lineage
docs.text:
Entity continuity across revisions is distinct from snapshot ancestry.

For an entity:

P@PR1 -> P@PR2 -> P@PR3

the system may expose lineage such as:

previous revision
next revision
change that introduced the revision
branch on which it appeared
snapshot where it became visible

For replacements that create a new conceptual entity rather than another revision of the same entity, migrations may express relationships such as:

split_into
merged_from
replaces
supersedes
extracted_from

Lineage belongs to change history rather than being forced into entity identity.

docs.title: 34. Creation, Deletion, and Absence
docs.text:
Deletion in a snapshot does not necessarily mean physical destruction.

If an entity is removed from the canonical scope represented by a branch, historical snapshots may still resolve it.

Conceptually:

S1:
E -> R1

S2:
E no longer visible in this canonical scope

The migration records the semantic removal.

The immutable historical revision may remain retained because another snapshot, branch, session, provenance record, or policy still references it.

Physical garbage collection is therefore separate from semantic deletion.

Similarly, creation means an entity becomes part of the relevant canonical state; it does not imply that no equivalent immutable content existed elsewhere in storage.

docs.title: 35. Moves Should Preserve Entity Continuity
docs.text:
Moving a semantic entity should not normally be represented as delete plus unrelated create when the system can determine continuity.

Examples include:

  • moving a paragraph to another section;
  • moving a function to another module or projected file;
  • moving a table row;
  • reorganizing a session branch;
  • moving an object between collections.

The entity may retain the same EntityId while structural owners receive new revisions.

The migration can then express the move explicitly.

This produces better history, more stable references, and better agent context than reconstructing identity from location.

docs.title: 36. Branch Descriptions Are Navigation Knowledge
docs.text:
A branch should be cheap to understand without opening its full history.

A branch may expose a short description or summary such as:

"Investigate immutable node identity and render-cache invalidation."

Completed branches may additionally expose an outcome:

"Use stable entities, immutable revisions, and local cache dependencies."

These descriptions are navigation aids for humans and agents.

They should be addressable and have provenance like other derived or authored descriptions.

A parent session or project view may retain only the compact branch descriptor by default while keeping the full branch available for deeper inspection.

docs.title: 37. Agent Work Uses the Same Change Model
docs.text:
Agents do not receive a separate mutation architecture.

An agent starts from an exact snapshot or branch head.

Its work creates one or more descendant snapshots in an isolated workspace.

Conceptually:

base S1
   |
   +-- S2 attempt
   |     validation failed
   |
   +-- S3 attempt
         validation passed

If S3 is accepted, the relevant named root may advance to it or merge it with newer concurrent state.

The agent does not directly mutate the previous canonical state.

The same model applies whether the agent changes source code, a document, a session, a decision, or another domain.

docs.title: 38. User Interfaces Use the Same Change Model
docs.text:
The CLI, API server, TUI, browser editor, external libraries, and agent runtime should all expose the same conceptual operations.

For example, editing a paragraph in the browser and editing the same paragraph through an agent should both result in:

base snapshot
semantic change
new revisions
result snapshot
migration
optional validation
promotion

This makes behavior consistent across product surfaces and ensures that history, merge, provenance, and validation do not depend on which interface initiated the change.

The system-level consequence is shown below: every write surface converges on the same semantic pipeline. Interfaces can offer very different interaction models, but none may bypass revision creation, migration/provenance, validation policy, and atomic promotion with a hidden direct-update path.

Figure 6. All product surfaces share one canonical write model, which keeps history, merge, validation, and concurrency behavior consistent.

docs.title: 39. Validation and Change Are Separate Concerns
docs.text:
A migration describes a transition.

Validation determines whether that transition is acceptable for a particular purpose.

Examples include:

  • schema validation;
  • source parsing;
  • type checking;
  • tests;
  • document invariants;
  • domain-specific constraints;
  • policy checks.

A candidate snapshot may exist in a workspace even if validation fails.

Promotion policy decides whether failed or incomplete validation prevents a named canonical root from advancing.

Keeping these concepts separate allows the same migration model to work across domains with different validation requirements.

Detailed trust and validation policy belongs in the dedicated Level 1 design for those concerns.

docs.title: 40. Deterministic Convergence Is Valuable
docs.text:
When two independent operations produce the same exact canonical state, the resulting snapshot identity should converge when the identity model permits it.

Likewise, identical immutable revisions should be reusable.

This means two branches may independently arrive at the same state and be recognized as equivalent without replaying their entire history.

However, identical state does not erase provenance.
