Two histories may reach the same snapshot through different migrations.

The system may preserve both historical explanations while sharing the identical resulting state.

docs.title: 41. State Equality and History Equality Are Different
docs.text:
Two branches may have the same current SnapshotId while having different historical paths.

For example:

S1 -> S2 -> S4

S1 -> S3 -> S4

The current canonical state is identical at S4.

The histories are not identical.

Applications must therefore distinguish questions such as:

Are these branches currently in the same state?

from:

Did these branches arrive here through the same history?

Snapshot identity answers the first question.

History topology and migrations answer the second.

docs.title: 42. Change Queries
docs.text:
The architecture should support queries such as:

what changed between snapshots A and B?
what migration introduced revision R?
what is the history of entity E?
which branch first introduced entity E?
what changed since snapshot S?
what branches descend from snapshot S?
what is the common ancestor of A and B?
what conflicts prevent merging A and B?
which migrations touched entity E?
which changes came from a particular branch or agent workspace?

These queries are core platform capabilities, not agent-specific features.

Agents are one class of consumer.

A database-only application should be able to use the same history and merge facilities.

docs.title: 43. Change Descriptions and Summaries
docs.text:
Migrations, diffs, branches, and merge results may be large.

They should support progressively disclosed descriptions like other Scriberig objects.

For example:

Migration M
"Add timeout handling to payment processing."

changed entities: 4
created entities: 1
removed entities: 0
validation: passed

A deeper view may expose semantic operations.

A deeper view still may expose exact before and after revisions.

This allows humans and agents to navigate history without consuming every low-level change immediately.

Descriptions may be authored, mechanically derived, or model-generated, and their provenance should remain visible.

docs.title: 44. Fine-Grained Dependencies Survive Branching
docs.text:
A global snapshot changes whenever canonical state changes, but branch creation and unrelated changes must not invalidate all derived work.

Derived results should continue to depend on exact local inputs.

For example:

Function summary
  depends on Function F@R7

Render cache
  depends on Section S@R3 and Style T@R2

Compiler analysis
  depends on exact source and configuration revisions

If a branch changes unrelated entity P, those results remain reusable.

The change and merge model must therefore preserve exact local revision identity through branching and merging whenever state is unchanged.

docs.title: 45. Named Roots Express Policy, Not State Identity
docs.text:
Names such as:

main
feature-x
agent-workspace-17
active-session
published

are mutable references selected by an application or user policy.

They are not immutable state identities.

A name can move:

main -> S1
main -> S2

The snapshots cannot.

A branch name may be deleted without deleting its historical snapshots if other retained roots still reach them.

This distinction is essential for both concurrency and garbage collection.

docs.title: 46. Retention of Change History Is Policy-Driven
docs.text:
The architecture permits rich immutable history, but not every speculative state must be retained forever.

Retention policy may differ for:

  • promoted canonical history;
  • published states;
  • session branches;
  • failed agent attempts;
  • abandoned workspaces;
  • merge experiments;
  • imported temporary states;
  • derived caches.

A retained migration must remain readable with the historical state it references.

Unretained unreachable states may eventually be garbage-collected according to persistence policy.

History semantics and physical retention are related but distinct concerns.

docs.title: 47. Cross-Domain Changes
docs.text:
One migration may legitimately span multiple domains because Scriberig stores one knowledge universe.

For example, a single accepted operation may:

change source code
update a design decision
resolve a task
append a session branch result

If those changes must become visible atomically, they may belong to one resulting snapshot and one composite migration.

The system must not assume that a migration belongs to exactly one file, one language, or one document type.

This is one of the advantages of a universal snapshot model.

docs.title: 48. Partial Domain Availability
docs.text:
Not every consumer needs every domain adapter installed.

A generic consumer should still be able to understand universal change information such as:

entity changed
relation changed
collection changed
snapshot ancestry
migration provenance

A consumer with the relevant domain adapter may additionally understand:

function renamed
paragraph split
table row moved
session decision superseded

History therefore needs a universal base representation with optional richer domain interpretation.

docs.title: 49. Change Model Invariants
docs.text:
Lower-level designs and implementations must preserve the following invariants.

  1. Existing snapshots are never mutated.
  2. Existing immutable revisions are never rewritten to mean different state.
  3. Every canonical state transition produces a new snapshot.
  4. A committed migration identifies its exact base and result states.
  5. Historical topology is explicit rather than inferred from write order.
  6. Branches and workspaces reference snapshots; they do not copy the whole knowledge store.
  7. Concurrent descendants of one snapshot are normal and independently valid.
  8. Promotion of a named root is atomic.
  9. Concurrent promotion must not silently overwrite a newer root.
  10. Merge uses an explicit common base or equivalent ancestry information.
  11. Disjoint semantic changes should merge without unnecessary conflict.
  12. Conflicts are represented semantically and at the smallest practical scope.
  13. Merge never mutates its input states.
  14. Rebase creates new history rather than rewriting immutable historical state.
  15. Semantic deletion is not physical destruction.
  16. Moves should preserve entity continuity when continuity is known.
  17. All write surfaces converge on the same migration/snapshot model.
  18. Formatting-only or derived-data changes do not create semantic history unless canonical knowledge changes.
  19. Snapshot equality and history equality are distinct concepts.
  20. Generic change remains understandable even without a domain-specific adapter.

docs.title: 50. What This Design Does Not Decide
docs.text:
This Level 1 design deliberately does not prescribe:

  • the database schema for migrations;
  • the exact migration operation enum;
  • the hash algorithm for migration identity;
  • the persistent-map implementation;
  • the exact branch metadata schema;
  • one merge algorithm for all domains;
  • one collection merge strategy;
  • one conflict-resolution UI;
  • one rebase algorithm;
  • one textual diff format;
  • one validation pipeline;
  • retention durations;
  • garbage-collection implementation;
  • whether every intermediate workspace snapshot is persisted eagerly;
  • how semantic operations are encoded on the wire.

Those decisions belong in Level 2 designs derived from these architectural rules.

docs.title: 51. Architectural Summary
docs.text:
Scriberig change history is a graph of immutable states connected by explicit semantic transitions.

The model can be summarized as:

stable entities
      |
      v
immutable revisions
      |
      v
immutable snapshots
      |
      +--------------------+
      |                    |
      v                    v
  migration             branch
      |                    |
      v                    v
new snapshot        descendant snapshots
      |                    |
      +---------+----------+
                |
                v
              merge
                |
                v
         new immutable snapshot

The essential separation is:

Snapshot
  exact canonical state

Migration
  explanation of a state transition

Branch
  named or semantic line of work over snapshots

Diff
  comparison between exact states

Merge
  combination of concurrent semantic changes

Conflict
  explicit unresolved semantic choice

Together these concepts allow Scriberig to support human editing, agents, external projections, concurrent clients, speculative work, history, rollback, semantic review, and reproducible merging without introducing in-place mutation as the foundation of the system.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig stores canonical knowledge as structured semantic entities and revisions rather than treating files, transcripts, rendered pages, or user-interface trees as the primary source of truth.

Humans and external tools still need familiar representations. Source code must appear as source files. Markdown must appear as Markdown. Sessions may appear as chronological transcripts. A browser may show a semantic tree, a rich editor, a diff, or a task-oriented view. An agent may receive a compact context containing only the information relevant to its current work.

These are all projections of semantic state.

A projection is not merely exported text. It is a controlled representation of canonical knowledge for a particular consumer, format, style, and purpose.

Some projections are read-only. Some are editable. For editable projections, changes made outside Scriberig must be interpreted and brought back into the canonical knowledge system as semantic changes.

This document defines the architectural rules for projection, style, rendering, external editing, import, reconciliation, and conflict handling.

The central principle is:

Canonical knowledge and its representations are separate. Rendering moves from semantic state to a projection; reconciliation interprets edited projections back into semantic migrations.

This document intentionally does not prescribe parser libraries, filesystem watcher libraries, pretty-print algorithms, editor frameworks, wire protocols, or concrete reconciliation data structures. Those belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Projection Is a General System Concept
docs.text:
Projection is not limited to files.

Examples include:

semantic Markdown document + Markdown style
    -> .md file

semantic Rust module + Rust style
    -> .rs file

session graph + human chat style
    -> chronological transcript

session graph + agent context policy
    -> model context

knowledge graph + browser view configuration
    -> interactive tree

semantic diff + presentation style
    -> human-readable change view

PDF knowledge + page layout projection
    -> rendered page view

The same canonical object may have several projections at the same time.

The same projection kind may also have several styles.

For example, one semantic Rust module may be rendered with different formatting preferences without creating different semantic programs.

This gives Scriberig one consistent mental model:

canonical knowledge
       |
       +----> projection A
       |
       +----> projection B
       |
       +----> projection C

The database remains authoritative. Projections exist to make that knowledge useful to humans, agents, compilers, external tools, and user interfaces.

Figure 1 makes the important direction of authority explicit: Markdown, source code, transcripts, agent context, and interactive UI views are different renderings of one canonical semantic state. None of the projected forms becomes a competing source of truth merely because it is easier for a particular consumer to use.

Figure 1 — One semantic state can support many simultaneous projections for different consumers and purposes.

docs.title: 3. Canonical State and Projection State Are Different
docs.text:
A projection must not become accidental canonical state merely because it is visible or editable.

Consider a semantic paragraph entity P.

Its canonical revision may contain:

text: "Objects are immutable."

A Markdown projection may render it as:

Objects are immutable.

An HTML projection may render it as:

<p>Objects are immutable.</p>

An agent summary projection may render it as:

Paragraph P: explains object immutability.

These representations are not three competing versions of the paragraph.

They are representations derived from one canonical semantic state.

The system must preserve this direction of authority even when a projection is editable.

An edited projection is therefore interpreted as a proposal for semantic change, not as an unconditional replacement for canonical knowledge.

docs.title: 4. Projection Classes
docs.text:
Different projections have different editing and synchronization requirements.

At Level 1, Scriberig should distinguish at least the following classes.

docs.title: 4.1 Read-only projections
docs.text:
These are generated views with no reverse-editing contract.

Examples may include:

  • rendered reports;
  • generated HTML;
  • diagnostic views;
  • some PDF renderings;
  • summaries;
  • temporary previews.

A consumer may copy or transform them externally, but Scriberig does not interpret those external changes as edits to canonical state.

docs.title: 4.2 Editable projections
docs.text:
These have a defined parser and reconciliation path back into semantic state.

Examples include:

  • Markdown files;
  • source-code files;
  • structured configuration files;
  • other formats for which the domain adapter can recover enough semantic structure.

An editable projection participates in synchronization with canonical state.

docs.title: 4.3 Ephemeral projections
docs.text:
These are generated for one operation or interaction and need not have persistent external identity.

Examples include:

  • agent context;
  • command output;
  • temporary semantic summaries;
  • preview fragments;
  • transient UI renderings.

Ephemeral projections may still be cached, but they are not independently authoritative.

docs.title: 4.4 Interactive projections
docs.text:
A user interface may project the graph into an interactive tree, editor, table, form, or diagram.

Interactive editing should still produce the same semantic operations and migrations as other editing paths.

The UI must not become a privileged back door that mutates canonical database rows directly.

docs.title: 5. A Projection Has Explicit Inputs
docs.text:
A projection should be understood as the result of exact declared inputs.

Conceptually:

Projection = render(
    semantic scope,
    snapshot,
    projection kind,
    style,
    renderer version,
    rendering context
)

Not every projection needs every input, but the dependencies must be explicit enough to support reproducibility and caching.

A projection may depend on:

  • one entity or a semantic scope;
  • exact revisions visible in a snapshot;
  • a projection format;
  • a style revision;
  • a renderer implementation/version;
  • domain-specific configuration;
  • layout context;
  • environment information that genuinely affects the result.

Implicit dependencies should be minimized.

If a projection changes because an undeclared global setting changed, it becomes difficult to cache, reproduce, compare, or reconcile reliably.

docs.title: 6. Styles Are Separate from Semantic Content
docs.text:
Formatting and presentation choices should not normally change semantic identity.

A style is itself semantic configuration and may be stored as a normal entity with immutable revisions.

For example:

RustStyle

max_width: 100
indent_width: 4
brace_style: same_line
imports: grouped

A second user may prefer:

RustStyle

max_width: 120
indent_width: 4
brace_style: same_line
imports: grouped

The Rust module does not change merely because the style changes.

Only the projection changes.

Conceptually:

semantic module M + style A -> source A
semantic module M + style B -> source B

The same principle applies beyond source code.

Styles or projection policies may control:

  • Markdown formatting;
  • table alignment;
  • line wrapping;
  • whitespace;
  • source-code formatting;
  • transcript verbosity;
  • UI presentation;
  • agent context detail;
  • human diff presentation.

Styles should have stable conceptual identity and immutable revisions like other semantic configuration.

A user-facing style alias may move to a newer style revision without rewriting semantic content.

Figure 2 shows why style belongs beside semantic content rather than inside it. The same exact semantic module can be combined with different immutable style revisions to produce different bytes and layouts while preserving one program identity.

Figure 2 — Style is an independent rendering input; changing presentation does not by itself change semantic identity.

docs.title: 7. Style Must Not Hide Semantic Transformation
docs.text:
A style controls representation, not meaning.

The boundary must be conservative.

For example, line wrapping, spacing, indentation, and brace placement are suitable style concerns.

Replacing one programming construct with another merely because they are currently equivalent is not ordinary formatting.

For example:

if-let

and:

match

may express related behavior, but choosing between them is a semantic/syntactic authoring decision rather than a simple style preference.

Likewise, a Markdown renderer should not silently rewrite the conceptual document structure merely to satisfy aesthetic preferences.

The canonical domain representation must preserve author-significant choices.

A projection adapter may support optional semantic transformations, but those must be explicit operations rather than invisible style effects.

docs.title: 8. Rendering Is Deterministic Over Declared Inputs
docs.text:
Given the same exact semantic inputs, style, renderer version, and relevant rendering context, rendering should produce the same projection.

Conceptually:

render(inputs) -> exact output

This property enables:

  • caching;
  • reproducibility;
  • projection hashing;
  • reliable dirty detection;
  • deterministic tests;
  • synchronization across clients;
  • safe reuse of unchanged fragments.

If a renderer intentionally uses nondeterministic information, such as current time, randomness, or environment state, those inputs must become explicit or the result must be treated as non-reproducible derived output.

Deterministic rendering is especially important for editable file projections because Scriberig must know what it last produced before interpreting an external edit.

docs.title: 9. Rendering May Be Incremental
docs.text:
A projection of a large semantic scope should not require complete recomputation whenever a small part changes.

The immutable revision model allows rendering to reuse unchanged fragments.

For example:

Module
  Function A unchanged
  Function B changed
  Function C unchanged

A renderer may reuse cached representations for Function A and Function C while recomputing only the affected portion of Function B and the minimum enclosing layout context.

The conceptual cache key should use exact immutable inputs rather than mutable paths or global snapshot identity.

For example:

(revision, style revision, renderer version)
    -> render intermediate

Some final layouts depend on surrounding width or indentation. In such cases the reusable cache value may be an intermediate layout representation rather than final text.

The Level 1 requirement is not a particular pretty-print algorithm.

It is:

Projection architecture must permit reuse at semantic boundaries and must not require global invalidation for unrelated local changes.

docs.title: 10. Persistent Projection Records
docs.text:
Editable external projections need persistent synchronization metadata.

Conceptually, a projection record identifies:

  • what semantic scope is projected;
  • what snapshot or exact revisions formed its synchronization base;
  • the projection kind;
  • the style revision;
  • the renderer version;
  • the external location, if any;
  • the exact output Scriberig last considered synchronized;
  • enough metadata to detect external modification.

For a file projection this may include a path and a hash of the last rendered file.

The exact schema is a lower-level concern.

The Level 1 requirement is:

Scriberig must retain enough information to distinguish its last synchronized projection from both current canonical state and current externally edited state.

This is necessary for correct three-way reconciliation.

Figure 3 is a conceptual schema, not a database table prescription. What matters at this level is that the synchronization record connects an exact semantic base to an exact external representation and records every input needed to reproduce or safely compare that representation.

Figure 3 — An editable projection record remembers enough exact state to reproduce output, detect drift, and support later reconciliation.

docs.title: 11. External Files Remain Normal Files
docs.text:
Although source files are projections rather than canonical storage, Scriberig must preserve ordinary filesystem workflows.

Users may:

  • open files with their preferred editor;
  • modify files with command-line tools;
  • run formatters;
  • move files;
  • use IDE refactoring tools;
  • switch Git branches;
  • generate files with external programs;
  • stop using Scriberig temporarily and continue editing.

The system must not require hidden identifiers embedded into every source file merely to maintain internal object identity.

A projected repository should remain understandable and usable by ordinary tools to the greatest extent allowed by the domain.

Scriberig therefore treats filesystem changes as external observations that may need semantic import.

This gives the system an intentional asymmetry:

canonical state -> projection

external projection edit -> semantic reconciliation -> canonical change

The filesystem is a human interoperability surface, not the final authority.

docs.title: 12. Editing a Projection Produces a Candidate Semantic State
docs.text:
When an editable projection changes externally, Scriberig should not directly replace canonical data with new parsed data.

The basic flow is:

last synchronized projection
          |
          v
external edit
          |
          v
parse edited projection
          |
          v
candidate semantic representation
          |
          v
reconcile with canonical knowledge
          |
          v
semantic migration
          |
          v
new snapshot

Parsing answers:

What semantic structure can be recovered from the edited representation?

Reconciliation answers:

How does that recovered structure correspond to the entities and revisions already known to Scriberig?

These are separate problems.

A parser may produce a structurally correct candidate graph without knowing which existing entity each candidate node should correspond to.

Figure 4 shows the complete round trip. The critical point is that an external edit passes through parsing, identity reconciliation, migration, and validation before it becomes canonical; after commit, Scriberig renders again so the external artifact once more has a known synchronization base.

Figure 4 — Bidirectional editing is a controlled semantic round trip, not direct replacement of the database with edited bytes.

docs.title: 13. Reconciliation Preserves Conceptual Identity Where Justified
docs.text:
Because Scriberig separates stable entity identity from immutable revisions, external editing needs to determine continuity.

Suppose the canonical state contains:

Paragraph P
revision R1:
"Sessions form a tree."

The user edits the projection to:

"Sessions form a persistent tree."

The usual interpretation is not:

delete P
create unrelated paragraph Q

It is:

P: R1 -> R2

The paragraph entity survives; its revision changes.

Similarly, inserting another paragraph before P should not change P merely because its textual position moved.

Reconciliation should therefore use semantic and structural evidence to preserve entity continuity when justified.

Possible evidence may include:

  • exact unchanged content;
  • semantic type;
  • structural role;
  • neighboring entities;
  • collection order;
  • parent context;
  • names or signatures;
  • similarity of content;
  • domain-specific identity rules;
  • explicit metadata when a format naturally provides it.

The exact matching algorithm belongs in domain-specific lower-level design.

Figure 5 illustrates the intended identity behavior. A modified paragraph normally keeps its stable entity and receives a new immutable revision, an inserted block gets a new entity, and an unchanged paragraph is reused exactly; position helps matching but does not define identity.

Figure 5 — Reconciliation preserves conceptual continuity where evidence supports it instead of treating every edited block as an unrelated new object.

docs.title: 14. Reconciliation Must Not Pretend Certainty
docs.text:
Some external edits are ambiguous.

For example, if two identical paragraphs exist and one is modified, positional and contextual information may be sufficient to infer which entity changed, or it may not.

A code transformation may resemble either:

  • an update to one function;
  • deletion plus insertion;
  • extraction into another function;
  • a move followed by modification.

The system must not silently invent lineage when confidence is insufficient.

Ambiguous cases should result in one of:

  • a conservative generic migration;
  • explicit conflict or ambiguity information;
  • user choice;
  • agent-assisted interpretation when permitted;
  • creation of new entities rather than unsupported continuity claims.

Incorrect stable identity is more damaging than creating a new entity when continuity cannot be established safely.

docs.title: 15. Content Changes and Structural Changes Must Remain Distinct
docs.text:
Projection reconciliation should preserve the distinction defined by the storage model.

Example content change:

Paragraph P
R1: "Files are projections."
R2: "Files are editable projections."

The containing section may still contain the same entity P and therefore may not require a structural revision.

Example structural change:

Section S
before: [P1, P2]
after:  [P1, P3, P2]

The section's child collection changed.

This distinction matters because it:

  • minimizes revision churn;
  • improves semantic diffs;
  • improves cache reuse;
  • makes history easier to understand;
  • helps agents reason about the effect of changes.

Textual diff alone cannot reliably preserve this distinction.

docs.title: 16. Formatting-Only Changes Are Not Semantic Changes
docs.text:
A central benefit of separating semantic state from projection style is that formatting-only edits need not create semantic history.

For example, a user may change:

foo(a,b,c)

to:

foo(a, b, c)

If the domain parser determines that both projections describe the same canonical syntax and the difference belongs entirely to presentation, then canonical semantic state does not change.

Scriberig may choose to:

  • recognize the edit as style information;
  • update a user or projection style;
  • normalize the projection back to the configured style;
  • preserve selected formatting hints outside semantic identity;
  • report that no semantic migration occurred.

The exact policy may differ by domain.

The invariant is:

Presentation-only differences must not be mistaken for semantic knowledge changes merely because textual bytes differ.

docs.title: 17. Canonical Syntax May Still Include Author-Significant Form
docs.text:
Formatting independence does not mean that every syntactic difference is irrelevant.

For source code especially, some choices belong to canonical syntax even when multiple forms compile to similar behavior.

Examples may include:

  • expression structure;
  • control-flow construct choice;
  • macro invocation syntax;
  • attributes;
  • comments with semantic or explanatory purpose;
  • chosen module structure;
  • author-visible syntactic organization.

A domain adapter must define the boundary between:

canonical syntax/meaning

and:

projection formatting

That boundary is domain-specific but must be explicit.

Scriberig should prefer preserving meaningful author intent rather than aggressively normalizing programs into a compiler-oriented intermediate representation.

docs.title: 18. Three-Way Reconciliation Is the Normal Concurrency Model
docs.text:
An external projection may be edited while canonical state also changes independently.

Therefore reconciliation cannot assume that the edited file was based on the current snapshot.

The system should retain three conceptual states:

B = synchronization base
D = current canonical database state
F = current externally edited projection

Conceptually:

      B
     / \
    D   F

The task is not simply to replace D with F.

It is to understand both changes relative to B and combine them semantically where possible.

This is analogous to three-way version-control merging, but the comparison happens through domain semantics rather than only through lines.

If database-side and external edits affect disjoint semantic entities, they should normally merge automatically.

If both affect the same semantic state incompatibly, the system should produce a structured conflict.

Figure 6 shows why the synchronization base must be retained. Current database state D and externally edited state F are both interpreted relative to the same base B; compatible semantic changes combine into a migration and new snapshot, while incompatible changes remain explicit structured conflicts rather than one side silently overwriting the other.

Figure 6 — Three-way semantic reconciliation combines independent changes and preserves conflicts when both sides changed the same meaning incompatibly.

docs.title: 19. Conflicts Are Semantic Objects, Not Error Strings
docs.text:
A reconciliation conflict should preserve enough structured information for a human, agent, UI, CLI, or API client to inspect and resolve it.

A conflict may identify:

  • the synchronization base;
  • the current canonical revision;
  • the candidate imported revision;
  • the affected entity or relation;
  • the conflicting semantic operations;
  • available alternatives;
  • domain-specific diagnostics;
  • provenance of each side.

Different interfaces may render the same conflict differently.

For example:

CLI -> concise textual conflict
Web -> interactive semantic diff
Agent -> structured conflict tool result
API -> typed conflict object

The conflict itself should not be reduced to one presentation.

docs.title: 20. Successful Reconciliation Produces a Migration
docs.text:
External editing is one source of migrations, not a special mutation mechanism.

After reconciliation succeeds:

external edit
   -> semantic operations
   -> migration
   -> validation
   -> new snapshot

The migration provides provenance and lineage between old and new canonical state.

This is the same conceptual path used by:

  • a web editor;
  • a TUI edit;
  • an API client;
  • an agent;
  • a semantic refactoring command;
  • a merge operation.

There should not be one mutation model for users and another for agents.

All canonical writes should converge on semantic operations, migrations, validation, and snapshot creation.

docs.title: 21. Re-Rendering Establishes the New Synchronization Point
docs.text:
After an externally edited projection has been successfully reconciled and committed, Scriberig should be able to render the resulting canonical state again.

That rendering becomes the new synchronized projection baseline.

Conceptually:

external edit
    |
    v
semantic migration
    |
    v
new canonical snapshot
    |
    v
canonical render
    |
    v
new synchronization base

This step is important even if the resulting text is visually similar to the user's edit.

It makes ownership clear:

Once imported, the semantic state is authoritative and the external representation is again a projection of that state.

If configured style differs from the user's temporary formatting, the file may be normalized during this render.

The system should make such behavior predictable and domain-configurable.

docs.title: 22. Projection Ownership Must Be Explicit
docs.text:
Not every file found in a project should automatically be rewritten by Scriberig.

A projection must have an ownership/synchronization relationship that is explicit enough to answer:

  • Is Scriberig responsible for rendering this artifact?
  • May external edits be imported?
  • Is this artifact read-only?
  • What semantic scope does it represent?
  • Which style applies?
  • What was the last synchronization base?

This prevents accidental capture of unrelated files and allows mixed projects where only some artifacts are managed projections.

A project may contain:

managed editable projections
managed read-only generated projections
unmanaged ordinary files
external artifacts imported as knowledge

These categories must not be conflated.

docs.title: 23. Renames and Moves Are Projection Changes Unless Semantics Say Otherwise
docs.text:
A semantic entity's identity should not normally depend on its projected filesystem path.

Moving a function, document, or module projection may change layout or containment metadata without changing the underlying conceptual entities.

For example:

src/foo.rs

moving to:

src/network/foo.rs

must not automatically imply that every contained function became a new conceptual function.

However, some programming languages assign semantic meaning to file/module placement.

Therefore the rule is:

Projection location is separate from semantic identity, except where a domain schema explicitly models location as semantically significant.

Domain adapters are responsible for expressing those cases.

docs.title: 24. Source Code Projections
docs.text:
For source code, the semantic representation should preserve author-significant syntax while formatting remains a projection concern.

Conceptually:

canonical syntax/semantic graph
        |
        +-- style A -> source projection A
        |
        +-- style B -> source projection B

Users remain free to edit the generated source file using ordinary tools.

On import:

source text
    -> parser
    -> candidate syntax graph
    -> entity matching
    -> semantic migration

Source-code projection adapters should not use line numbers as primary identity.

Line numbers are useful presentation coordinates but are unstable semantic handles.

Stable entities and exact revisions should remain the primary internal references.

Compiler-derived facts such as symbol resolution, types, call graphs, and diagnostics may participate in reconciliation or validation but remain derived knowledge unless a domain design explicitly says otherwise.

docs.title: 25. Markdown and Document Projections
docs.text:
Markdown is a particularly suitable first editable projection because its semantic structure maps naturally to knowledge objects such as:

  • sections;
  • headings;
  • paragraphs;
  • lists;
  • list items;
  • tables;
  • rows;
  • cells;
  • code blocks;
  • links;
  • quotations.

The Markdown file should remain normal readable Markdown without requiring hidden database IDs in every paragraph.

External edits are reconciled through structure and content.

For example:

old:
Section S -> [P1, P2]

edited projection:
Section S -> [P1 changed, P3 inserted, P2 unchanged]

The preferred semantic interpretation is:

P1 receives a new revision
P3 is created
P2 is reused
Section S receives a structural revision because its child collection changed

This demonstrates the general bidirectional model without requiring source-code compiler semantics.

docs.title: 26. PDF and Other Less-Editable Formats
docs.text:
Not every projection must support arbitrary round-trip editing.

A PDF may be:

  • an external artifact from which semantic knowledge is extracted;
  • a generated read-only projection of canonical knowledge;
  • a visual view with annotations represented separately as semantic entities.

The presence of a parser does not imply that a format is suitable for lossless bidirectional editing.

Adapters should explicitly declare their capabilities.

For example:

renderable
parseable
editable
round-trip capable
structure preserving
style preserving

Scriberig should prefer an honest limited adapter over pretending that a lossy format has a reliable reverse mapping.

docs.title: 27. Sessions and Agent Context Are Projections Too
docs.text:
The same projection model applies to sessions.

A canonical session may be stored as structured entities such as:

  • goals;
  • branches;
  • turns;
  • tool invocations;
  • tool results;
  • decisions;
  • summaries;
  • tasks;
  • artifact references.

A human transcript is one projection:

session graph + chat style -> chronological conversation

An agent context is another:

session graph + context policy -> compact working context

The agent context may deliberately omit completed branch bodies while including their short descriptions and outcomes.

That omission does not delete session knowledge.

It is merely a projection optimized for limited model context.

This reinforces the architectural rule that views should be tailored to consumers without changing canonical knowledge.

docs.title: 28. User Interfaces Are Projection Clients
docs.text:
The web editor, TUI, CLI, and third-party applications should all operate on the same semantic state and operation model.

A browser may show:

  • raw database entities and relations;
  • domain-oriented trees;
  • rich document editors;
  • source-code views;
  • semantic diffs;
  • migration history;
  • session branches;
  • agent activity.

These are projections and interactions over shared canonical state.

A UI edit should create the same kind of semantic migration that would result from an equivalent external file edit.

The integrated Scriberig editor must not rely on private mutation semantics unavailable to third-party clients.

This helps keep reusable libraries, CLI, API, agent tools, and the reference web application aligned.

docs.title: 29. Agents Use Semantic Editing Rather Than Projection Mutation
docs.text:
Agents should normally operate directly on semantic capabilities rather than editing source text blindly.

For example, an agent may request operations such as:

replace paragraph
insert section
rename symbol
replace expression
move code group

These operations create candidate semantic migrations.

The system may then render affected projections.

An agent can still inspect a source projection when textual form matters, but projection bytes should not become the primary mutation interface merely because they are familiar.

This keeps agent work aligned with stable entities, exact revisions, semantic diffs, validation, and branch-based workflows.

docs.title: 30. Projection Reconciliation Must Be Domain-Aware but Architecturally Uniform
docs.text:
Markdown, Rust, PDFs, sessions, and future domains require different parsers and semantic matching rules.

The framework should nevertheless preserve one common lifecycle:

render
observe external state
parse
build candidate semantic representation
reconcile
produce semantic operations
validate
commit migration
render again

Domain adapters specialize the middle of that flow.

They define:

  • canonical semantic boundaries;
  • parse behavior;
  • rendering behavior;
  • style capabilities;
  • identity matching evidence;
  • structural equivalence;
  • formatting equivalence;
  • conflict semantics;
  • validation rules;
  • round-trip guarantees.

The surrounding projection system should remain domain-independent.

docs.title: 31. Projection Adapters Must Declare Loss and Guarantees
docs.text:
A projection may not contain every fact present in canonical state.

For example, an agent context intentionally contains only a subset of a session.

A Markdown file may not encode every piece of provenance attached to its semantic entities.

A rendered source file may omit derived analysis.

Therefore adapters should distinguish between:

information represented by the projection
information preserved externally
information recoverable on parse
information intentionally omitted

Bidirectional editing is safe only when the adapter understands what can and cannot be reconstructed.

The system must not assume that parsing a projection recreates the whole canonical universe.

Reconciliation occurs against existing canonical state precisely so omitted knowledge can remain intact.

docs.title: 32. Reconciliation Should Preserve Unrepresented Knowledge
docs.text:
Suppose a paragraph has canonical relationships to:

  • a decision;
  • provenance metadata;
  • an agent summary;
  • a source citation.

A Markdown projection may contain only the paragraph text.

Editing that text must not silently delete the relationships that the projection cannot represent.

The imported candidate representation describes only the semantic dimensions governed by that projection.

Reconciliation must therefore modify the projected semantic surface while preserving unrelated canonical knowledge unless the edit explicitly changes it.

This is a major difference between:

replace database from parsed file

and:

reconcile a partial external projection with existing semantic state

The second is the required model.

docs.title: 33. Validation Happens Before Promotion
docs.text:
Successfully parsing and reconciling an edit does not necessarily mean the resulting semantic state is valid.

Before promoting a migration to the intended canonical branch or root, the system may apply domain validation such as:

  • schema validation;
  • syntax validation;
  • type checking;
  • compiler checks;
  • linting;
  • tests;
  • project invariants;
  • projection round-trip checks.

Validation results should be structured derived knowledge with exact dependencies.

The projection system should be able to report failure without destroying either the external user edit or the previous valid canonical state.

Immutable snapshots and migration branches make this natural.

docs.title: 34. Failed Imports Must Be Recoverable
docs.text:
External files are controlled by users and other programs. They may temporarily contain invalid or incomplete state.

For example, while typing, a source file may not parse.

The system must not interpret every temporary invalid state as corruption of canonical knowledge.

A failed import should preserve:

  • the last valid canonical snapshot;
  • the last synchronized projection base;
  • the externally observed content or enough information to retry;
  • diagnostics explaining why import could not complete.

When the file becomes valid again, reconciliation can resume from the correct base.

This is necessary for normal editor workflows where files frequently pass through transient invalid states.

docs.title: 35. Synchronization Must Avoid Feedback Loops
docs.text:
Rendering a projection may itself trigger filesystem or UI change notifications.

Those notifications must not be mistaken for independent external edits.

Conceptually, the projection system must distinguish:

change produced by Scriberig rendering

from:

change produced independently by a user or external tool

The mechanism is a lower-level concern, but the architectural invariant is important:

Rendering and observation must converge to a stable synchronized state rather than repeatedly re-importing Scriberig's own output.

Projection hashes, operation identities, synchronization records, or equivalent mechanisms may be used to establish this distinction.

docs.title: 36. Projection History and Semantic History Are Related but Different
docs.text:
Canonical migrations describe semantic history.

Projection changes may include additional non-semantic events such as:

  • formatting changes;
  • style changes;
  • path moves;
  • regeneration;
  • transient invalid edits;
  • local presentation settings.

Not every projection event belongs in canonical semantic history.

The system may retain projection operation history for diagnostics or auditing, but it must preserve the distinction between:

knowledge changed

and:

representation changed

This distinction is essential for meaningful version history.

docs.title: 37. Projection Diff and Semantic Diff Serve Different Purposes
docs.text:
A textual or visual projection diff answers:

How did this representation change?

A semantic diff answers:

How did canonical knowledge change?

Both are useful.

For example, a source formatter may produce a large textual diff and an empty semantic diff.

A semantic refactoring may produce a small high-level semantic diff but touch many rendered lines.

Scriberig should support both views without confusing them.

The semantic diff is the primary description of canonical change.

Projection diffs remain valuable for interoperability, review, debugging, and user familiarity.

docs.title: 38. Projection Configuration Is Knowledge
docs.text:
Projection definitions and styles may themselves be stored in the universal knowledge system.

Examples include:

  • which semantic module maps to which path;
  • which style a user prefers;
  • which projection format is active;
  • whether an artifact is editable or read-only;
  • which context policy an agent session uses.

These configuration entities benefit from the same identity, revisions, snapshots, provenance, branching, and history as other knowledge.

However, derived runtime synchronization state may remain outside canonical knowledge when it is purely operational and rebuildable.

The distinction should follow the general rule:

User-meaningful configuration belongs to knowledge; disposable acceleration and observation state belongs to derived/runtime storage.

docs.title: 39. The Projection System Must Be Usable Without Agents
docs.text:
Projection, rendering, parsing, and reconciliation are platform capabilities.

A consumer may use Scriberig purely as:

  • a semantic document store with editable Markdown files;
  • a structured source-code database;
  • a formatter-independent code repository;
  • a bidirectional document conversion system;
  • a semantic synchronization engine;
  • a database-backed editor platform.

Therefore projection libraries must not depend on model providers, prompts, agent sessions, or agent-specific tool protocols.

Agents consume projection and semantic APIs like any other client.

This keeps the platform reusable and allows the agent system to evolve independently.

docs.title: 40. Core Invariants
docs.text:
All lower-level projection and editing designs must preserve the following invariants.

  1. Canonical knowledge is stored independently from its projections.
  2. A projection is derived from explicit semantic state and rendering inputs.
  3. Formatting style is separate from semantic content unless a domain explicitly defines otherwise.
  4. Styles and projection configuration may have normal stable identities and immutable revisions.
  5. Rendering should be deterministic over declared inputs.
  6. Editable projections require an explicit reverse mapping through parse and reconciliation.
  7. Parsing an edited projection creates a candidate representation; it does not directly replace canonical state.
  8. Reconciliation preserves stable entity identity only when continuity is justified.
  9. Ambiguous identity must not be silently invented.
  10. Content changes and structural changes remain distinct.
  11. Formatting-only changes should not create semantic history.
  12. Unrepresented canonical knowledge must survive edits to partial projections.
  13. External edits become semantic migrations rather than privileged direct writes.
  14. Web, CLI, TUI, API, and agent edits converge on the same migration model.
  15. Concurrent canonical and external changes use a three-way reconciliation model.
  16. Conflicts are structured semantic data, not only textual error messages.
  17. Failed imports preserve the last valid canonical state and remain recoverable.
  18. Re-rendering after successful reconciliation establishes a new synchronization base.
  19. Projection paths and visual layout do not define semantic identity unless a domain explicitly makes them semantic.
  20. Fine-grained render caches depend on exact local immutable inputs rather than global snapshot identity.
  21. Domain adapters declare their round-trip guarantees and information loss honestly.
  22. Projection infrastructure remains useful without the agent runtime.

docs.title: 41. Decisions Deferred to Lower-Level Design
docs.text:
This document does not decide:

  • filesystem watcher implementation;
  • parser libraries;
  • formatter libraries;
  • exact pretty-print representation;
  • projection database tables;
  • synchronization record schema;
  • reconciliation scoring algorithms;
  • confidence thresholds;
  • exact conflict object schema;
  • editor autosave behavior;
  • debounce intervals;
  • file-locking policy;
  • HTTP endpoints;
  • Rust traits;
  • TypeScript interfaces;
  • web component APIs;
  • source-language-specific AST structure;
  • exact style properties;
  • storage format for cached fragments.

Those decisions should be derived from the invariants in this document and specified in Level 2 and Level 3 designs.

docs.title: 42. Summary
docs.text:
Scriberig treats files, transcripts, agent contexts, and user-interface views as projections of one semantic knowledge system.

The canonical database does not compete with normal human workflows. Instead, Scriberig renders ordinary representations that humans and tools can use, then interprets supported external edits back into semantic migrations.

The fundamental cycle is:

canonical semantic state
        |
        v
      render
        |
        v
    projection
        |
        v
 human or external edit
        |
        v
       parse
        |
        v
candidate semantic structure
        |
        v
    reconcile
        |
        v
semantic migration
        |
        v
validation and new snapshot
        |
        v
      render

Styles control representation without redefining semantic identity.

Stable entities preserve conceptual continuity across external edits. Immutable revisions preserve exact historical state. Snapshot identity provides whole-world consistency. Reconciliation connects edited external representations back to those concepts without requiring hidden IDs in ordinary files.

This model allows Scriberig to combine a database-first semantic architecture with ordinary source files, Markdown editors, web interfaces, external tools, and agents without making any one representation the permanent source of truth.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Scriberig uses one universal knowledge model, but useful systems are built from domains with their own semantics.

Markdown has sections, paragraphs, lists, tables, links, and code blocks. Source code has modules, functions, parameters, statements, expressions, comments, attributes, and language-specific syntax. PDFs have pages, text regions, tables, figures, annotations, and layout. Sessions have branches, turns, goals, decisions, tool invocations, and results.

These domains must not become independent storage systems.

They specialize the universal knowledge model through schemas, adapters, projections, validation, semantic operations, descriptions, and derived analysis.

The central rule is:

A domain defines meaning and behavior over the universal knowledge model. An adapter translates between that meaning and external representations or tools without creating a second source of truth.

This document defines the architectural role of domains and adapters, the boundary between canonical and derived information, and the rules that domain implementations must preserve.

It intentionally does not prescribe Rust traits, parser libraries, compiler APIs, SQL layouts, HTTP endpoints, or concrete UI components. Those belong in lower-level designs.

docs.title: 2. Design Goals
docs.text: Domain modeling must satisfy the following goals.

docs.title: 2.1 Preserve one universal substrate
docs.text:
A new domain must not require a new persistence architecture.

Markdown, Rust, PDFs, sessions, and future domains should all use the same concepts for:

  • entities;
  • revisions;
  • snapshots;
  • typed properties;
  • relations;
  • collections;
  • migrations;
  • provenance;
  • descriptions;
  • derived knowledge;
  • querying;
  • history;
  • branching;
  • merging.

The domain defines vocabulary and constraints. It does not replace the substrate.

docs.title: 2.2 Preserve domain meaning
docs.text:
Universality must not flatten important distinctions.

A Rust expression is not merely text. A Markdown table row is not merely a list of strings. A PDF table cell may have extraction uncertainty and page geometry. A session branch has purpose, outcome, and provenance that differ from document containment.

Each domain must be able to preserve the choices that matter to its users and tools.

docs.title: 2.3 Support progressive disclosure
docs.text:
Domains must expose useful semantic boundaries that let consumers move from coarse structure to fine detail.

A consumer should be able to inspect a document before paragraphs, a function before expressions, a PDF before regions, and a session before turns.

The canonical model should therefore preserve or derive meaningful navigation units rather than forcing every consumer to traverse raw low-level syntax.

docs.title: 2.4 Separate canonical knowledge from derived analysis
docs.text:
A parser, compiler, OCR system, static analyzer, model, renderer, or external service may produce valuable information.

That information should be storable and queryable, but it must not silently become canonical knowledge merely because it exists in the same database.

docs.title: 2.5 Support ordinary external tools
docs.text:
A domain adapter should make Scriberig interoperable with the existing tools of that domain whenever practical.

Examples include:

  • normal Markdown editors;
  • source-code editors and formatters;
  • compilers and language servers;
  • PDF viewers and extraction tools;
  • browser applications;
  • third-party API clients.

docs.title: 2.6 Remain useful without agents
docs.text:
Domain schemas, parsing, rendering, querying, reconciliation, and analysis must not depend on an agent runtime.

Agents are consumers of domain capabilities, not a prerequisite for them.

docs.title: 3. Domain Specialization
docs.text:
A domain specializes the universal model by defining a coherent vocabulary and rules over it.

The key point is that all domains share the same persistence, identity, history, graph, query, migration, and provenance foundations. A language specialization such as Rust may refine the source-code domain further, but it still does not introduce a separate knowledge system.

Figure 1. Domain specialization over one universal knowledge substrate.

The reader should notice that specialization happens upward: the universal layer supplies generic knowledge mechanics, while each domain supplies its own vocabulary and constraints. Source code is itself a domain family, allowing Rust, TypeScript, and future languages to share broad concepts without flattening their language-specific syntax.

A domain may define:

  • entity types;
  • property types;
  • relation types;
  • collection semantics;
  • canonical structure;
  • validation rules;
  • semantic operations;
  • navigation summaries;
  • descriptions;
  • projection kinds;
  • reconciliation rules;
  • derived analyses;
  • domain-specific queries;
  • domain-specific commands;
  • domain-specific UI views.

The universal store does not need hard-coded knowledge of these concepts.

For example, the store does not need to understand that a Rust match expression has arms or that a Markdown table contains rows. Those meanings belong to domain schemas and adapters.

docs.title: 4. Domain Schemas and Adapters Are Different
docs.text:
A schema and an adapter have related but distinct responsibilities.

A schema defines what knowledge means once it is inside Scriberig. An adapter connects that knowledge to some external representation, tool, parser, compiler, or environment.

Figure 2. Schema and adapter responsibilities are intentionally separate.

The important boundary is that schemas define meaning inside the knowledge system, while adapters translate to and from external systems. A domain may have several adapters, and a schema may exist even when there is no file format at all. The universal store remains unaware of Markdown parsing, Rust compiler APIs, PDF extraction, or session rendering.

A schema may define:

  • entity and property types;
  • relation types and valid endpoints;
  • ordered and unordered collection semantics;
  • required and optional structure;
  • canonical versus derived fields;
  • validation rules;
  • supported projections;
  • semantic operations;
  • schema version.

An adapter may provide some or all of:

  • parsing;
  • importing;
  • canonicalization;
  • rendering;
  • reconciliation;
  • validation;
  • analysis;
  • domain-specific queries;
  • semantic operations;
  • descriptions;
  • external coordinate mapping.

Not every adapter needs every capability.

For a programming language, separate adapters may eventually connect to source syntax, formatting, compiler analysis, language-server analysis, test execution, and package metadata. For PDFs, different extractors may coexist with different quality, speed, licensing, or platform requirements.

Adapters must operate through public knowledge-model operations rather than bypassing the model with domain-specific persistence tables that become independent sources of truth.

Domain-specific indexes are allowed, but they must be rebuildable or explicitly classified as canonical domain state.

docs.title: 5. Canonical, Derived, Projection-Only, and External Knowledge
docs.text:
Every important field or relation in a domain must have a clear authority class.

Canonical knowledge is the state that participates in snapshots, semantic history, branching, merging, and semantic editing. Derived knowledge is computed from canonical knowledge or external evidence and must retain provenance and dependency information. Projection-only information affects representation but not normally semantic identity. External evidence preserves source artifacts or observations independently from interpretations made from them.

Figure 3. Domain information is classified by authority and purpose.

The reader should notice that all four classes may coexist in the same database without having equal authority. A compiler fact can be queryable without becoming canonical source syntax; a PDF extraction can be useful without being treated as identical to the original PDF bytes; a formatting choice can affect a rendered file without changing the program's semantic revision.

docs.title: 5.1 Canonical does not mean minimal
docs.text:
Canonical state should not be reduced to the smallest representation that happens to preserve execution or rendering today.

If an author made a meaningful syntactic or structural choice, the domain should normally preserve it.

For example, two source constructs that currently compile to equivalent behavior may still represent different chosen syntax and should not automatically collapse to the same canonical state.

docs.title: 5.2 Canonical does not mean exact bytes
docs.text:
Presentation details that do not carry domain meaning should not automatically become canonical.

Formatting, line wrapping, indentation width, table alignment spacing, and similar choices may belong to projection style rather than semantic identity.

The domain owns this distinction.

docs.title: 5.3 Derived knowledge records its dependencies
docs.text:
Examples of derived knowledge include:

  • symbol resolution;
  • inferred types;
  • call, control-flow, and data-flow graphs;
  • compiler and lint diagnostics;
  • macro expansion;
  • document summaries and topic labels;
  • PDF text extraction and table detection;
  • OCR results and reading order;
  • branch summaries and relevance indexes;
  • model-generated descriptions.

A derived result should identify exact inputs, producer, configuration, and profile whenever those affect the result.

If the inputs and producer configuration remain unchanged, the result may be reused. If they change, the result may need recomputation even though the conceptual entity identity remains stable.

docs.title: 6. Adapter Boundaries and Dependency Direction
docs.text:
Adapters should have narrow, explicit boundaries.

The dependency direction is always from domain-specific integration toward the universal platform:

  1. external format or tool;
  2. adapter;
  3. domain schema;
  4. universal graph and knowledge model;
  5. universal persistence.

Higher layers depend on lower layers. Lower layers do not call back into specific domains.

This keeps the universal store reusable for applications that never install a particular adapter and allows smaller deployments to install only the domains they need.

Multiple adapters may serve the same schema. Derived results therefore identify the adapter or producer that created them when that identity affects interpretation.

docs.title: 7. Domain Composition and Cross-Domain Relations
docs.text:
Real knowledge frequently crosses domain boundaries.

A Markdown document may contain a code block. A PDF may contain a source-code excerpt. A session branch may reference a function, paragraph, PDF page, migration, or test result. A source-code comment may link to a design decision.

These relationships should use the same universal graph machinery rather than forcing domains into isolated silos.

Figure 4. Cross-domain relations connect knowledge without transferring ownership.

The distinction to notice is between containment and reference. A Markdown document can own a code block while that code block references a source function; the document does not thereby own the function. A session branch can touch a function without copying it. A decision can be supported by a PDF page without absorbing the PDF content into the decision.

Examples include:

SessionBranch --touches--> Function
Decision --supported_by--> PDFPage
MarkdownCodeBlock --represents--> FunctionRevision
Comment --references--> Decision
Migration --changes--> Paragraph
Migration --changes--> Function

Cross-domain links must not require either domain to copy the other's content or force unrelated revisions to churn.

docs.title: 8. Markdown and Structured Documents
docs.text:
Markdown is the first recommended document-domain specialization because it has meaningful structure while remaining easy to inspect and edit with ordinary tools.

A Markdown model should support semantic entities such as:

MarkdownDocument
Section
Heading
Paragraph
List
ListItem
Table
TableRow
TableCell
CodeBlock
QuoteBlock
Link
ImageReference
InlineContent

The exact set may evolve, but several principles are architectural.

docs.title: 8.1 Sections are semantic navigation units
docs.text: A document should expose top-level sections before paragraphs. Nested sections provide natural progressive disclosure.

docs.title: 8.2 Paragraphs are independently addressable
docs.text: Paragraphs should be entities that can be inspected, described, referenced, changed, and searched without requiring a consumer to load the full file.

docs.title: 8.3 Tables expose rows and cells
docs.text: Search and editing should be able to return or modify a row or cell semantically rather than only by byte coordinates.

docs.title: 8.4 Formatting is not automatically canonical
docs.text: Whitespace, table alignment, wrapping, and similar choices normally belong to projection style unless the domain explicitly decides otherwise.

docs.title: 8.5 External editing remains supported
docs.text: A .md file is an editable projection. The Markdown adapter parses an external edit, matches semantic entities where possible, and produces semantic changes rather than treating the file as an opaque replacement blob.

docs.title: 9. Source Code as a Domain Family
docs.text:
Source code should be modeled as a family of related domains rather than one universal AST that pretends all programming languages are identical.

A language-independent code layer may define broad concepts such as:

Module
Type
Function
Parameter
CodeGroup
Statement
Expression
Comment
Symbol
Reference

Language-specific schemas then refine those concepts.

The common layer exists to enable shared operations where semantics genuinely overlap. It must not erase language-specific constructs merely to force uniformity.

docs.title: 9.1 Canonical source syntax preserves meaningful author choices
docs.text:
The canonical code model should normally include:

  • declarations;
  • parameters;
  • statements;
  • expressions;
  • patterns;
  • type syntax;
  • attributes or annotations;
  • macro invocations or equivalent language constructs;
  • intentionally preserved comments;
  • meaningful ordering;
  • other syntax that affects author intent or round-trip fidelity.

Compiler intermediate representation should not be the primary canonical program representation because it may erase syntax choices, comments, macros, and source-level structure needed by humans and agents.

docs.title: 9.2 AST nodes may have semantic identity
docs.text:
AST nodes may be normal domain entities where independent identity is useful. This enables inspection and semantic operations at function, code-group, statement, and expression levels.

Storage granularity and semantic granularity do not need to be identical. Lower-level implementations may optimize physical representation while preserving logical addressability.

docs.title: 9.3 Comments are first-class source knowledge
docs.text:
Comments should not automatically be discarded as parser trivia.

They may encode documentation, explanations, invariants, safety arguments, TODOs, warnings, directives, and user intent. A source comment is authored source content; a generated description is derived knowledge unless explicitly promoted.

docs.title: 9.4 Code groups provide a human-oriented layer
docs.text:
Raw AST depth is often too fine-grained for navigation.

A function should be able to expose conceptual groups such as validation, loading, persistence, event emission, and result construction. A CodeGroup may be based on preserved grouping, comments, blocks, blank-line boundaries, explicit editor actions, static analysis, or generated descriptions.

The domain must distinguish which aspects are canonical and which are inferred.

docs.title: 9.5 Concrete syntax is preserved where required
docs.text:
Some constructs cannot safely round-trip through a simplified AST alone. Rust macros are a representative example.

The code domain may therefore need several structural layers.

Figure 5. Source code is represented through several layers rather than one flattened AST.

The important distinction is that source-level syntax, comments, macros, and token structures needed for faithful round-trip may be canonical, while compiler semantics such as inferred types, call graphs, control flow, and diagnostics remain derived. Human-oriented code groups sit above low-level syntax to reduce the information cost of understanding code.

docs.title: 9.6 Compiler and static-analysis integration is derived
docs.text:
Compiler-derived information may depend on:

  • compiler version;
  • dependency graph;
  • enabled features;
  • build target;
  • environment;
  • configuration.

The producer and dependency set must therefore be explicit enough to support correct invalidation and reproducibility.

Compiler facts should remain queryable through the same universal graph even though they are not canonical program syntax.

docs.title: 10. PDFs and Imported Documents
docs.text:
PDFs differ from Markdown and source code because they are often imported artifacts rather than editable semantic projections.

The original PDF should be preservable as exact source evidence. An adapter may then derive structured entities such as:

PDFDocument
PDFPage
TextRegion
Paragraph
Table
TableRow
TableCell
Figure
Annotation

Some extracted structure may be certain; some may be inferred. The domain must preserve provenance and confidence where extraction is uncertain.

A consumer must be able to distinguish:

  • exact imported PDF bytes;
  • parser or extractor interpretation;
  • page geometry and source regions;
  • model-generated descriptions or summaries.

These may coexist in the same database without having equal authority.

Page coordinates remain important, but they should not replace semantic identity. A semantic paragraph can retain page and bounding-region metadata for highlighting while still being searchable, referenceable, summarizable, and related to other entities through semantic handles.

If a later extractor produces improved structure, the system should preserve provenance and lineage instead of pretending the earlier extraction never existed.

docs.title: 11. Sessions as a Domain
docs.text:
Sessions use the same universal model as documents and code.

A session-domain schema may define:

Session
Branch
Goal
HumanInput
AgentOutput
Observation
Question
Decision
ToolInvocation
ToolResult
BranchResult
Summary
Task

Typical relations include:

Session --contains--> Branch
Branch --contains--> Turn
Branch --touches--> Entity
Decision --derived_from--> Branch
ToolResult --produced_by--> ToolInvocation
BranchResult --produced_by--> Branch

A branch may have a short description, purpose, outcome, state, and touched entities so that it can be navigated without loading all contained turns.

The session domain may render several projections from the same underlying session knowledge:

  • human transcript;
  • agent context;
  • branch tree;
  • audit history;
  • decision log.

The session domain must not be tied to one model provider or one chat UI.

docs.title: 12. Progressive Disclosure and Capability Discovery
docs.text:
Each domain should define natural levels of inspection.

The agent, CLI, API server, browser, and third-party applications should not need to load complete objects by default. An inspection response should provide concise descriptions, child counts, semantic handles, and available capabilities before finer content is requested.

Figure 6. Generic clients discover domain capabilities and descend from coarse structure to fine detail.

The reader should notice that the navigation grammar stays universal while the domain hierarchy differs. A generic client can call inspect without understanding every installed domain, discover what the entity supports, and then choose a relevant relation, projection, analysis, or semantic command.

Natural hierarchies include:

Markdown:
Document -> Section -> Block -> Paragraph/Table/List -> Cell/Item/InlineContent

Code:
Project -> Module -> Function/Type -> CodeGroup -> Statement -> Expression

PDF:
Document -> Page -> Region -> Paragraph/Table/Figure -> Row/Cell

Session:
Session -> Branch -> Episode/Turn -> Message/ToolInteraction

These are views over the graph, not a requirement that the universal database be stored as one tree.

Important entities should expose concise descriptions suitable for navigation, with provenance identifying whether the description is authored, parsed, compiler-derived, statically inferred, model-generated, or imported.

Generated descriptions should normally remain derived knowledge and should not alter the canonical revision of the described entity.

docs.title: 13. Search and Semantic Handles
docs.text:
Search should return semantic domain objects whenever possible rather than only coordinates in an external representation.

Examples include:

Markdown search result
  Paragraph P
  containing Section S

Table search result
  TableRow R
  containing Table T

Code search result
  Function F
  CodeGroup G
  Statement S

PDF search result
  Paragraph P
  Page 12
  source region ...

Session search result
  Branch B
  Decision D

External coordinates such as filenames, line numbers, page numbers, and byte ranges remain useful metadata, but semantic handles should be preferred for continued interaction.

A consumer should be able to receive a semantic handle and immediately use it for later operations such as inspect, follow, diff, history, render, or a domain-specific command.

docs.title: 14. Domain Semantic Operations
docs.text:
Domains may define semantic operations that are more meaningful than generic graph edits.

Examples include:

Markdown:
  rename heading
  insert paragraph
  move section
  add table row

Code:
  rename symbol
  replace expression
  add parameter
  move statement
  extract function

Session:
  start branch
  complete branch
  promote decision
  reopen task

These operations ultimately produce ordinary revisions and universal migrations.

A domain-specific command is therefore an ergonomic and validation layer, not an alternate history mechanism.

Generic graph operations remain available where appropriate, especially for infrastructure and debugging, but normal domain users should not need to express every change as raw relation manipulation.

docs.title: 15. Validation Belongs to the Domain Boundary
docs.text:
The universal store can validate universal invariants, but domain correctness requires domain knowledge.

Examples include:

Markdown:
  structural validity

Rust:
  parse validity
  language constraints
  compiler validation

PDF:
  source-region consistency
  extractor output shape

Session:
  valid branch state transitions
  valid result references

Adapters and domain services should provide validation before changes are promoted when correctness matters.

Validation results should be stored as derived knowledge with explicit provenance rather than silently mutating canonical state.

docs.title: 16. Reconciliation Is Domain-Specific
docs.text:
Bidirectional editing requires domain knowledge.

The universal projection system can orchestrate change detection, base-projection tracking, snapshot references, conflict representation, and migration commit. Only the domain adapter can decide what an external edit means.

Figure 7. External edits become semantic migrations through domain-aware reconciliation.

The critical point is that the adapter must infer semantic continuity explicitly. External files often contain no Scriberig entity IDs, so a reconciler may use exact content equality, structural role, parent context, sibling order, names or signatures, text similarity, syntax similarity, or stable external identifiers. When continuity is uncertain, the system should create a new entity or report ambiguity rather than silently inventing identity.

For Markdown, reconciliation may match sections and paragraphs. For source code, it may match declarations and syntax subtrees. Another structured format may match rows, records, or semantic keys.

The adapter produces semantic changes rather than directly updating persistence internals.

docs.title: 17. Adapter Versioning and Schema Evolution
docs.text:
Adapters evolve independently from schemas.

A parser may improve. A PDF extractor may identify tables more accurately. A compiler integration may change. A reconciliation algorithm may gain new behavior. Derived results must therefore identify the adapter version or producer profile that created them when that version affects interpretation.

Schema evolution changes what stored domain knowledge means. It may add entity types or relations, refine validation rules, split one concept into several, introduce richer canonical structure, or deprecate old structures.

The distinction is:

schema version
  defines what stored domain knowledge means

adapter version
  defines how an external representation or tool maps to that schema

Existing history must remain interpretable.

Schema migrations are different from ordinary user-content migrations. Both should remain inspectable and reproducible.

docs.title: 18. Generic Operations and Domain Extensions
docs.text:
All domains remain reachable through the universal interaction grammar:

inspect
list
follow
find
query
diff
history
render
branch
apply
commit

Domain-specific operations extend this grammar rather than replacing it.

For example, inspecting a function may advertise parameters, code groups, references, callers, history, and source rendering. Inspecting a PDF page may advertise paragraphs, tables, figures, source image, and reading order.

The agent, CLI, API server, browser, TUI, and third-party libraries should all consume the same underlying domain capabilities.

Adapters are part of the knowledge platform, not part of the agent runtime. Markdown parsing, Rust analysis, PDF extraction, and session storage must all work without an agent model provider.

docs.title: 19. Domain UI Views
docs.text:
Domains may provide reusable UI views, but UI code is not the canonical domain model.

Examples include:

  • Markdown section browser;
  • source-code function inspector;
  • PDF page viewer;
  • session branch tree.

These views should consume the same public domain APIs available to other clients.

A full Scriberig application may compose low-level graph browsing with high-level semantic views, but neither should require privileged access to private storage internals.

The UI should be able to move between a raw universal graph view and a domain-specific semantic view without changing the underlying entity being inspected.

docs.title: 20. Future Domains and Minimal Installations
docs.text:
The architecture must support domains that were not anticipated when the core system was written.

Possible future domains include spreadsheets, notebooks, CAD or geospatial structures, database schemas, API specifications, diagrams, issue trackers, email, calendars, media transcripts, scientific datasets, and build graphs.

A new domain should ideally require:

schema
adapter(s)
projection(s)
validation
optional derived analysis
optional UI views

It should not require modification of the fundamental entity, revision, or snapshot architecture.

If adding a reasonable new domain requires changing the universal storage model, that is evidence that an architectural assumption should be re-examined.

The same modularity allows deployments to stop at different layers:

  • storage-only deployment: universal store;
  • knowledge-graph deployment: store + schemas + queries;
  • Markdown deployment: knowledge graph + Markdown domain;
  • code-analysis deployment: knowledge graph + code domain + language adapter;
  • full Scriberig deployment: multiple domains + sessions + agents + web editor.

No domain should make unrelated domains mandatory dependencies.

docs.title: 21. Domain Testing and Conformance
docs.text:
Every domain should be testable against common architectural invariants.

Important checks include:

  • canonical data round-trips without semantic loss;
  • derived data can be rebuilt;
  • provenance remains visible;
  • semantic identities survive irrelevant projection changes;
  • external edits produce migrations rather than direct mutation;
  • domain validation is applied at the domain boundary;
  • unchanged entities and revisions can be reused;
