The complete reference editor application belongs to the AGPL product layer.

Private packages should still declare their license when doing so clarifies the architectural boundary.

The implementation must not make MUI usage itself an AGPL boundary. Reusable MUI components remain part of the Apache platform unless they contain integrated product/runtime behavior.

docs.title: 6. SPDX Source Identifiers
docs.text:
The Level 1 design permits SPDX identifiers in source files where appropriate, but does not require a repository-wide source-header migration.

Therefore this design does not require adding headers to every source file.

Package metadata and complete license texts are mandatory. Source SPDX headers may be added later under a separate focused task if the repository adopts that convention.

docs.title: 7. Third-Party Notices and Attribution
docs.text:
The project must preserve notices and attribution required by third-party dependencies, assets, generated code, fonts, parsers, UI frameworks, and other distributed material.

The implementation must not invent attribution obligations where dependencies do not require them.

Use the following repository artifact when there is material that must or should be surfaced centrally:

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md

If the initial repository has no distributable third-party material requiring a notice, the file may contain a short statement that dependency-specific notices will be added as distributable dependencies are introduced, or creation may be deferred until such material exists. The implementation agent must not fabricate a list of dependencies that are not present.

Dependency license review is required when adding a new externally distributed component.

docs.title: 8. Contribution Policy
docs.text:
CONTRIBUTING.md must include a licensing section with these rules:

  • contributions to Apache-licensed components are contributed under terms compatible with Apache-2.0;
  • contributions to AGPL-covered product components are contributed under terms compatible with AGPL-3.0;
  • contributors must not add third-party material without preserving its applicable license and notices;
  • the repository does not implicitly obtain rights to commercially relicense third-party contributions beyond the licenses and contributor terms actually in force;
  • no CLA, DCO, copyright assignment, or commercial relicensing grant is implied by this document.

If the project later adopts a formal CLA, DCO, or commercial relicensing policy, that must be introduced deliberately and the contributor documentation must be updated explicitly.

docs.title: 9. Protocol Specifications, Schemas, and Fixtures
docs.text:
The Level 1 design requires public protocol specifications, schemas, and conformance fixtures to live with the reusable platform rather than only inside the AGPL reference server.

This document does not create those protocol artifacts because their content is defined by protocol designs, not by licensing policy.

When those files are created, they must live in an Apache-licensed reusable package or platform directory and must not require the AGPL product runtime merely to be consumed.

No Level 3 implementation task in this licensing stream should invent protocol semantics merely to satisfy this placement rule.

docs.title: 10. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The expected licensing dependency direction matches the architecture:

Apache reusable platform
        ^
        |
AGPL integrated product

AGPL product components may depend on Apache platform components.

Reusable Apache platform components must not depend on integrated AGPL product components.

This is an architectural rule first and a licensing clarity rule second.

An implementation agent that discovers such a reverse dependency must report it rather than hiding it with metadata changes.

docs.title: 11. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Apply this design in four focused steps.

  1. Create the repository license texts and LICENSING.md.
  2. Apply license declarations to Rust crates once their manifests exist.
  3. Apply license declarations to web/TypeScript packages once their manifests exist.
  4. Create or update contributor licensing guidance and preserve third-party notices required by dependencies that actually exist.

These steps are intentionally separable so a simple implementation agent does not have to classify the whole repository while also retrieving legal text.

docs.title: 12. Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
This design is implemented when all applicable statements below are true.

  • LICENSES/Apache-2.0.txt contains the complete Apache License 2.0 text.
  • LICENSES/AGPL-3.0.txt contains the complete GNU Affero General Public License version 3 text selected by the project.
  • LICENSING.md explains the platform/product split and points developers to package metadata for component-level licensing.
  • Every existing distributable Rust crate declares the license appropriate to its architectural responsibility.
  • Every existing distributable web package declares the license appropriate to its architectural responsibility.
  • The integrated server/runtime/editor are not accidentally labeled as permissive platform components.
  • Reusable libraries are not accidentally labeled AGPL merely because the reference product consumes them.
  • Contributor documentation preserves the two-license model without inventing relicensing rights.
  • Required third-party attribution is preserved for dependencies and assets actually present in distributed components.
  • No reusable Apache component depends on an integrated AGPL product component.

docs.title: 13. Non-Goals
docs.text:
Do not use this design to:

  • introduce a plugin registry;
  • define package publication policy;
  • define protocol semantics;
  • add a CLA or DCO;
  • promise commercial licensing;
  • choose a legal entity or copyright holder;
  • rewrite dependency licenses;
  • add speculative third-party notices;
  • make every source file carry a license header;
  • move reusable functionality into AGPL packages for licensing leverage.

Those decisions require separate designs when they become necessary.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns the persistence guarantees in design/level-1/004. persistence and storage model.md into Rust crate boundaries.

This level chooses implementation structure. It does not change the Level 1 model.

docs.title: Required crates
docs.text:
The initial persistence slice must create these workspace crates:

crates/
├── sr-core/
├── sr-store/
├── sr-store-memory/
└── sr-store-sqlite/

The dependency direction is:

sr-core
   ↑
sr-store
   ↑        ↑
sr-store-memory  sr-store-sqlite

No crate in this slice may depend on agents, sessions, Markdown, source-code adapters, the CLI, the API server, or web code.

docs.title: sr-core
docs.text:
sr-core owns universal identifiers and value types that must not depend on a backend.

Initial public concepts:

  • EntityId
  • RevisionId
  • SnapshotId
  • RootName
  • ObjectType
  • EncodingVersion

Identifiers must be strongly typed. Do not use raw String or byte arrays throughout the public API when a specific identifier type exists.

The crate may contain deterministic encoding support shared by persistence crates, but it must not contain SQLite code or storage traits.

docs.title: sr-store
docs.text:
sr-store owns the backend-independent persistence API and logical storage types.

It must define traits or equivalent interfaces for:

  • immutable revision insertion and retrieval;
  • snapshot lookup;
  • snapshot construction from a base snapshot plus changes;
  • named-root lookup and atomic promotion;
  • ancestry/history traversal needed by higher layers;
  • integrity verification hooks;
  • reachability enumeration;
  • index rebuild hooks where the backend owns physical indexes.

It also owns storage-level error types.

The public API must describe semantic persistence operations, not SQL statements, paths, pages, or table layouts.

docs.title: sr-store-memory
docs.text:
sr-store-memory implements the sr-store interfaces entirely in memory.

Its purposes are:

  • executable specification of store behavior;
  • fast unit and conformance tests;
  • deterministic testing of concurrency and root promotion;
  • a backend usable by embedding applications that do not need persistence.

It must implement the same externally visible behavior as the SQLite backend.

docs.title: sr-store-sqlite
docs.text:
sr-store-sqlite provides the first durable embedded backend.

It must hide SQLite-specific details behind sr-store interfaces.

It owns:

  • schema creation and upgrades for storage-internal tables;
  • transactions;
  • durable immutable revision storage;
  • persistent snapshot structures;
  • named roots;
  • backend indexes;
  • integrity metadata needed for recovery.

No consumer outside this crate should issue SQL against Scriberig's internal tables.

docs.title: Workspace files prescribed by this design
docs.text:
The first implementation agent must create at least:

Cargo.toml
crates/sr-core/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-core/src/lib.rs
crates/sr-store/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-store/src/lib.rs
crates/sr-store-memory/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-store-memory/src/lib.rs
crates/sr-store-sqlite/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-store-sqlite/src/lib.rs

Additional modules should be introduced only when their responsibility is clear from the other Level 2 storage designs.

docs.title: Architectural rules
docs.text:
• sr-core must remain backend-independent.
  • sr-store must remain backend-independent.
  • Backend crates depend on sr-store; sr-store never depends on a backend crate.
  • The memory and SQLite implementations must pass the same conformance tests.
  • Named roots are mutable references to immutable snapshots. Snapshots themselves are never updated in place.
  • Public persistence APIs must not assume an agent exists.

docs.title: Completion criteria
docs.text: This design is satisfied when the workspace builds with the four crates, the dependency direction is enforced, and both backend crates can implement one shared storage conformance suite without exposing backend-specific operations.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document translates design/level-1/002. universal knowledge model.md into reusable Rust model libraries.

It is intentionally limited to the domain-independent semantic vocabulary required for entities, properties, typed relations, collections, schemas, provenance, descriptions, derived knowledge, and snapshot-bound graph inspection.

This design does not own repository bootstrapping, identity generation, content addressing, snapshot-map persistence, database backends, migrations, domain parsers, projections, agents, transports, or UI.

Those concerns are defined by other design lineages and must be treated as prerequisites or later layers rather than reimplemented here.

docs.title: 2. Prerequisites and Ownership Boundaries
docs.text:
Before implementing this design, the repository-wide Rust workspace and the shared identity types must already exist.

In particular, this work consumes existing equivalents of:

EntityId
RevisionId
SnapshotId
TypeId or EntityTypeId

It must not redefine how those IDs are generated, hashed, serialized canonically, or persisted.

The repository-wide workspace design currently names the relevant crates:

scriberig-core
scriberig-schema
scriberig-graph

If prerequisite implementation work has already instantiated the same architectural crates under an equivalent established name, implementation agents must extend the existing canonical crate rather than create a duplicate crate with another prefix.

The rule is:

There is one shared core identity crate, one universal schema crate, and one universal graph crate in the workspace. This design adds model functionality to those layers; it does not fork them.

docs.title: 3. Files Prescribed by This Design
docs.text:
Within the already-established shared core crate, add the universal value/provenance modules if they do not already exist:

src/value.rs
src/provenance.rs

Within the universal schema crate, create:

src/lib.rs
src/entity.rs
src/property.rs
src/relation.rs
src/collection.rs
src/validation.rs

Within the universal graph crate, create:

src/lib.rs
src/revision.rs
src/relation.rs
src/collection.rs
src/description.rs
src/derived.rs
src/view.rs

tests/universal_model.rs

If a prescribed file already exists because another prerequisite design created the crate skeleton, modify that file instead of creating a competing module.

Do not create a new root Cargo.toml or a second core/store crate as part of this design.

docs.title: 4. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The model-layer dependency direction remains:

shared core
   ↑
   ├──────── universal schema
   │
   └──────── universal graph
                 ↑
                 └── schema definitions

The universal schema layer depends on the shared core types.

The universal graph layer depends on shared core types and schema contracts. It may also consume storage-facing traits from the established store layer where snapshot resolution requires them, but graph semantics must not become tied to one database backend.

None of these model modules may depend on:

  • an agent runtime;
  • an HTTP framework;
  • a CLI or TUI crate;
  • a UI toolkit;
  • a Markdown/Rust/PDF/session parser;
  • a concrete database driver merely to represent semantic values.

docs.title: 5.1 Universal property values
docs.text:
Add a domain-neutral property value representation capable of representing at least:

null
boolean
signed integer
unsigned integer
floating-point number
string
bytes
list of values
string-keyed record/map

This value type is for local property payloads.

Do not use it to hide semantic entity relationships that should be represented as typed relations or collections.

Do not add domain-specific variants such as RustExpression, MarkdownParagraph, PdfPage, or SessionBranch.

docs.title: 5.2 Canonical versus derived classification
docs.text:
Provide one shared classification vocabulary for distinguishing canonical semantic state from derived knowledge.

The concrete type may be named KnowledgeClass, DataClass, or another clear equivalent, but it must at least express:

Canonical
Derived

docs.title: 5.3 Provenance
docs.text:
Add reusable provenance data capable of recording:

  • origin/source kind;
  • optional producer identity;
  • exact entity/revision dependencies when known;
  • optional profile/configuration identity;
  • optional human-readable note.

Source kinds must support known categories such as user, authoritative import, parser, compiler, static analysis, agent, model-generated output, system, external tool, and migration, while remaining extensible.

Provenance records origin, not trust policy.

Do not add authorization or trust scoring to this layer.

docs.title: 6. Universal Schema Library
docs.text:
The schema library defines how domains add strong meaning to the universal graph without changing storage architecture.

It must not contain concrete production schemas for Markdown, Rust, PDF, sessions, or any other domain.

docs.title: 6.1 Entity type schemas
docs.text:
An entity type schema must support:

  • entity type identifier;
  • human-readable name;
  • optional description;
  • schema version association;
  • declared properties;
  • declared relation types;
  • declared collection types.

docs.title: 6.2 Property schemas
docs.text:
A property schema must represent:

  • property key;
  • expected value shape;
  • required versus optional;
  • canonical versus derived classification where applicable;
  • small schema-level constraints;
  • optional description.

The value-shape system should cover the universal value variants without becoming a general-purpose type language.

docs.title: 6.3 Relation schemas
docs.text:
A relation schema must represent:

  • relation type identifier;
  • semantic name;
  • permitted source entity types;
  • permitted target entity types;
  • canonical versus derived classification;
  • cardinality;
  • optional description;
  • whether reverse navigation is expected to be derived/index-backed.

Reverse edges must not be required as duplicated canonical state.

docs.title: 6.4 Collection schemas
docs.text:
Collections are modeled separately from generic relations because sequence semantics matter.

A collection schema must represent:

  • collection type identifier;
  • owner entity type;
  • permitted member entity types;
  • ordered versus unordered semantics;
  • cardinality constraints;
  • canonical versus derived classification;
  • optional description.

docs.title: 6.5 Validation contracts
docs.text:
Schema validation must return structured issues rather than plain strings.

A validation issue must contain at least:

  • severity;
  • stable machine-readable code;
  • human-readable message;
  • optional semantic location such as entity/property/relation/collection.

The schema crate must not depend on the graph crate merely to validate graph-shaped data. Define a small validation-subject/context trait using shared core types; graph revision records can implement that trait from the graph side.

Schema validation covers schema-level structure only. Parser validity, compiler validity, tests, and product policy belong elsewhere.

docs.title: 7. Universal Graph Library
docs.text:
The graph library provides immutable semantic revision records and snapshot-bound read contracts.

It must not become a persistence backend.

docs.title: 7.1 Revision record
docs.text:
A universal semantic revision record represents one exact entity state and includes, conceptually:

entity type
property values
owned canonical relation values
owned canonical collection values

It must not require:

  • mutable parent pointers;
  • database row IDs;
  • a database connection;
  • reverse-edge caches;
  • current-snapshot mutable state;
  • file paths as semantic identity.

Exact RevisionId generation remains owned by the identity/storage design.

docs.title: 7.2 Relation values
docs.text:
A relation value identifies a typed semantic relation and target entity handles.

Targets are semantic entities, not filenames or line numbers.

Derived relations such as compiler-computed call edges may be stored as derived knowledge rather than silently inserted into canonical revision payloads.

docs.title: 7.3 Collection values
docs.text:
Ordered and unordered collections must be semantically distinct.

Requirements:

  • ordered collections preserve order exactly;
  • unordered collections do not expose incidental insertion/storage order as meaning;
  • members use semantic entity handles;
  • moving a member changes collection state but does not require changing the member entity identity;
  • child entities do not require parent pointers for containment.

docs.title: 7.4 Descriptions
docs.text:
Descriptions are navigation objects that bind to an exact entity revision and contain:

  • description profile;
  • provenance;
  • textual content;
  • optional information-cost metadata.

Generated descriptions are derived knowledge by default and must not silently become canonical entity content.

docs.title: 7.5 Derived artifacts
docs.text:
A generic derived artifact must identify:

  • artifact/profile kind;
  • exact immutable input dependencies;
  • producer/configuration identity;
  • provenance;
  • result payload or result reference;
  • status/validation metadata where useful.

The exact dependency list is essential for later incremental reuse.

This design does not implement a cache.

docs.title: 7.6 Snapshot-bound graph view
docs.text:
Define a storage-independent read interface that can, conceptually:

resolve an entity to its revision in a snapshot
read a revision
inspect properties
follow owned relations
read collections
obtain reverse relations through an index/view abstraction
obtain schema information

Operations that depend on entity state must be explicitly snapshot-bound. Do not introduce ambiguous implicit-current-state APIs as the universal contract.

Universal search, history, diff, migrations, and writes are outside this design.

docs.title: 8. Canonical Versus Derived Data
docs.text:
The implementation must keep canonical and derived knowledge visibly distinct.

Canonical data participates in semantic snapshots and history.

Derived data is computed from canonical data or external evidence and records exact dependencies and provenance.

Do not simplify the model by inserting these directly into canonical revision payloads by default:

  • model-generated descriptions;
  • summaries;
  • compiler call graphs;
  • reverse indexes;
  • cached render output;
  • validation runs;
  • embeddings.

docs.title: 9. No Hard-Coded Domain Vocabulary
docs.text:
Production universal libraries must not define enums or structs whose variants hard-code domain types such as:

MarkdownSection
RustFunction
PdfPage
SessionBranch

Domain crates will provide schemas and adapters later.

Examples with Document, Section, and Paragraph are allowed inside tests and documentation only.

docs.title: 10. Conformance Tests
docs.text:
The graph library integration test tests/universal_model.rs must demonstrate the Level 1 invariants without requiring SQLite, networking, parsers, or an agent runtime.

Required scenarios:

  1. one conceptual entity can be represented at two exact revisions without changing its entity identity;
  2. one entity resolves to different revisions in two snapshots through a test/mocked view;
  3. ordered collection order is preserved and reordering changes only collection state;
  4. unordered collection semantics do not depend on insertion order;
  5. a child revision does not need a canonical parent pointer;
  6. a typed relation is validated against a test schema;
  7. invalid property/relation structure yields machine-readable validation issues;
  8. a description binds to an exact entity revision with provenance;
  9. a derived artifact exposes exact dependency revisions;
  10. domain names used by the test come from the test schema, not hard-coded production variants.

docs.title: 11. Documentation Requirements
docs.text:
Public modules and types must document semantic purpose and important exclusions.

In particular, generated API documentation should make clear:

EntityId   = conceptual continuity
RevisionId = exact immutable state
SnapshotId = exact consistent graph view

The universal-model modules consume these identities but do not redefine their generation semantics.

Documentation must also make clear that:

  • relation direction is canonical ownership/meaning, while reverse navigation may be derived;
  • ordering is a collection semantic;
  • descriptions and derived artifacts carry provenance;
  • these libraries remain useful without an agent runtime.

docs.title: 12. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This design is implemented when:

  • [ ] the existing shared core library exposes a domain-neutral property value type;
  • [ ] the existing shared core library exposes provenance and canonical/derived classification;
  • [ ] the universal schema crate defines entity/property/relation/collection schemas;
  • [ ] schema-level validation returns structured issues;
  • [ ] the universal graph crate defines storage-independent revision/relation/collection records;
  • [ ] child records do not require parent pointers;
  • [ ] ordered and unordered collections are distinct;
  • [ ] descriptions are separate derived navigation objects;
  • [ ] derived artifacts declare exact immutable dependencies;
  • [ ] a snapshot-bound storage-independent graph view exists;
  • [ ] conformance tests demonstrate the Level 1 semantics;
  • [ ] no duplicate core/workspace layer was introduced;
  • [ ] no database, parser, projection, migration, agent, transport, or UI subsystem was implemented by this work.

docs.title: 13. Work Decomposition
docs.text:
Create focused Level 3 implementation tasks in this order:

  1. extend the established shared core crate with universal values and provenance;
  2. implement the universal schema contracts;
  3. implement universal graph semantic records and snapshot-bound views;
  4. add universal-model conformance tests and public documentation.

Every implementation task must first inspect the existing workspace and reuse the canonical shared crates already established by prerequisite designs. A task must never create a second competing core/schema/graph crate merely because another design used a different provisional prefix.

docs.title: Web Workspace, Packages, and Integrated Editor
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document refines design/level-1/012. web platform and integrated editor.md into a concrete TypeScript/React workspace and file plan.

It is intentionally implementation-oriented but still architectural. It defines package boundaries, dependency directions, required public surfaces, and the initial reference-editor composition. Exact function bodies and component implementations belong in Level 3 tasks.

Read before implementing:

  1. design/level-1/010. universal query and operation model.md
  2. design/level-1/011. runtime libraries protocol and product surfaces.md
  3. design/level-1/012. web platform and integrated editor.md

The controlling invariant is:

The complete Scriberig editor must be buildable entirely from public protocol, client, model, interaction, and component packages.

docs.title: 2. Web Workspace Location
docs.text:
Create a dedicated web workspace under:

web/

The web workspace is separate from the Rust Cargo workspace but lives in the same repository.

Use pnpm workspaces for JavaScript/TypeScript package management.

Initial top-level files:

web/package.json
web/pnpm-workspace.yaml
web/tsconfig.base.json

The workspace contains reusable packages and applications:

web/
├── package.json
├── pnpm-workspace.yaml
├── tsconfig.base.json
├── packages/
│   ├── protocol/
│   ├── client/
│   ├── model/
│   ├── react/
│   ├── editor-core/
│   ├── components/
│   └── components-mui/
└── apps/
    └── scriberig/

Do not place reusable logic directly in apps/scriberig if it can live in one of the public packages.

docs.title: 3. Package Names
docs.text:
Use these package names:

@scriberig/protocol
@scriberig/client
@scriberig/model
@scriberig/react
@scriberig/editor-core
@scriberig/components
@scriberig/components-mui

The reference application package is private and uses:

@scriberig/app

All reusable packages must be publishable independently even if publication is not enabled initially.

docs.title: 4. Common Package Shape
docs.text:
Every reusable package starts with this minimum shape:

package-name/
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
├── src/
│   └── index.ts
└── test/

Additional source files should be introduced only when they correspond to a defined responsibility.

Each package must:

  • use TypeScript;
  • emit declarations when built as a library;
  • avoid importing from another package's private source paths;
  • export supported APIs through src/index.ts;
  • expose package boundaries through package exports rather than repository-relative imports.

The Level 3 tasks may add focused files below src/ as required.

docs.title: 5. Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The package dependency graph is:

@scriberig/protocol
        |
        v
@scriberig/client
        |
        v
 @scriberig/model
      /      \
     v        v
@scriberig/react   @scriberig/editor-core
      \            /
       \          /
        v        v
      reusable React UI
       /             \
      v               v
@scriberig/components   @scriberig/components-mui
             \          /
              \        /
               v      v
              @scriberig/app

The graph is conceptual; a package should depend only on what it actually imports.

Hard rules:

  • @scriberig/protocol depends on no other Scriberig web package.
  • @scriberig/client may depend on @scriberig/protocol, but not React or MUI.
  • @scriberig/model may depend on protocol and client, but not React or MUI.
  • @scriberig/editor-core may depend on protocol and model, but not React or MUI.
  • @scriberig/react may depend on protocol, client, model, and editor-core, but not MUI.
  • @scriberig/components may depend on React bindings and headless interaction packages, but not MUI.
  • @scriberig/components-mui may depend on MUI and the public reusable packages.
  • @scriberig/app may depend on all public web packages but must not import server internals or database code.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Represent the public wire contract used by browser and Node clients.

It owns TypeScript representations for public concepts such as:

  • entity, revision, and snapshot references;
  • descriptions and typed summaries;
  • relations and collections;
  • query expressions;
  • semantic diffs;
  • migrations;
  • validation results;
  • operations and operation events;
  • sessions and branches;
  • projections;
  • capability information;
  • structured errors and stale-state conditions.

docs.title: Required boundary
docs.text:
This package must not independently redesign server semantics.

The authoritative protocol definition comes from the shared runtime/protocol design. When protocol generation becomes available, generated definitions should land behind this package's public exports.

docs.title: Initial source organization
docs.text:
web/packages/protocol/src/
├── index.ts
├── ids.ts
├── objects.ts
├── query.ts
├── changes.ts
├── operations.ts
├── sessions.ts
├── projections.ts
├── capabilities.ts
└── errors.ts

If generation produces different internal files, index.ts remains the stable import boundary.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Provide a framework-independent transport client over the public protocol.

The package exposes operations equivalent to:

inspect
list
follow
query
diff
history
branch
migrate
validate
render
session operations
agent operations
operation inspection
event subscriptions

docs.title: Initial source organization
docs.text:
web/packages/client/src/
├── index.ts
├── client.ts
├── transport.ts
├── http-transport.ts
├── event-stream.ts
└── errors.ts

transport.ts defines a transport abstraction so tests and alternate deployments can provide non-HTTP implementations.

The client must not contain React hooks, view state, MUI types, or reference-editor concerns.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Coordinate client-side semantic state without becoming a second canonical database.

It owns:

  • immutable revision cache entries;
  • current snapshot awareness;
  • entity-to-current-revision resolution for loaded data;
  • relation-page caches;
  • operation records;
  • event application;
  • stale-view detection;
  • local navigation state where reusable;
  • migration preview state;
  • opened session/branch state.

docs.title: Initial source organization
docs.text:
web/packages/model/src/
├── index.ts
├── workspace-model.ts
├── revision-cache.ts
├── snapshot-state.ts
├── relation-cache.ts
├── operation-store.ts
├── event-reducer.ts
└── stale-state.ts

Canonical server state and browser-local state must be represented separately.

The model must preserve unchanged immutable revisions when a new snapshot arrives.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Provide framework-independent interaction models for semantic browsing and editing.

Initial primitives:

  • universal semantic selection;
  • relation/tree expansion;
  • semantic navigation;
  • command discovery and execution descriptors;
  • history navigation;
  • diff navigation;
  • branch navigation;
  • migration review state;
  • operation-progress coordination;
  • projection/editor coordination.

docs.title: Initial source organization
docs.text:
web/packages/editor-core/src/
├── index.ts
├── selection.ts
├── commands.ts
├── knowledge-tree.ts
├── navigation.ts
├── history.ts
├── diff.ts
├── branches.ts
├── migration-review.ts
└── projection-session.ts

This package must contain behavior and state transitions, not JSX.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Expose React bindings for client, model, and editor-core without imposing a visual design system.

Initial source organization:

web/packages/react/src/
├── index.ts
├── provider.tsx
├── use-object.ts
├── use-children.ts
├── use-snapshot.ts
├── use-operation.ts
├── use-session.ts
├── use-selection.ts
└── use-commands.ts

Bindings should subscribe to reusable model/controller state rather than reproduce state logic inside each hook.

No MUI dependency is allowed.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Provide reusable React views with minimal visual assumptions.

Initial component set:

ObjectTree
ObjectInspector
RelationBrowser
HistoryView
SemanticDiffView
MigrationPreview
SessionTree
BranchView
ValidationResults
OperationView
ProjectionHost
AgentOperationView

Initial source organization:

web/packages/components/src/
├── index.ts
├── ObjectTree.tsx
├── ObjectInspector.tsx
├── RelationBrowser.tsx
├── HistoryView.tsx
├── SemanticDiffView.tsx
├── MigrationPreview.tsx
├── SessionTree.tsx
├── BranchView.tsx
├── ValidationResults.tsx
├── OperationView.tsx
├── ProjectionHost.tsx
└── AgentOperationView.tsx

The package may expose slots, render callbacks, data attributes, and semantic class names, but must not require MUI.

Accessibility and keyboard behavior that belongs to shared interaction semantics should be implemented through editor-core and React bindings rather than duplicated per visual package.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
Provide an application-ready Material UI interpretation of Scriberig's public interaction and data model.

Initial source organization:

web/packages/components-mui/src/
├── index.ts
├── MuiObjectTree.tsx
├── MuiObjectInspector.tsx
├── MuiRelationBrowser.tsx
├── MuiHistoryView.tsx
├── MuiSemanticDiffView.tsx
├── MuiMigrationPreview.tsx
├── MuiSessionTree.tsx
├── MuiBranchView.tsx
├── MuiValidationResults.tsx
├── MuiOperationView.tsx
├── MuiProjectionHost.tsx
└── MuiAgentPanel.tsx

The MUI package may choose strong visual defaults.

It must not reimplement semantic caching, selection, command resolution, event handling, migration logic, or protocol access.

docs.title: 13. Reference Application
docs.text:
Create the full editor under:

web/apps/scriberig/

Initial files:

web/apps/scriberig/package.json
web/apps/scriberig/tsconfig.json
web/apps/scriberig/index.html
web/apps/scriberig/vite.config.ts
web/apps/scriberig/src/main.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/App.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/app-shell.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/routes.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/

The reference application uses React, Vite, and the MUI integration package.

The app must use only public Scriberig web packages for semantic behavior and server communication.

docs.title: 14. Required Reference Editor Views
docs.text:
Create view modules corresponding to the Level 1 conceptual surfaces:

web/apps/scriberig/src/views/RawKnowledgeView.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/SemanticView.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/ProjectionView.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/HistoryView.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/SessionAgentView.tsx
web/apps/scriberig/src/views/OperationsView.tsx

These are application composition views. Reusable widgets must remain in reusable packages.

The initial application shell may use a simple layout. Panel docking, persistence of layout, and sophisticated workspace UX are deferred.

docs.title: 15. Universal Selection
docs.text:
Define one reusable selection model in @scriberig/editor-core.

It must be able to represent:

entity
optional exact revision
snapshot
optional relation/path context
optional projection location

It should support both current-resolution selection and exact historical selection.

Views use this model to coordinate:

  • graph reveal;
  • semantic inspection;
  • projection highlighting;
  • history loading;
  • relation browsing;
  • agent scope;
  • migration highlighting.

The reference application owns which selection is active; packages own how that selection is interpreted.

docs.title: 16. Universal Commands
docs.text:
Define a command descriptor model in @scriberig/editor-core.

A command descriptor must be able to express at least:

  • stable command identifier;
  • human title;
  • applicability to a selection/capability context;
  • whether it is read-only or mutating;
  • invocation through a shared application operation;
  • optional keyboard/menu metadata;
  • optional domain extension metadata.

The UI may expose the same command through:

  • a palette;
  • a context menu;
  • a toolbar;
  • a button;
  • an agent-oriented action.

The command descriptor must not embed MUI components.

docs.title: 17. Events and Snapshot Synchronization
docs.text:
The transport client exposes the shared event stream.

The model consumes events and updates loaded state incrementally.

Minimum event handling behavior:

  • a snapshot-advanced event updates current snapshot identity;
  • unchanged cached revisions remain available;
  • changed loaded entities may be marked for resolution/refetch;
  • operation progress updates operation records;
  • branch/session events update relevant loaded models;
  • disconnect state is explicit;
  • reconnect may resume or re-establish subscriptions according to server capability.

The browser must never pretend that a historical snapshot has silently become current.

docs.title: 18. Drafts and Mutations
docs.text:
Browser-local drafts are not canonical knowledge.

Mutation flow:

UI intent
  -> public command/application operation
  -> migration proposal or domain operation
  -> validation
  -> resulting snapshot
  -> protocol event
  -> client model update

The reference application may show optimistic local state, but must keep candidate state distinguishable from accepted canonical state.

No package may implement direct database writes.

docs.title: 19. Projection Integration
docs.text:
Projection components receive semantic selection and snapshot context.

Where an adapter provides location mappings, projection views should support:

semantic selection -> projection location
projection location -> semantic selection

The initial package architecture must not hard-code source-code-only assumptions because Markdown, PDFs, sessions, and future domains use the same projection concept.

Domain-specific editors can be plugged into ProjectionHost through extension registration defined in a later design.

docs.title: 20. Domain UI Extensions
docs.text:
The initial extension contract should allow domains to contribute descriptors for:

  • semantic inspectors;
  • projection renderers/editors;
  • diff renderers;
  • relation views;
  • commands;
  • icons/labels;
  • validation presentation.

The concrete registry API may be finalized during Level 3 implementation of editor-core, but registration must happen through public web packages rather than direct imports into the app shell.

docs.title: 21. Testing Layers
docs.text:
Each package has tests at its own boundary.

Required categories:

protocol: serialization/type contract fixtures where applicable
client: transport and event-stream behavior with fake transport
model: snapshot/event/cache transitions
editor-core: pure interaction/controller behavior
react: provider and hook subscription behavior
components: accessible rendering and interaction contracts
components-mui: integration/smoke tests
app: end-to-end composition and public-boundary conformance

The reference application must include a conformance test that fails if application source imports private paths from reusable packages or server/database code.

docs.title: 22. Initial Tooling
docs.text:
Use:

  • pnpm workspaces;
  • TypeScript;
  • React for framework bindings and the reference app;
  • Vite for the reference browser application;
  • Material UI for the opinionated component package and reference app;
  • Vitest for package-level unit tests;
  • React Testing Library for React component/hook tests where appropriate.

Do not introduce a global client-state framework until @scriberig/model requirements demonstrate that one is necessary. The model should initially be implemented with explicit TypeScript state and subscription primitives.

Do not introduce Storybook, Electron/Tauri, code generation frameworks, or a browser E2E runner in the first web bootstrap unless a later design requires them.

docs.title: 23. Implementation Order
docs.text:
Implement in this order:

1. web workspace bootstrap
2. @scriberig/protocol
3. @scriberig/client
4. @scriberig/model
5. @scriberig/editor-core
6. @scriberig/react
7. @scriberig/components
8. @scriberig/components-mui
9. reference editor application
10. cross-package and conformance tests

Packages may initially be small, but each step must preserve the dependency direction.

Do not build the reference editor first and extract libraries afterward.

docs.title: 24. Completion Criteria
docs.text:
This Level 2 design is satisfied when:

  • the web/ workspace exists;
  • all seven public packages exist with the prescribed dependency direction;
  • the reference editor exists as a separate app;
  • no lower package depends on React unless it is a React/UI package;
  • no lower package depends on MUI;
  • protocol semantics are not independently reinvented in the browser;
  • one semantic selection can coordinate multiple application views;
  • commands are represented independently of visual controls;
  • snapshot and stale-state information are explicit;
  • web edits flow through public migrations/operations rather than database writes;
  • the editor exposes at least skeletal raw, semantic, projection, history, session/agent, and operation views;
  • the reference app communicates only through public web packages;
  • package tests and conformance checks enforce these boundaries.

docs.title: 25. Level 3 Work Items
docs.text:
Level 3 should split implementation into focused tasks:

  1. bootstrap the web workspace and reusable package scaffolds;
  2. implement the protocol package boundary;
  3. implement the framework-independent transport client;
  4. implement the client semantic model and incremental event handling;
  5. implement headless editor-core selection, tree, command, and navigation primitives;
  6. implement React providers and hooks;
  7. implement neutral reusable components;
  8. implement Material UI components;
  9. implement the reference integrated editor;
  10. add cross-package boundary and conformance tests.

Each Level 3 task must state exact files, prerequisites, required checks, and explicit non-goals so a focused implementation agent can execute it without redesigning the architecture.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns the architectural constraints in design/level-1/001. vision and principles.md into a concrete repository and package layout.

It defines boundaries and dependency direction. It does not define the internal data model, persistence schema, migration algorithms, protocol payloads, or domain-specific semantics. Those require later Level 1 and Level 2 decisions.

The layout must preserve these Level 1 requirements:

  • storage and domain libraries are useful without an agent runtime;
  • CLI, API, TUI, web, and agents are peer consumers of shared application capabilities;
  • the official web editor uses the same public libraries available to third parties;
  • domain adapters plug into shared storage, query, migration, and projection systems;
  • all write surfaces converge on one change model;
  • product capabilities can be developed vertically across interfaces;
  • lower layers never depend on higher product layers.

docs.title: 2. Repository Shape
docs.text:
Scriberig is a monorepo containing a Rust workspace and a TypeScript/web workspace.

The target top-level layout is:

/
├── Cargo.toml
├── rust-toolchain.toml
├── crates/
│   ├── scriberig-core/
│   ├── scriberig-store/
│   ├── scriberig-schema/
│   ├── scriberig-graph/
│   ├── scriberig-query/
│   ├── scriberig-migration/
│   ├── scriberig-projection/
│   ├── scriberig-session/
│   ├── scriberig-app/
│   ├── scriberig-protocol/
│   ├── scriberig-client/
│   ├── scriberig-agent-core/
│   ├── scriberig-agent-runtime/
│   ├── scriberig-server/
│   ├── scriberig-tui/
│   ├── scriberig-cli/
│   └── domains/
│       └── ... domain crates added by later designs
├── apps/
│   └── scriberig/
├── web/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── pnpm-workspace.yaml
│   ├── tsconfig.base.json
│   ├── packages/
│   │   ├── protocol/
│   │   ├── client/
│   │   ├── model/
│   │   ├── editor-core/
│   │   ├── react/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── components-mui/
│   │   └── agent-ui/
│   └── apps/
│       └── editor/
└── design/
    ├── level-1/
    ├── level-2/
    └── level-3/

The exact domain crates under crates/domains/ are intentionally deferred. A later domain design may add Markdown, Rust/code, PDF, or other adapters without changing the foundation layout.

docs.title: 3.1 Foundation
docs.text: These crates define the reusable knowledge platform.

docs.title: scriberig-core
docs.text:
Owns universal identifiers and small cross-cutting types that must not depend on storage, agents, transport, UI, or domain adapters.

It is the bottom of the dependency graph.

docs.title: scriberig-store
docs.text:
Defines persistence-facing abstractions for revisions, snapshots, and stored objects.

It depends on scriberig-core only at this stage.

A concrete storage backend must remain replaceable. Backend-specific persistence should not leak into higher layers.

docs.title: scriberig-schema
docs.text:
Defines the reusable schema/type vocabulary used by domains to describe structured knowledge.

It depends on scriberig-core.

docs.title: scriberig-graph
docs.text:
Defines the universal entity/relation graph view over stored knowledge.

It may depend on:

  • scriberig-core;
  • scriberig-store;
  • scriberig-schema.

It must not depend on agents, server code, CLI code, TUI code, or web-specific concepts.

docs.title: scriberig-query
docs.text:
Defines domain-independent query and traversal concepts over the graph.

It may depend on scriberig-core and scriberig-graph.

docs.title: scriberig-migration
docs.text:
Defines the common change boundary used by all mutation surfaces.

It may depend on the core graph/storage abstractions but not on product interfaces.

docs.title: scriberig-projection
docs.text:
Defines common projection concepts: render/import/reconcile boundaries and projection state abstractions.

It may depend on the graph and migration layers.

It must not contain Markdown-, Rust-, PDF-, or UI-specific implementations.

docs.title: scriberig-session
docs.text:
Defines sessions, branches, goals, tool interactions, and related structured session concepts as another domain over the universal system.

It must remain usable without an agent runtime.

docs.title: scriberig-app
docs.text:
This crate is the shared application-operation boundary.

The CLI, server, TUI, web server integration, and agent runtime must call application capabilities through this layer rather than reproduce business logic in their own surfaces.

Examples of future operations include inspecting semantic objects, querying, rendering, proposing changes, validating changes, branching, and committing. Their exact APIs are deferred.

scriberig-app may depend on the foundation crates and selected domain adapters. Foundation crates must never depend on it.

docs.title: scriberig-protocol
docs.text:
Owns stable serializable transport-facing data types used between remote clients and the server.

It must not contain server business logic.

It should depend on small stable identifier/value types, not on backend implementation details.

The exact schema-generation mechanism for TypeScript is deferred, but the Rust and TypeScript protocol packages must represent one wire contract rather than diverging manually.

docs.title: scriberig-client
docs.text:
Provides a reusable Rust client for a running Scriberig server.

It depends on scriberig-protocol, not on server internals.

docs.title: scriberig-server
docs.text:
Adapts remote requests onto scriberig-app operations and emits protocol responses/events.

The server is an adapter. It is not the owner of application semantics.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-core
docs.text:
Contains reusable agent-facing concepts such as tool descriptions, capability exposure, semantic navigation adapters, and context construction interfaces.

It consumes application/session capabilities. Nothing in the foundation may depend on it.

docs.title: scriberig-agent-runtime
docs.text:
Contains integrated agent execution/orchestration behavior and model-provider integration.

It depends on scriberig-agent-core and higher product-level capabilities.

Splitting agent concepts from runtime orchestration keeps the reusable knowledge platform independent from agent execution.

docs.title: scriberig-tui
docs.text:
Implements the terminal UI over shared application capabilities.

It must not own storage or mutation semantics.

docs.title: scriberig-cli
docs.text:
Defines command parsing and command dispatch for the Scriberig executable.

Commands may invoke local application operations, TUI mode, server mode, or agent runtime behavior. Core business logic belongs below this crate.

docs.title: apps/scriberig
docs.text:
Contains the final Rust executable named scriberig.

The executable is composition only. It wires together the CLI, application layer, server, TUI, and agent runtime. It should contain minimal logic of its own.

The same executable is expected to support the product modes selected by later designs, including command-style operation, server mode, TUI mode, and agent operation.

docs.title: 8. Domain Adapter Location
docs.text:
Domain-specific Rust crates belong under:

crates/domains/

A domain adapter may provide:

  • schemas;
  • parsers;
  • renderers;
  • reconcilers;
  • validators;
  • derived indexes;
  • specialized queries;
  • semantic operations.

A domain crate may depend on the shared foundation appropriate to its function. It may not introduce an alternative persistence, snapshot, migration, or agent-access architecture.

The first concrete domain directories must be introduced only by a design document that defines that domain sufficiently to implement it.

docs.title: 9. TypeScript and Web Workspace
docs.text:
The web workspace uses pnpm and lives entirely under web/.

Public packages use the @scriberig/ namespace.

docs.title: @scriberig/protocol
docs.text:
TypeScript representation of the wire contract exposed by scriberig-protocol.

It has no React or MUI dependency.

docs.title: @scriberig/client
docs.text:
Browser/Node client for the Scriberig server.

It depends on @scriberig/protocol.

docs.title: @scriberig/model
docs.text:
Client-side domain/application state: object caches, snapshot awareness, selections, navigation state, operation state, and other UI-independent client behavior.

It depends on the client/protocol layer and has no MUI dependency.

docs.title: @scriberig/editor-core
docs.text:
Headless reusable editor and browser controllers for semantic trees, selection, commands, diffs, history, and structured editing behavior.

It must not impose product styling.

docs.title: @scriberig/react
docs.text:
React bindings/hooks over the public model and client capabilities.

It must not require MUI.

docs.title: @scriberig/components
docs.text:
Reusable non-MUI Scriberig UI components or component primitives built on the public React/editor layers.

It must remain styleable by consumers.

docs.title: @scriberig/components-mui
docs.text:
Opinionated MUI implementation built on the reusable web layers.

MUI-specific dependencies must stop here or in the integrated editor application.

docs.title: @scriberig/agent-ui
docs.text: Reusable agent/session UI primitives built on the same model, selection, protocol, and operation concepts used by other web surfaces.

docs.title: web/apps/editor
docs.text:
The complete Scriberig browser editor.

It is a consumer of the public packages above. It must not import private server implementation code or bypass the public client/model abstractions.

The editor must eventually combine low-level and high-level views, including raw knowledge/revision browsing, semantic views, projection views, history/diffs, session branches, and agent commands scoped to semantic selections.

docs.title: 10. Required Dependency Direction
docs.text:
The conceptual Rust dependency direction is:

scriberig-core
    |
    +--> scriberig-store
    +--> scriberig-schema
              |
              v
         scriberig-graph
          /      |      \
         v       v       v
      query   migration  projection
         \       |       /
          \      |      /
           +-- session --+
                 |
                 v
            scriberig-app
              /      \
             v        v
        protocol     agent-core
           |             |
           v             v
        client       agent-runtime
           |
           +----> server

scriberig-app ---> tui
scriberig-app ---> cli/product composition

This diagram is directional, not exhaustive. The invariant is more important than exact edges:

reusable foundation -> application operations -> adapters/product surfaces

Never the reverse.

The web dependency direction is:

@scriberig/protocol
        |
        v
@scriberig/client
        |
        v
@scriberig/model
      /     \
     v       v
editor-core  react
     \       /
      \     /
      components
        |
        +--> components-mui
        +--> agent-ui
                 |
                 v
          integrated editor

No public package may depend on web/apps/editor.

docs.title: 12. Scaffold Rules
docs.text:
The initial scaffold must obey all of the following:

  • use Rust edition 2024;
  • keep package versions at 0.1.0 until release/versioning design exists;
  • use workspace dependency declarations where practical;
  • keep all newly created Rust crates compileable with cargo check --workspace;
  • keep source files minimal and documentation-oriented;
  • do not implement placeholder fake domain behavior;
  • do not add concrete database schemas;
  • do not define wire payloads beyond what is required for an empty package to compile;
  • do not create domain adapter crates yet;
  • do not create private APIs solely for the official editor;
  • do not add MUI dependencies outside components-mui or the integrated editor;
  • do not add agent dependencies to foundation crates.

docs.title: 13. Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
The scaffold is complete when:

  • the Rust workspace recognizes all prescribed Rust members;
  • cargo check --workspace succeeds;
  • every Rust package has a clear crate-level statement of its architectural role;
  • the Scriberig executable builds without containing substantive application behavior;
  • pnpm recognizes all prescribed web packages and the editor app;
  • TypeScript package boundaries match this document;
  • the public web packages do not import from the integrated editor app;
  • MUI is isolated to the MUI-specific package/editor boundary;
  • .gitignore covers generated artifacts for both workspaces;
  • no semantic implementation has been invented ahead of its design.

docs.title: 14. Level 3 Decomposition
docs.text:
The scaffold should be implemented by focused Level 3 tasks rather than one agent changing the whole repository at once:

  1. initialize the Rust workspace and foundation crates;
  2. scaffold Rust application, protocol, agent, and native surface crates;
  3. initialize the TypeScript/web workspace and headless/public packages;
  4. scaffold UI packages and the integrated editor shell.

Each Level 3 document must repeat the dependency constraints relevant to its task and include explicit acceptance checks.

docs.title: Change History and Merge Crate Design
Purpose
docs.text:
This document turns design/level-1/005. changes migrations branches and merge.md into a concrete Rust library boundary and file plan.

It depends on the persistence boundaries already defined in design/level-2/001. persistence crate boundaries.md.

This design does not change the Level 1 model. It chooses where the change model lives in code, which public concepts it exposes, and which implementation files must exist.

docs.title: Required crate
docs.text:
Create one backend-independent crate:

crates/sr-change/

Dependency direction:

sr-core
   ↑
sr-store
   ↑
sr-change

sr-change may depend on sr-core and the public storage interfaces from sr-store.

sr-change must not depend on:

  • SQLite;
  • a concrete storage backend;
  • agents;
  • sessions;
  • Markdown;
  • a programming-language adapter;
  • CLI, HTTP, TUI, or web UI code.

Domain adapters and product surfaces depend on sr-change, not the reverse.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
sr-change owns the domain-independent model and algorithms for:

  • migrations;
  • generic change operations;
  • provenance of changes;
  • explicit history topology;
  • branches and isolated workspaces;
  • optimistic promotion of named roots;
  • semantic snapshot diffs;
  • structured conflicts;
  • three-way merge;
  • semantic replay and rebase;
  • change-history and lineage queries;
  • progressively disclosed change summaries.

It does not own revision persistence, snapshot persistence, or named-root storage. Those remain storage capabilities supplied through sr-store.

docs.title: Migration model
docs.text:
A committed migration identifies one exact transition:

base SnapshotId
result SnapshotId

The migration must contain enough universal information to describe the exact changed set even when no domain adapter is installed.

The minimum universal entity delta is:

EntityDelta {
    entity: EntityId,
    before: Option<RevisionId>,
    after: Option<RevisionId>,
}

Interpretation:

  • None -> Some means creation or introduction into the relevant canonical state;
  • Some -> None means semantic removal from that state;
  • Some(old) -> Some(new) means the visible revision changed;
  • equal before and after values must not be stored as a change.

A migration may additionally record generic semantic operations and domain-specific semantic operation references.

docs.title: Generic operations
docs.text:
The initial generic operation vocabulary must support at least:

CreateEntity
ReplaceRevision
RemoveEntity
AddRelation
RemoveRelation
InsertCollectionMember
RemoveCollectionMember
MoveCollectionMember
ReplaceCollectionStructure

These operations describe intent where known. They do not replace the authoritative base/result snapshots and entity deltas.

Do not require every migration to contain a perfect semantic operation list. Exact before/after state remains sufficient for correctness.

docs.title: Domain-specific operations
docs.text:
sr-change must allow richer operations without knowing their domain schemas.

The generic crate should represent a domain operation as a typed reference or opaque domain payload with explicit domain/type identity.

Do not add Rust-specific, Markdown-specific, PDF-specific, or session-specific variants to the universal operation enum.

Domain adapters may provide interpretation and replay support through extension traits.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
A migration must support provenance describing where the change came from.

The universal source categories should cover at least:

User
ExternalProjection
Agent
Cli
Api
WebEditor
Tui
Importer
Refactoring
Merge
Synchronization
System
Other

The model must allow additional structured references such as:

  • actor or tool identity;
  • workspace or branch identity;
  • external projection identity;
  • parent migration identities;
  • validation-result references;
  • free-form or typed metadata owned by higher layers.

Provenance does not bypass validation or promotion rules.

docs.title: History topology
docs.text:
History is a DAG, not a list.

The crate must expose structures and queries that preserve:

  • base and result snapshot for each migration;
  • linear parentage where applicable;
  • multiple merge parents where applicable;
  • lookup of migrations that introduced a revision or touched an entity;
  • common-ancestor discovery through snapshot ancestry supplied by storage.

Physical write order and timestamps must never be used as the authoritative history topology.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
A branch is a named or semantic line of work whose current head is a snapshot.

The crate should model branch state independently from snapshot state.

At minimum, branch-facing code must be able to represent:

branch entity/reference
base snapshot
current snapshot
status
optional title
optional purpose
optional short description
optional outcome
optional resulting migration

The stable semantic representation of branch metadata may later live in the universal graph, but sr-change owns the branch/workspace operations that use snapshots and named roots.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is an isolated branch used for speculative work.

It must always have an exact base snapshot and a current snapshot.

Failed validation or abandoned work must not modify the base snapshot or target named root.

Workspace APIs must make it possible to:

  • create from a base snapshot;
  • advance through descendant snapshots;
  • inspect base/current state;
  • abandon without promotion;
  • promote or merge completed work later.

docs.title: Promotion
docs.text:
Promotion advances a named root from an expected snapshot to a result snapshot.

The operation must use optimistic concurrency.

Conceptually:

promote(root, expected = S1, result = S2)

If the current root no longer resolves to S1, promotion must fail with a conflict result containing the actual current snapshot.

It must never silently overwrite concurrent work.

The storage backend performs the atomic compare-and-promote. sr-change provides the higher-level operation and error semantics.

docs.title: Semantic diff
docs.text:
A diff compares any two snapshots. It does not require direct ancestry.

The universal diff must report at least:

  • entities introduced;
  • entities removed from the compared state;
  • entities whose revision changed.

Where canonical relation/collection information is available through generic graph interfaces, the diff may additionally expose relation and collection changes.

Domain adapters may enrich the same diff with domain meaning.

The diff API must not imply that every entity changed merely because the global SnapshotId changed.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text:
The universal merge entry point is three-way:

base
left
right

The engine first compares entity-resolution changes against the base.

Rules:

  1. Changes made by only one side are adopted.
  2. Equal resulting revisions on both sides converge without conflict.
  3. Independent entities merge without conflict.
  4. Same-entity changes are passed to progressively deeper merge logic.
  5. The generic engine may resolve generic relation/collection changes when intent is unambiguous.
  6. Domain-specific strategies may resolve conflicts more deeply.
  7. Ambiguity must remain a structured conflict; the engine must not choose silently.

Merge creates a new result state. It never mutates base, left, or right.

docs.title: Structured conflicts
docs.text:
The universal conflict model must carry enough information to inspect the disagreement without rendering textual conflict markers.

At minimum:

Conflict {
    entity: EntityId,
    base: Option<RevisionId>,
    left: Option<RevisionId>,
    right: Option<RevisionId>,
    kind: ConflictKind,
}

Initial conflict kinds should distinguish at least:

BothModified
DeleteModify
CompetingCreate
RelationConflict
CollectionConflict
DomainConflict

Conflicts may carry a minimal affected field/relation/collection path and domain-specific detail.

A merge result may contain resolved deltas plus unresolved conflicts. Promotion policy decides whether unresolved results may become current; the default project workflow should require resolution first.

docs.title: Rebase and replay
docs.text:
Rebase creates new history from an existing line of work and a new base.

It must never rewrite retained historical snapshots or migrations.

Replay should prefer recorded semantic operations when they are available and still valid.

If only exact state deltas are available, the rebase engine may use generic replay rules or surface a conflict rather than inventing intent.

Domain-specific replay must be supplied through extension traits.

docs.title: Change queries
docs.text:
The crate must expose a service layer capable of answering Level 1 queries such as:

what changed between snapshots A and B?
what migration introduced revision R?
what is the history of entity E?
which migrations touched entity E?
what branches descend from snapshot S?
what is the common ancestor of A and B?
what conflicts prevent merging A and B?

Queries must use explicit history and storage ancestry, never physical insertion order.

docs.title: Summaries and progressive disclosure
docs.text:
Migration, diff, branch, and merge-result objects must support compact inspection before full detail.

The crate should expose deterministic structural summaries such as:

changed entity count
created entity count
removed entity count
conflict count
base/result snapshots
source category
validation status reference count

Human-authored or model-generated descriptions belong to higher layers but can reference these objects.

docs.title: Public extension traits
docs.text:
The crate should provide narrow extension points for domain adapters.

At minimum, design for traits equivalent in responsibility to:

DomainDiffInterpreter
DomainMergeStrategy
DomainReplayStrategy

Exact trait names and method signatures may be adjusted during implementation, but the dependency direction is mandatory: sr-change defines extension points; domain crates implement them.

docs.title: Prescribed files
docs.text:
The implementation of this Level 2 design must create at least:

crates/sr-change/Cargo.toml
crates/sr-change/src/lib.rs
crates/sr-change/src/migration.rs
crates/sr-change/src/operation.rs
crates/sr-change/src/provenance.rs
crates/sr-change/src/history.rs
crates/sr-change/src/branch.rs
crates/sr-change/src/workspace.rs
crates/sr-change/src/promotion.rs
crates/sr-change/src/diff.rs
crates/sr-change/src/conflict.rs
crates/sr-change/src/merge.rs
crates/sr-change/src/rebase.rs
crates/sr-change/src/query.rs
crates/sr-change/src/summary.rs
crates/sr-change/tests/change_conformance.rs

The workspace Cargo.toml must include crates/sr-change once the crate is implemented.

docs.title: Required dependency behavior
docs.text:
The crate should rely on public storage capabilities for:

  • resolving an entity in a snapshot;
  • enumerating changes between snapshot mappings efficiently where available;
  • snapshot ancestry traversal;
  • constructing a descendant snapshot from entity-resolution changes;
  • named-root compare-and-promote.

If a required storage capability is not yet present in sr-store, the implementation must extend the backend-independent sr-store trait first and add conformance coverage for both memory and SQLite backends. It must not reach around sr-store into a backend implementation.

docs.title: Testing strategy
docs.text:
The conformance suite must cover at least:

  • direct migration with one revision replacement;
  • create and remove entity deltas;
  • branch creation without copying state;
  • failed optimistic promotion when the expected root is stale;
  • diff of unrelated sibling snapshots;
  • automatic merge of disjoint changes;
  • automatic convergence when both sides produce the same revision;
  • structured conflict for competing same-entity edits;
  • delete/modify conflict;
  • rebase that creates new history while preserving the original line;
  • history query using explicit topology rather than insertion order;
  • cross-domain migration represented only through universal entity deltas;
  • no semantic migration for representation-only changes.

Tests should use the in-memory store whenever possible. Durable backend behavior belongs to shared store conformance tests rather than being duplicated here.

docs.title: Completion criteria
docs.text:
This design is satisfied when:

  • sr-change builds without a concrete backend dependency;
  • all prescribed modules exist with focused responsibilities;
  • migrations preserve exact base/result snapshots and universal entity deltas;
  • branches and workspaces operate on snapshot references rather than copied state;
  • named-root promotion uses optimistic concurrency;
  • diff works between arbitrary snapshots;
  • disjoint three-way changes merge automatically;
  • unresolved ambiguity is represented as structured conflicts;
  • rebase produces new history;
  • generic history remains useful without any domain adapter;
  • the conformance suite passes against the in-memory persistence backend.

docs.title: Repository Scaffold, Conventions, and Native Command Surface
1. Purpose
docs.text:
This document reconciles the implemented repository scaffold with the Level 1 architecture and the earlier Level 2 package designs. It records repository-wide implementation conventions that apply across Rust, TypeScript, tooling, tests, and product composition.

It complements:

  1. design/level-2/011. application operations protocol and runtime boundaries.md;
  2. design/level-2/017. web workspace packages and integrated editor.md;
  3. design/level-2/018. workspace and package layout.md.

The controlling rule is:

The scaffold defines dependency and ownership boundaries, not proof that runtime behavior exists.

A crate, package, command, view, or application may exist as a documented stub while its semantic implementation remains pending in a focused Level 3 task.

docs.title: 2. Native Product Identity
docs.text:
The native product composition root remains:

apps/scriberig/

Its Cargo package name remains:

scriberig

The executable produced by that package is named:

srig

Package identity and executable spelling are intentionally distinct. Documentation, examples, shell commands, installers, and help output must use srig when referring to the executable.

apps/scriberig remains composition-only. Reusable command parsing belongs in scriberig-cli; runtime behavior belongs in the server, TUI, agent runtime, application, storage, and domain crates that own it.

docs.title: 3. Native Command Surface
docs.text:
The stable top-level command names are:

srig tui
srig serve
srig run <PROMPT>
srig agent <PROMPT>
srig maintenance

The executable must also provide conventional:

srig --help
srig --version

The initial serve command accepts endpoint-selection arguments equivalent to:

--host <HOST>
--port <PORT>

These commands may initially be stubs. A stub must:

  • parse successfully;
  • appear in generated help;
  • reject malformed arguments through the CLI parser;
  • state clearly that its runtime behavior is not implemented;
  • avoid direct persistence, server, TUI, or agent behavior in the CLI crate.

Later tasks replace individual stubs by delegating to the owning runtime APIs without changing the top-level command grammar unnecessarily.

docs.title: 4. Implemented Rust Scaffold
docs.text:
The current Rust workspace is organized around these reusable and product-facing boundaries:

crates/
├── scriberig-core/
├── scriberig-store/
├── scriberig-store-memory/
├── scriberig-store-sqlite/
├── scriberig-schema/
├── scriberig-graph/
├── scriberig-query/
├── scriberig-migration/
├── scriberig-derive/
├── scriberig-projection/
├── scriberig-session/
├── scriberig-app/
├── scriberig-protocol/
├── scriberig-client/
├── scriberig-agent-core/
├── scriberig-agent-runtime/
├── scriberig-server/
├── scriberig-tui/
├── scriberig-cli/
└── domains/
    ├── scriberig-domain-markdown/
    ├── scriberig-domain-code/
    ├── scriberig-domain-rust/
    └── scriberig-domain-pdf/

apps/
└── scriberig/

The existence of these crates establishes ownership and dependency boundaries only. Empty or documentation-only lib.rs files must not be interpreted as implemented semantic behavior.

docs.title: 5. Implemented Web Scaffold
docs.text:
The current web workspace is rooted at web/ and uses pnpm.

Reusable packages are:

@scriberig/protocol
@scriberig/client
@scriberig/model
@scriberig/editor-core
@scriberig/react
@scriberig/components
@scriberig/components-mui
@scriberig/agent-ui

The integrated reference browser application is:

web/apps/scriberig/

with private package identity:

@scriberig/app

agent-ui is a first-class reusable package. It must use the same protocol/model/editor abstractions as the rest of the web platform and must not become a product-only shortcut into agent or server internals.

The integrated application consumes public packages. Reusable packages must never depend on web/apps/scriberig.

docs.title: 6. Repository Guidance Files
docs.text:
Important architectural directories contain AGENTS.md files.

An AGENTS.md file explains:

  • the purpose of its directory;
  • ownership boundaries;
  • allowed dependency directions;
  • relationships with sibling/lower/higher layers;
  • local exceptions or refinements to repository-wide implementation rules.

Agents must read the repository root AGENTS.md and the nearest applicable nested AGENTS.md before editing a subsystem.

A nested file may refine a repository rule but must not silently reverse architectural invariants defined by Level 1 or Level 2 design.

docs.title: 7. Source File Size
docs.text:
Source-code files are limited to 400 lines after excluding the leading preamble.

The preamble may contain:

  • file/module documentation;
  • license headers;
  • attributes/directives;
  • imports and Rust use declarations.

Markdown and other prose/text files are exempt.

When a source file grows beyond the limit, split by responsibility rather than compressing unrelated logic. A preferred strategy is to replace an oversized file by a directory with the same stem and focused child modules while preserving the public re-export boundary.

docs.title: 8. Documentation and Logical Blocks
docs.text:
Every source file has a file-level description.

Every public or private function and method has documentation containing:

  • a one-line brief description;
  • optional extended explanation;
  • parameter documentation;
  • return-value documentation when meaningful;
  • thrown/returned error documentation when applicable.

Class-like constructs document their purpose and members. Class documentation separates public and private members where the language supports that distinction.

Each logical code block has a one- or two-line plain intent comment. For a documented declaration, place the comment after its documentation. In Rust, put the intent comment immediately after the /// lines without a blank line, so Clippy does not report empty_line_after_doc_comments. Do not add a special prefix to explanatory comments.

These rules apply to implementation work, not only public APIs.

docs.title: 9. Formatting Policy
docs.text:
Formatting policy is intentionally language-specific:

TypeScript / JavaScript: 2 spaces
Rust:                    4 spaces

Prettier is authoritative for supported web source files. rustfmt is authoritative for Rust formatting.

CI verifies formatting without modifying the tree.

Pre-commit automation may modify staged files when the modification is deterministic and safe.

docs.title: 10. Repository Lint and Auto-Fix
docs.text:
Repository-specific conventions are enforced by tools/lint_repo.py and its tools/repo_lint/ implementation package.

The linter should prefer deterministic safe fixes when possible. Rules that require semantic judgment may reject a file with a precise diagnostic rather than applying a risky rewrite.

The linter itself follows the same source-size and documentation rules. If it grows, split it into focused modules rather than exempting it merely because it is tooling.

tools/fix.sh is the repository-wide safe-fix entry point. tools/check.sh is the non-mutating verification entry point.

docs.title: 11. Pre-Commit Behavior
docs.text:
The repository uses pre-commit hooks to prevent malformed source files from entering Git history.

The intended separation is:

pre-commit: fix safe deterministic issues, then verify
CI:         verify only

For staged TypeScript/JavaScript files, the pre-commit formatter runs Prettier with --write and re-stages the exact files it formatted. This lets a normal add-and-commit operation succeed with formatter corrections included in the same commit attempt.

Hooks must not silently stage unrelated files.

Developers and agents must not bypass the hook to land known malformed source.

docs.title: 12. Tests and Cross-Surface Verification
docs.text:
Repository-level test structure includes dedicated locations for:

tests/conformance/
tests/protocol/
tests/end-to-end/
tests/fixtures/

These directories provide shared homes for tests that do not belong exclusively to one crate/package.

The presence of these directories is scaffolding. Concrete conformance behavior is completed only when the corresponding Level 3 test task and its assertions exist.

docs.title: 13. Scaffold Task Status Rules
docs.text:
Level 3 task bookkeeping must distinguish these states:

  • Complete: every completion criterion that remains applicable is implemented and verified.
  • Partial: structural work exists, but one or more applicable completion checks remain outstanding.
  • Superseded: a later task/design replaced the instructions before completion; the old task remains for history but is no longer implementation authority.
  • Pending: implementation has not materially started.

A task must not be marked Complete merely because its directories exist.

When a later design intentionally changes a path, package name, executable name, framework choice, or dependency boundary, reconciliation should mark the older conflicting task Superseded rather than forcing the repository backward to satisfy obsolete instructions.

docs.title: 14. Renumbering References
docs.text:
Level 2 and Level 3 filename prefixes are unique identifiers in the current design tree, but earlier documents were authored before the numbering was normalized.

All new or edited design references must use the current filename.

Important current mappings include:

design/level-2/017. web workspace packages and integrated editor.md
design/level-2/018. workspace and package layout.md
design/level-3/028. initialize rust foundation workspace.md
design/level-3/048. initialize web workspace and headless packages.md
design/level-3/088. scaffold runtime application and product crates.md

When touching an older task, repair stale numbered references in that task as part of the change.

docs.title: 15. Reconciliation Principle
docs.text:
The repository tree, Level 1 invariants, and the newest non-superseded Level 2 design together determine the intended scaffold.

Reconciliation must not mark semantic work complete simply because a placeholder file exists.

Conversely, once a later decision is explicit—such as the srig executable name, the web/apps/scriberig application path, the reusable agent-ui package, or repository-wide quality automation—older scaffold instructions should be updated or marked superseded instead of remaining as contradictory implementation guidance.

docs.title: Implement: Bootstrap Persistence Workspace and Core IDs
Objective
docs.text:
